paragraphs: This paper constructs a class of associative memories by starting with the properties the memories should have. An associative memory retrieves stored information through its relationship to an input. The design therefore concerns both how much information can be stored and how the system moves toward a remembered item during retrieval.

The desired properties are high capacity, controllable basins of attraction, and fast convergence. A basin of attraction is the collection of starting states that lead to the same recalled state. Controlling these basins concerns which inputs retrieve which memories, while convergence speed concerns how quickly that retrieval settles. These are distinct aspects of a memory's behavior.

The resulting construction can be implemented as an artificial neural network. The significance is the direction of the design process: the authors begin with requirements for storage and retrieval, then arrive at a neural realization. This links the network's intended function to its construction, bringing capacity, the organization of recall, and retrieval speed into a single memory-design problem.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs neural associative memories from desired requirements for capacity, controllable recall basins, and convergence speed.

title: HIGH DENSITY ASSOCIATIVE MEMORIES

paragraphs: This paper proposes a parallel architecture for image compression with the goal of achieving substantial data reduction while maintaining reconstructed image quality. It frames the task as requiring two things together: a useful model of images and an efficient representation of the particular information contained in each image being compressed.

The architecture combines a Markov image model with interactions among many filter banks. The image model supplies a mathematical basis for representing image structure, while the interacting filters form part of the proposed data representation. Bringing these elements into one coherent architecture is the paper's approach to connecting assumptions about images with the machinery used to encode them.

The design draws inspiration from physiological knowledge of multiple channels in human vision and the interactions between those channels. Its emphasis is therefore on coordinated processing across filters, with parallel organization built into the proposal. The contribution described is an architecture aimed at balancing compression and reconstruction quality through an image model and interacting representations.
summary.tldr: A proposed image-compression architecture combines a Markov image model with parallel, interacting filter banks inspired by human vision.

title: Model Based Image Compression and Adaptive Data Representation by Interacting Filter Banks

abstract: We present a methodological framework enabling a detailed de(cid:173) scription of the performance of Hopfield-like attractor neural net(cid:173) works (ANN) in the first two iterations. Using the Bayesian ap(cid:173) proach, we find that performance is improved when a history-based term is included in the neuron's dynamics. A further enhancement of the network's performance is achieved by judiciously choosing the censored neurons (those which become active in a given itera(cid:173) tion) on the basis of the magnitude of their post-synaptic poten(cid:173) tials. The contribution of biologically plausible, censored, history(cid:173) dependent dynamics is especially marked in conditions of low firing activity and sparse connectivity, two important characteristics of the mammalian cortex. In such networks, the performance at(cid:173) tained is higher than the performance of two 'independent' iter(cid:173) ations, which represents an upper bound on the performance of history-independent networks.

paragraphs: The paper examines how the recent history of neural activity can improve Hopfield-like attractor networks. It develops a framework for describing performance over the first two iterations. This short-time analysis lets the authors investigate how information from an earlier update should affect the next one.

Using a Bayesian approach, they find that adding a history-dependent term to neuron dynamics improves performance. A further improvement comes from selecting which neurons become active according to the magnitude of their postsynaptic potentials. The method therefore changes both how a neuron uses past information and which neurons participate in a particular iteration.

The benefits are especially strong when firing activity is low and connectivity is sparse, conditions the abstract relates to mammalian cortex. In these networks, performance exceeds that of two independent iterations, which the analysis treats as an upper bound for history-independent networks. The result makes history an active computational resource: successive updates can achieve more when their dynamics exploit the relationship between them.
summary.tldr: History-dependent updates and selective neuron activation improve attractor-network performance, especially with sparse connections and low firing activity.

title: History-Dependent Attractor Neural Networks

abstract: This paper presents a neural network able to control saccadic movements. The input to the network is a specification of a stimulation site on the collicular motor map. The output is the time course of the eye position in the orbit (horizontal and vertical angles). The units in the network exhibit a one-to-one correspondance with neurons in the intermediate layer of the superior colliculus (collicular motor map), in the brainstem and with oculomotor neurons. Simulations carried out with this network demonstrate its ability to reproduce in a straightforward fashion many experimental observations.

The units in the network exhibit a one-to-one correspondance with neurons in the intermediate layer of the superior colliculus (collicular motor map), in the brainstem and with oculomotor neurons. Simulations carried out with this network demonstrate its ability to reproduce in a straightforward fashion many experimental observations.

paragraphs: The paper presents a recurrent neural network for controlling saccades, the rapid movements that change eye position. The task is to connect a command expressed at a neural motor map to an unfolding physical movement. This makes the model an account of movement generation over time, including both horizontal and vertical components.

The network receives the location of a stimulation site on the collicular motor map. It produces the eye's position in the orbit as a time course of two angles. Its units have a one-to-one correspondence with neurons in the intermediate superior colliculus, the brainstem, and the oculomotor system, giving the network an explicit relationship to the biological structures involved.

Simulations demonstrate that the model can reproduce many experimental observations. The stated finding supports the usefulness of this network organization as a model of saccade control. Its contribution is to connect an anatomically specified input, corresponding neural processing units, and a complete movement trajectory within a single computational system.
summary.tldr: A recurrent network with biologically corresponding units converts collicular stimulation locations into simulated eye-movement trajectories.

title: A Recurrent Neural Network for Generation of Occular Saccades

abstract: Existing recurrent net learning algorithms are inadequate. We in(cid:173) troduce the conceptual framework of viewing recurrent training as matching vector fields of dynamical systems in phase space. Phase(cid:173) space reconstruction techniques make the hidden states explicit, reducing temporal learning to a feed-forward problem. In short, we propose viewing iterated prediction [LF88] as the best way of training recurrent networks on deterministic signals. Using this framework, we can train multiple trajectories, insure their stabil(cid:173) ity, and design arbitrary dynamical systems.

In short, we propose viewing iterated prediction [LF88] as the best way of training recurrent networks on deterministic signals. Using this framework, we can train multiple trajectories, insure their stabil(cid:173) ity, and design arbitrary dynamical systems.

paragraphs: The paper reframes recurrent network training as learning the dynamics of a system in phase space. A point in this space represents a system state, and a vector field describes how that state changes. Under this view, training seeks a match between the network’s dynamics and those of the process being modeled.

The authors use phase-space reconstruction to make hidden states explicit. With those states available, temporal learning becomes a feedforward prediction problem: learn how an explicit state evolves, then repeatedly apply the learned prediction. They advocate this iterated-prediction approach for deterministic signals, which is the stated setting for their training proposal.

The framework is presented as supporting several related goals: learning multiple trajectories, ensuring their stability, and designing dynamical systems. These goals concern the behavior produced by repeated prediction, not just isolated outputs. The contribution is therefore a way to organize recurrent learning around state-space structure, making trajectories and stability direct objects of training and design.
summary.tldr: Phase-space reconstruction turns learning deterministic recurrent dynamics into explicit-state prediction, supporting trajectory learning and stability.

title: Phase-Space Learning

abstract: When a sensory system constructs a model of the environment from its input, it might need to verify the model's accuracy. One method of verification is multivariate time-series prediction: a good model could predict the near-future activity of its inputs, much as a good scientific theory predicts future data. Such a predict(cid:173) ing model would require copious top-down connections to compare the predictions with the input. That feedback could improve the model's performance in two ways: by biasing internal activity to(cid:173) ward expected patterns, and by generating specific error signals if the predictions fail. A proof-of-concept model-an event-driven, computationally efficient layered network, incorporating "cortical" features like all-excitatory synapses and local inhibition- was con(cid:173) structed to make near-future predictions of a simple, moving stim(cid:173) ulus. After unsupervised learning, the network contained units not only tuned to obvious features of the stimulus like contour orienta(cid:173) tion and motion, but also to contour discontinuity ("end-stopping") and illusory contours.

paragraphs: This paper explores prediction as a way for a sensory system to check its model of the environment. If the model captures useful structure, it should anticipate near-future input activity. Top-down connections allow those expectations to be compared with incoming signals, potentially biasing activity toward expected patterns and generating specific errors when predictions fail.

The author constructs a proof-of-concept layered network that predicts a simple moving stimulus. The model is event-driven and designed for computational efficiency. It also incorporates cortical-inspired features, including all-excitatory synapses and local inhibition, to investigate prediction within a particular kind of neural architecture.

After unsupervised learning, units respond to contour orientation and motion, as well as contour discontinuities and illusory contours. The significance is that learning to predict input produces sensitivity to several visual features, including ones beyond obvious stimulus properties. The demonstration links a temporal prediction task to the development of visual representations in the model, with the simple moving stimulus defining the reported setting.
summary.tldr: A network trained without supervision to predict a moving stimulus develops units sensitive to motion, contours, and illusory contours.

title: Unsupervised Pixel-prediction

abstract: Time series prediction is one of the major applications of neural net(cid:173) works. After a short introduction into the basic theoretical foundations we argue that the iterated prediction of a dynamical system may be in(cid:173) terpreted as a model of the system dynamics. By means of RBF neural networks we describe a modeling approach and extend it to be able to model instationary systems. As a practical test for the capabilities of the method we investigate the modeling of musical and speech signals and demonstrate that the model may be used for synthesis of musical and speech signals.

paragraphs: Predicting a time series and modeling the process that generates it are closely related tasks. This paper argues that repeatedly applying a predictor can be interpreted as a model of a dynamical system. Once predictions are iterated, the model describes how a signal develops over time rather than supplying only an isolated forecast.

The authors build their modeling approach with radial basis function neural networks. They then extend it to handle nonstationary systems, whose behavior changes over time. That extension is important to the stated goal because a model of changing dynamics must accommodate more than a single unchanging pattern of signal evolution.

Musical and speech signals provide practical tests of the approach. The paper demonstrates that the resulting model can synthesize both types of signal. This links the prediction viewpoint to generation: a learned account of temporal evolution can be used to produce a continuing signal. The reported contribution is therefore a modeling method whose usefulness extends from forecasting to audio synthesis.
summary.tldr: Iterated radial basis function predictions model changing signal dynamics and enable synthesis of speech and music.

title: Neural Network Modeling of Speech and Music Signals

abstract: We discuss the development of a Multi-Layer Perceptron neural network classifier for use in preoperative differentiation between benign and malignant ovarian tumors. As the Mean Squared classification Error is not sufficient to make correct and objective assessments about the performance of the neural classifier, the concepts of sensitivity and specificity are introduced and combined in Receiver Operating Characteristic curves. Based on objective observations such as sonomorphologic criteria, color Doppler imaging and results from serum tumor markers, the neural network is able to make reliable predictions with a discriminating performance comparable to that of experienced gynecologists.

paragraphs: This paper develops a multilayer perceptron to help distinguish benign from malignant ovarian tumors before surgery. The classifier uses objective observations, including ultrasound morphology, color Doppler imaging, and serum tumor markers. Its purpose is to combine these measurements into a prediction relevant to preoperative assessment.

The authors emphasize that mean squared classification error does not adequately characterize performance for this task. They instead examine sensitivity and specificity, which describe detection of malignant cases and correct recognition of benign cases. Receiver operating characteristic curves combine these considerations, showing how the balance changes as the decision threshold varies.

The network is reported to make reliable predictions with discrimination comparable to that of experienced gynecologists. This concerns its ability to distinguish the two tumor categories. The paper's contribution includes both the classifier and the choice of evaluation framework: assessing a diagnostic model requires examining the types of decisions it makes, rather than relying only on a single averaged numerical error. The measurements and evaluation are tied to the preoperative classification problem.
summary.tldr: A neural classifier combines preoperative tumor measurements and achieves discrimination reported as comparable to experienced gynecologists.

title: Use of a Multi-Layer Perceptron to Predict Malignancy in Ovarian Tumors

abstract: This paper describes a Bayesian graph matching algorithm for data-mining from large structural data-bases. The matching algorithm uses edge-consistency and node attribute similarity to determine the a posteriori probability of a query graph for each of the candidate matches in the data-base. The node feature-vectors are constructed by computing normalised histograms of pairwise geometric attributes. Attribute similarity is assessed by computing the Bhattacharyya distance between the histograms. Recognition is realised by selecting the candidate from the data-base which has the largest a posteriori probability. We illustrate the recognition technique on a data-base containing 2500 line patterns extracted from real-world imagery. Here the recognition technique is shown to significantly outperform a number of algorithm alternatives.

paragraphs: The paper presents a Bayesian method for retrieving shapes represented as graphs from a large structural database. Matching considers both whether graph edges are consistent and whether node attributes are similar. These two kinds of evidence contribute to a posterior probability for each candidate match, combining structural agreement with agreement in geometric description.

Node features are built from normalized histograms of pairwise geometric attributes. The method compares these histograms using Bhattacharyya distance, providing a measure of similarity between their distributions. Recognition then selects the database candidate with the highest posterior probability. This connects the feature comparison and graph structure to one probabilistic decision rule.

The authors demonstrate the method on a database of 2,500 line patterns extracted from real-world imagery. In that setting, it significantly outperforms several alternative algorithms. The result supports the usefulness of combining edge consistency with histogram-based node similarity for the reported recognition task. The contribution includes both a concrete geometric representation and a Bayesian way to use that representation when ranking candidate graph matches.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian graph matcher combines edge consistency and geometric histogram similarity, outperforming alternatives on a database of 2,500 line patterns.

title: Graph Matching for Shape Retrieval

abstract: Classifier systems are now viewed disappointing because of their prob(cid:173) lems such as the rule strength vs rule set performance problem and the credit assignment problem. In order to solve the problems, we have de(cid:173) veloped a hybrid classifier system: GLS (Generalization Learning Sys(cid:173) tem). In designing GLS, we view CSs as model free learning in POMDPs and take a hybrid approach to finding the best generalization, given the total number of rules. GLS uses the policy improvement procedure by Jaakkola et al. for an locally optimal stochastic policy when a set of rule conditions is given. GLS uses GA to search for the best set of rule conditions.

In order to solve the problems, we have de(cid:173) veloped a hybrid classifier system: GLS (Generalization Learning Sys(cid:173) tem). In designing GLS, we view CSs as model free learning in POMDPs and take a hybrid approach to finding the best generalization, given the total number of rules. GLS uses the policy improvement procedure by Jaakkola et al. for an locally optimal stochastic policy when a set of rule conditions is given. GLS uses GA to search for the best set of rule conditions.

paragraphs: This paper presents the Generalization Learning System, a hybrid classifier system designed to address credit assignment and the mismatch between individual rule strength and overall rule-set performance. The authors frame classifier systems as model-free learning in partially observable Markov decision processes. This places rule selection and rule-set behavior within a policy-learning perspective.

The system divides its search between choosing rule conditions and improving behavior under those conditions. Given a fixed set of rule conditions, it uses a policy-improvement procedure aimed at a locally optimal stochastic policy. A genetic algorithm searches for the set of rule conditions, with the total number of rules held fixed.

This division gives the two searches different responsibilities: one improves the policy for an existing description of situations, while the other changes that description to seek better generalization. The design aims to address the identified classifier-system problems through this combination. Its stated local policy objective should be distinguished from the broader search for the best rule conditions; the abstract does not assert a global optimum for the combined system.
summary.tldr: GLS combines local stochastic-policy improvement with genetic search over rule conditions in a model-free POMDP framework.

title: Viewing Classifier Systems as Model Free Learning in POMDPs

paragraphs: Maximum-margin classification can generalize well, but solving the associated optimization problem may be more expensive than simple online updates. ALMAp seeks an approximate large-margin separator through an incremental algorithm. The setting is linearly separable data with a margin measured under a chosen p-norm.

The analysis bounds the number of corrections needed to reach a margin close to the best achievable one. The method avoids quadratic or higher-order programming and is straightforward to implement. This places it computationally closer to a perceptron while explicitly pursuing the geometric margin that motivates support vector machines.

Experiments outperform the compared perceptron and ROMMA methods. Accuracy is slightly below the tested SVMs, but training is faster and simpler. The contribution is therefore a practical tradeoff: much of the benefit of large-margin learning can be obtained through lightweight incremental updates when exact optimization is not worth its additional cost.
summary.tldr: ALMAp approximates maximum-margin classification with simple incremental updates, trading a little SVM accuracy for speed and simplicity.

title: A New Approximate Maximal Margin Classification Algorithm

abstract: The choice of an SVM kernel corresponds to the choice of a rep(cid:173) resentation of the data in a feature space and, to improve per(cid:173) formance, it should therefore incorporate prior knowledge such as known transformation invariances. We propose a technique which extends earlier work and aims at incorporating invariances in non(cid:173) linear kernels. We show on a digit recognition task that the pro(cid:173) posed approach is superior to the Virtual Support Vector method, which previously had been the method of choice.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a support vector machine can use prior knowledge about transformations that should preserve a classification. Such knowledge is called invariance: an input may change in a known way while retaining the identity relevant to the task. Incorporating that knowledge can inform the representation used for learning.

An SVM's kernel determines how data are represented in a feature space. The authors therefore focus on putting invariance information into nonlinear kernels. Their technique extends earlier work and aims to make the chosen representation reflect known transformation relationships, connecting task knowledge directly to the kernel design.

The method is evaluated on digit recognition and outperforms the Virtual Support Vector method in that task. The comparison supports the proposed treatment of invariance in the reported setting. The contribution is both a technique for nonlinear kernels and evidence that this use of prior knowledge can improve recognition relative to the comparison method, without establishing superiority for every task or transformation.
summary.tldr: A technique for incorporating transformation invariances into nonlinear SVM kernels outperforms Virtual Support Vectors on a digit recognition task.

title: Incorporating Invariances in Non-Linear Support Vector Machines

abstract: Drawing on the correspondence between the graph Laplacian, the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a manifold , and the connections to the heat equation , we propose a geometrically motivated algorithm for constructing a representation for data sampled from a low di(cid:173) mensional manifold embedded in a higher dimensional space. The algorithm provides a computationally efficient approach to non(cid:173) linear dimensionality reduction that has locality preserving prop(cid:173) erties and a natural connection to clustering. Several applications are considered. In many areas of artificial intelligence, information retrieval and data mining, one is often confronted with intrinsically low dimensional data lying in a very high di(cid:173) mensional space. For example, gray scale n x n images of a fixed object taken with a moving camera yield data points in rn: n2 . However , the intrinsic dimensionality of the space of all images of t he same object is the number of degrees of freedom of the camera - in fact the space has the natural structure of a manifold embedded in rn: n2 . While there is a large body of work on dimensionality reduction in general, most existing approaches do not explicitly take into account the structure of the manifold on which the data may possibly reside. Recently, there has been some interest (Tenenbaum et aI, 2000 ; Roweis and Saul, 2000) in the problem of devel(cid:173) oping low dimensional representations of data in this particular context. In this paper , we present a new algorithm and an accompanying framework of analysis for geometrically motivated dimensionality reduction. The core algorithm is very simple, has a few local computations and one sparse eigenvalue problem. The solution reflects th e intrinsic geom etric structure of the manifold. The justification comes from the role of the Laplacian operator in pro(cid:173) viding an optimal emb edding. The Laplacian of the graph obtained from the data points may be viewed as an approximation to the Laplace-Beltrami operator defined on the manifold. The emb edding maps for the data come from approximations to a natural map that is defined on the entire manifold. The framework of analysis presented here makes this connection explicit. While this connection is known to geometers and specialists in spectral graph theory (for example , see [1, 2]) to the best of our knowledge we do not know of any application to data representation yet. The connection of the Laplacian to the heat kernel enables us to choose the weights of the graph in a principled manner. The locality preserving character of the Laplacian Eigenmap algorithm makes it rel(cid:173) atively insensitive to outliers and noise. A byproduct of this is that the algorithm implicitly emphasizes the natural clusters in the data. Connections to spectral clus(cid:173) tering algorithms developed in learning and computer vision (see Shi and Malik , 1997) become very clear. Following the discussion of Roweis and Saul (2000) , and Tenenbaum et al (2000), we note that the biological perceptual apparatus is con(cid:173) fronted with high dimensional stimuli from which it must recover low dimensional structure. One might argue that if the approach to recovering such low-dimensional structure is inherently local , then a natural clustering will emerge and thus might serve as the basis for the development of categories in biological perception.

Connections to spectral clus(cid:173) tering algorithms developed in learning and computer vision (see Shi and Malik , 1997) become very clear. Following the discussion of Roweis and Saul (2000) , and Tenenbaum et al (2000), we note that the biological perceptual apparatus is con(cid:173) fronted with high dimensional stimuli from which it must recover low dimensional structure. One might argue that if the approach to recovering such low-dimensional structure is inherently local , then a natural clustering will emerge and thus might serve as the basis for the development of categories in biological perception.
title: Laplacian Eigenmaps and Spectral Techniques for Embedding and Clustering

abstract: We use the k-core decomposition to develop algorithms for the analysis of large scale complex networks. This decomposition, based on a re- cursive pruning of the least connected vertices, allows to disentangle the hierarchical structure of networks by progressively focusing on their cen- tral cores. By using this strategy we develop a general visualization algo- rithm that can be used to compare the structural properties of various net- works and highlight their hierarchical structure. The low computational complexity of the algorithm, O(n + e), where n is the size of the net- work, and e is the number of edges, makes it suitable for the visualization of very large sparse networks. We show how the proposed visualization tool allows to ﬁnd speciﬁc structural ﬁngerprints of networks.

paragraphs: The paper uses k-core decomposition to analyze and visualize large complex networks. The decomposition repeatedly removes the least connected vertices, progressively exposing more central cores. This creates a way to examine network hierarchy by following how the structure changes through successive rounds of pruning.

Building on that decomposition, the authors develop a general visualization algorithm for comparing structural properties across networks. The visual organization is tied to the hierarchy revealed by the cores. This gives comparisons a structural basis, helping highlight how different networks are organized around their more central regions.

The algorithm's computational complexity is O(n + e), where n is the number of vertices and e the number of edges. Its cost therefore grows linearly with these measures of network size, making it suitable for very large sparse networks. The authors show that the visualization can reveal distinctive structural fingerprints. The contribution combines an efficient decomposition with a display strategy that makes network hierarchy and differences between networks visible.
summary.tldr: A linear-time visualization method uses k-core decomposition to reveal network hierarchies and distinctive structural fingerprints.

title: Large scale networks fingerprinting and visualization using the k-core decomposition

abstract: Embeddings of probability measures into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces have been proposed as a straightforward and practical means of representing and comparing probabilities. In particular, the distance between embeddings (the maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD) has several key advantages over many classical metrics on distributions, namely easy computability, fast convergence and low bias of finite sample estimates. An important requirement of the embedding RKHS is that it be characteristic: in this case, the MMD between two distributions is zero if and only if the distributions coincide. Three new results on the MMD are introduced in the present study. First, it is established that MMD corresponds to the optimal risk of a kernel classifier, thus forming a natural link between the distance between distributions and their ease of classification. An important consequence is that a kernel must be characteristic to guarantee classifiability between distributions in the RKHS. Second, the class of characteristic kernels is broadened to incorporate all strictly positive definite kernels: these include non-translation invariant kernels and kernels on non-compact domains. Third, a generalization of the MMD is proposed for families of kernels, as the supremum over MMDs on a class of kernels (for instance the Gaussian kernels with different bandwidths). This extension is necessary to obtain a single distance measure if a large selection or class of characteristic kernels is potentially appropriate. This generalization is reasonable, given that it corresponds to the problem of learning the kernel by minimizing the risk of the corresponding kernel classifier. The generalized MMD is shown to have consistent finite sample estimates, and its performance is demonstrated on a homogeneity testing example.

This supplies one distance when several kernels are appropriate and corresponds to learning a kernel by minimizing classifier risk. The authors establish consistent finite-sample estimates for this generalized measure and demonstrate it in a homogeneity-testing example.
summary.tldr: The paper connects MMD with classification risk, broadens characteristic kernels, and develops a consistently estimable distance over kernel families.

title: Kernel Choice and Classifiability for RKHS Embeddings of Probability Distributions

abstract: In this paper, we develop an efficient moments-based permutation test approach to improve the system’s efficiency by approximating the permutation distribution of the test statistic with Pearson distribution series. This approach involves the calculation of the first four moments of the permutation distribution. We propose a novel recursive method to derive these moments theoretically and analytically without any permutation. Experimental results using different test statistics are demonstrated using simulated data and real data. The proposed strategy takes advantage of nonparametric permutation tests and parametric Pearson distribution approximation to achieve both accuracy and efficiency.

This approach involves the calculation of the first four moments of the permutation distribution. We propose a novel recursive method to derive these moments theoretically and analytically without any permutation. Experimental results using different test statistics are demonstrated using simulated data and real data. The proposed strategy takes advantage of nonparametric permutation tests and parametric Pearson distribution approximation to achieve both accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: A permutation test assesses a statistic against the distribution it would have under rearrangements of the data. Constructing that reference distribution can require substantial computation. This paper proposes a shortcut: approximate the permutation distribution using the Pearson distribution family, with the approximation determined by its first four moments.

The key contribution is a recursive method that derives those moments analytically, without actually performing permutations. Moments summarize features of a distribution, so the method uses a compact description to build an approximate reference distribution. This separates the calculation of the needed summaries from the potentially expensive process of generating rearranged datasets.

The authors demonstrate the approach with different test statistics on both simulated and real data. They report a combination of accuracy and efficiency from joining a nonparametric permutation-test foundation with a parametric distribution approximation. The distinction matters: the moments are derived theoretically, while the resulting permutation distribution is approximated. The contribution is therefore an efficient route to permutation-based inference whose practical accuracy is supported by the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Analytically computed moments allow Pearson distributions to approximate permutation-test reference distributions without performing permutations.

title: Efficient Moments-based Permutation Tests

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) improves the prediction performance on multiple, different but related, learning problems through shared parameters or representations. One of the most prominent multi-task learning algorithms is an extension to svms by Evgeniou et al. Although very elegant, multi-task svm is inherently restricted by the fact that support vector machines require each class to be addressed explicitly with its own weight vector which, in a multi-task setting, requires the different learning tasks to share the same set of classes. This paper proposes an alternative formulation for multi-task learning by extending the recently published large margin nearest neighbor (lmnn) algorithm to the MTL paradigm. Instead of relying on separating hyperplanes, its decision function is based on the nearest neighbor rule which inherently extends to many classes and becomes a natural fit for multitask learning. We evaluate the resulting multi-task lmnn on real-world insurance data and speech classification problems and show that it consistently outperforms single-task kNN under several metrics and state-of-the-art MTL classifiers.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning shares information across related prediction problems. The paper identifies a restriction in a prominent multi-task support vector machine formulation: its class-specific weight vectors require the tasks to use the same class set. This can constrain how related problems are combined when their prediction categories differ.

The authors instead extend large margin nearest-neighbor learning to the multi-task setting. Predictions rely on the nearest-neighbor rule rather than a collection of separating hyperplanes. Because this decision rule naturally handles multiple classes, the formulation offers a way to share learning across tasks without organizing the model around the same class-specific construction.

The resulting method is evaluated on real-world insurance data and speech classification problems. It consistently outperforms single-task nearest-neighbor methods using several metrics and the state-of-the-art multi-task classifiers included in those evaluations. The findings support learning a shared approach to distance and neighborhood structure as a useful basis for multi-task prediction, especially in addressing the class-set restriction motivating the work.
summary.tldr: Extending large margin nearest-neighbor learning across tasks improves insurance and speech classification in the reported comparisons.

title: Large Margin Multi-Task Metric Learning

abstract: We consider Markov decision processes where the values of the parameters are uncertain. This uncertainty is described by a sequence of nested sets (that is, each set contains the previous one), each of which corresponds to a probabilistic guarantee for a different confidence level so that a set of admissible probability distributions of the unknown parameters is specified. This formulation models the case where the decision maker is aware of and wants to exploit some (yet imprecise) a-priori information of the distribution of parameters, and arises naturally in practice where methods to estimate the confidence region of parameters abound. We propose a decision criterion based on distributional robustness : the optimal policy maximizes the expected total reward under the most adversarial probability distribution over realizations of the uncertain parameters that is admissible (i.e., it agrees with the a-priori information). We show that finding the optimal distributionally robust policy can be reduced to a standard robust MDP where the parameters belong to a single uncertainty set, hence it can be computed in polynomial time under mild technical conditions.

paragraphs: Planning with a Markov decision process becomes harder when its parameters are uncertain. A decision maker may have some information about their distribution without knowing that distribution precisely. This paper represents such information through nested sets of parameter values, each associated with a probabilistic guarantee at a different confidence level.

Together, these guarantees specify which probability distributions over the unknown parameters are admissible. The proposed decision rule chooses a policy that maximizes expected total reward under the most adverse admissible distribution. Consequently, the policy accounts for uncertainty while still making use of the available prior information. The adversary is constrained by those probabilistic guarantees rather than being allowed to choose an arbitrary distribution.

The main computational result reduces this distributionally robust planning problem to a standard robust Markov decision process with a single uncertainty set. Under mild technical conditions, the optimal policy can therefore be computed in polynomial time. This connects a richer description of uncertainty to an established form of robust planning without abandoning computational tractability.
summary.tldr: The paper makes planning under imprecise parameter distributions tractable by reducing distributionally robust MDPs to standard robust MDPs.

title: Distributionally Robust Markov Decision Processes

abstract: This paper presents an analysis of importance weighting for learning from finite samples and gives a series of theoretical and algorithmic results. We point out simple cases where importance weighting can fail, which suggests the need for an analysis of the properties of this technique. We then give both upper and lower bounds for generalization with bounded importance weights and, more significantly, give learning guarantees for the more common case of unbounded importance weights under the weak assumption that the second moment is bounded, a condition related to the Renyi divergence of the training and test distributions. These results are based on a series of novel and general bounds we derive for unbounded loss functions, which are of independent interest. We use these bounds to guide the definition of an alternative reweighting algorithm and report the results of experiments demonstrating its benefits. Finally, we analyze the properties of normalized importance weights which are also commonly used.

paragraphs: Importance weighting adjusts the contributions of training examples when training and test distributions differ. This paper examines its behavior with finite samples, beginning with simple cases in which the technique can fail. The aim is to identify conditions that support generalization guarantees and use that analysis to inform a learning procedure.

The authors establish upper and lower generalization bounds when weights are bounded. They also provide guarantees for unbounded weights under the weaker requirement that their second moment is finite. That condition is related to Rényi divergence between the training and test distributions, connecting the guarantees to how those distributions differ.

The analysis develops general bounds for unbounded loss functions, which also have relevance beyond importance weighting. These bounds guide an alternative reweighting algorithm, and experiments demonstrate benefits of that algorithm. The paper additionally analyzes normalized importance weights. Together, the results explain why reweighting requires care with finite data and extend the theoretical treatment beyond the restrictive case of uniformly bounded weights.
summary.tldr: The paper gives finite-sample importance-weighting guarantees, including for unbounded weights with finite second moments, and derives an alternative reweighting algorithm.

title: Learning Bounds for Importance Weighting

abstract: Our objective is to train $p$-norm Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) and, more generally, linear MKL regularised by the Bregman divergence, using the Sequential Minimal Optimization (SMO) algorithm. The SMO algorithm is simple, easy to implement and adapt, and efficiently scales to large problems. As a result, it has gained widespread acceptance and SVMs are routinely trained using SMO in diverse real world applications. Training using SMO has been a long standing goal in MKL for the very same reasons. Unfortunately, the standard MKL dual is not differentiable, and therefore can not be optimised using SMO style co-ordinate ascent. In this paper, we demonstrate that linear MKL regularised with the $p$-norm squared, or with certain Bregman divergences, can indeed be trained using SMO. The resulting algorithm retains both simplicity and efficiency and is significantly faster than the state-of-the-art specialised $p$-norm MKL solvers. We show that we can train on a hundred thousand kernels in approximately seven minutes and on fifty thousand points in less than half an hour on a single core.

paragraphs: Sequential Minimal Optimization, or SMO, is an established way to train support vector machines because it is simple and scales efficiently. Applying the same strategy to multiple kernel learning has been difficult: the standard dual objective is not differentiable, preventing the usual SMO-style coordinate-ascent approach.

The paper shows that linear multiple kernel learning can use SMO when regularized by the squared p-norm or by certain Bregman divergences. This is a qualified result about particular regularizers, rather than all possible multiple-kernel objectives. It gives those formulations access to a training procedure valued for its implementation simplicity and efficiency.

The resulting algorithm is reported to be significantly faster than specialized state-of-the-art p-norm multiple-kernel solvers. The authors demonstrate training with one hundred thousand kernels in about seven minutes and with fifty thousand points in under half an hour, using a single core. These examples establish the reported scale of the method and show why resolving the optimization obstacle matters in practice.
summary.tldr: Squared p-norm and certain Bregman regularizers make linear multiple kernel learning compatible with efficient SMO training.

title: Multiple Kernel Learning and the SMO Algorithm

abstract: The Charles Bonnet Syndrome (CBS) is characterized by complex vivid visual hallucinations in people with, primarily, eye diseases and no other neurological pathology. We present a Deep Boltzmann Machine model of CBS, exploring two core hypotheses: First, that the visual cortex learns a generative or predictive model of sensory input, thus explaining its capability to generate internal imagery. And second, that homeostatic mechanisms stabilize neuronal activity levels, leading to hallucinations being formed when input is lacking. We reproduce a variety of qualitative findings in CBS. We also introduce a modification to the DBM that allows us to model a possible role of acetylcholine in CBS as mediating the balance of feed-forward and feed-back processing. Our model might provide new insights into CBS and also demonstrates that generative frameworks are promising as hypothetical models of cortical learning and perception.

And second, that homeostatic mechanisms stabilize neuronal activity levels, leading to hallucinations being formed when input is lacking. We reproduce a variety of qualitative findings in CBS. We also introduce a modification to the DBM that allows us to model a possible role of acetylcholine in CBS as mediating the balance of feed-forward and feed-back processing. paragraphs: Charles Bonnet syndrome involves vivid, complex visual hallucinations in people primarily affected by eye disease, without other neurological pathology. This paper uses a Deep Boltzmann Machine to explore a possible account of those hallucinations. The model links the brain's ability to generate internal imagery with mechanisms that stabilize neuronal activity.

The account rests on two hypotheses. First, the visual cortex learns a generative or predictive model of sensory input. Second, homeostatic mechanisms maintain activity levels, potentially causing internally generated visual content to emerge when sensory input is lacking. The computational model brings these hypotheses together and reproduces a variety of qualitative findings associated with the syndrome.

The authors also modify the model to represent a possible role for acetylcholine in balancing feed-forward and feedback processing. These results offer a hypothetical mechanism through which reduced input and activity regulation could interact. They suggest that generative models may help explain cortical learning and perception, without establishing the proposed biological account as the confirmed cause of the syndrome.
summary.tldr: A Deep Boltzmann Machine explores how learned visual imagery and activity-stabilizing mechanisms could produce hallucinations when sensory input is reduced.

title: Hallucinations in Charles Bonnet Syndrome Induced by Homeostasis: a Deep Boltzmann Machine Model

abstract: Many nonparametric regressors were recently shown to converge at rates that depend only on the intrinsic dimension of data. These regressors thus escape the curse of dimension when high-dimensional data has low intrinsic dimension (e.g. a manifold). We show that $k$-NN regression is also adaptive to intrinsic dimension. In particular our rates are local to a query $x$ and depend only on the way masses of balls centered at $x$ vary with radius. Furthermore, we show a simple way to choose $k = k(x)$ locally at any $x$ so as to nearly achieve the minimax rate at $x$ in terms of the unknown intrinsic dimension in the vicinity of $x$. We also establish that the minimax rate does not depend on a particular choice of metric space or distribution, but rather that this minimax rate holds for any metric space and doubling measure.

These regressors thus escape the curse of dimension when high-dimensional data has low intrinsic dimension (e.g. a manifold). We show that $k$-NN regression is also adaptive to intrinsic dimension. In particular our rates are local to a query $x$ and depend only on the way masses of balls centered at $x$ vary with radius. Furthermore, we show a simple way to choose $k = k(x)$ locally at any $x$ so as to nearly achieve the minimax rate at $x$ in terms of the unknown intrinsic dimension in the vicinity of $x$. We also establish that the minimax rate does not depend on a particular choice of metric space or distribution, but rather that this minimax rate holds for any metric space and doubling measure.

paragraphs: Data described by many coordinates may still have a much lower-dimensional local structure. This paper shows that k-nearest-neighbor regression can adapt to that intrinsic dimension. Its convergence analysis focuses on an individual query point, rather than assigning one dimensionality-based rate to the entire dataset.

The relevant local structure is expressed through how probability mass inside a ball changes as its radius grows around the query. This connects prediction rates to the distribution of nearby observations. The authors also give a simple rule for choosing the number of neighbors separately at each query, nearly achieving the local minimax rate despite not knowing the nearby intrinsic dimension.

The minimax result extends across metric spaces equipped with doubling measures, rather than relying on one particular space or distribution. Together, these findings explain how a familiar regression method can adapt to locally simple data structure. They also provide a reason to vary the neighborhood size across queries instead of treating every location alike.
summary.tldr: K-nearest-neighbor regression can adapt to local intrinsic dimension through a query-specific choice of neighborhood size.

title: k-NN Regression Adapts to Local Intrinsic Dimension

abstract: How do people determine which elements of a set are most representative of that set? We extend an existing Bayesian measure of representativeness, which indicates the representativeness of a sample from a distribution, to define a measure of the representativeness of an item to a set. We show that this measure is formally related to a machine learning method known as Bayesian Sets. Building on this connection, we derive an analytic expression for the representativeness of objects described by a sparse vector of binary features. We then apply this measure to a large database of images, using it to determine which images are the most representative members of different sets. Comparing the resulting predictions to human judgments of representativeness provides a test of this measure with naturalistic stimuli, and illustrates how databases that are more commonly used in computer vision and machine learning can be used to evaluate psychological theories.

paragraphs: People can judge some members of a collection to be more representative than others. This paper develops a mathematical account of that judgment by extending an existing Bayesian measure. The original measure concerns how representative a sample is of a distribution; the extension asks how representative an individual item is of a set.

The authors establish a formal connection to Bayesian Sets, a machine learning method. Using that connection, they derive an analytic expression for objects represented by sparse binary feature vectors. This makes the proposed psychological measure computable for objects described by a collection of present-or-absent features, linking the theoretical account to a practical representation.

They apply the measure to a large image database to identify representative members of different image sets, then compare its predictions with human judgments. That comparison tests the account using naturalistic stimuli. The abstract does not state the degree of agreement; the reported contribution is the formal measure and its evaluation, demonstrating how image databases can support tests of psychological theories.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian measure of item representativeness is connected to Bayesian Sets and tested against human judgments using image collections.

title: Testing a Bayesian Measure of Representativeness Using a Large Image Database

abstract: We present an optimization approach for linear SVMs based on a stochastic primal-dual approach, where the primal step is akin to an importance-weighted SGD, and the dual step is a stochastic update on the importance weights. This yields an optimization method with a sublinear dependence on the training set size, and the first method for learning linear SVMs with runtime less then the size of the training set required for learning!
originalAbstract: We present an optimization approach for linear SVMs based on a stochastic primal-dual approach, where the primal step is akin to an importance-weighted SGD, and the dual step is a stochastic update on the importance weights. This yields an optimization method with a sublinear dependence on the training set size, and the first method for learning linear SVMs with runtime less then the size of the training set required for learning!

paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly a linear support vector machine can be learned. Its focus is the computational cost of optimization as the training set grows. The proposed approach combines two stochastic updates within a primal-dual formulation, linking the update of the predictor to the update of weights that determine the importance assigned to training information.

On the primal side, the method resembles stochastic gradient descent with importance weighting. On the dual side, it makes a stochastic adjustment to those importance weights. These are coupled parts of the optimization procedure: the weights participate in learning rather than serving only as a fixed choice made before optimization begins.

The stated result is an optimization method whose dependence on training-set size is sublinear. The authors also claim the first linear-SVM learning method with runtime below the size of the training set required for learning. The significance is a computational one: the amount of data associated with a learning problem need not dictate a proportional amount of optimization work. The claim concerns linear SVM learning and the proposed stochastic primal-dual approach.
summary.tldr: A stochastic primal-dual method learns linear SVMs with sublinear dependence on training-set size by jointly updating the predictor and importance weights.

title: Beating SGD: Learning SVMs in Sublinear Time

abstract: Neurons typically respond to a restricted number of stimulus features within the high-dimensional space of natural stimuli. Here we describe an explicit model-based interpretation of traditional estimators for a neuron's multi-dimensional feature space, which allows for several important generalizations and extensions. First, we show that traditional estimators based on the spike-triggered average (STA) and spike-triggered covariance (STC) can be formalized in terms of the "expected log-likelihood" of a Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson (LNP) model with Gaussian stimuli. This model-based formulation allows us to define maximum-likelihood and Bayesian estimators that are statistically consistent and efficient in a wider variety of settings, such as with naturalistic (non-Gaussian) stimuli. It also allows us to employ Bayesian methods for regularization, smoothing, sparsification, and model comparison, and provides Bayesian confidence intervals on model parameters. We describe an empirical Bayes method for selecting the number of features, and extend the model to accommodate an arbitrary elliptical nonlinear response function, which results in a more powerful and more flexible model for feature space inference. We validate these methods using neural data recorded extracellularly from macaque primary visual cortex.

paragraphs: A neuron may respond to only a few features of a stimulus, even when the stimulus itself has many dimensions. This paper develops a model-based interpretation of methods that identify those features from neural spikes. It connects the spike-triggered average and covariance to an expected log-likelihood formulation of a Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson model under Gaussian stimulation.

That connection makes it possible to extend familiar estimators beyond their original setting. The authors define maximum-likelihood and Bayesian estimators that are statistically consistent and efficient across a wider range of conditions, including naturalistic, non-Gaussian stimuli. Bayesian inference also supplies ways to smooth estimates, encourage sparsity, compare models, and express uncertainty through confidence intervals on model parameters.

The paper further introduces an empirical Bayes method for choosing how many stimulus features to retain. It expands the response model to allow an arbitrary elliptical nonlinear function, making feature-space inference more flexible. Validation uses extracellular recordings from macaque primary visual cortex. The contribution is both an interpretation of established statistics and a framework for richer neural-response estimation.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic interpretation of spike-triggered statistics enables more flexible Bayesian estimation of the stimulus features that drive neural responses.

title: Bayesian Spike-Triggered Covariance Analysis

abstract: We present a reformulation of the information bottleneck (IB) problem in terms of copula, using the equivalence between mutual information and negative copula entropy. Focusing on the Gaussian copula we extend the analytical IB solution available for the multivariate Gaussian case to distributions with a Gaussian dependence structure but arbitrary marginal densities, also called meta-Gaussian distributions. This opens new possibles applications of IB to continuous data and provides a solution more robust to outliers.

paragraphs: The paper reformulates the information bottleneck problem using copulas, which describe dependence separately from the individual distributions of variables. Its mathematical starting point is the equivalence between mutual information and negative copula entropy. This makes the dependence structure a direct way to express the information quantities involved in the bottleneck problem.

In this family, the dependence structure is Gaussian, but the marginal densities can take arbitrary forms. The extension therefore relaxes the shape requirements on individual variables while retaining a particular structure for how those variables depend on one another.

This distinction broadens the continuous-data settings to which the analytical information bottleneck solution can apply. The authors also report that the resulting solution is more robust to outliers. The contribution is a change in the distributional requirements of the solution: Gaussian dependence remains central, while Gaussian marginal densities are no longer required.
summary.tldr: A copula reformulation extends the analytical information bottleneck solution to Gaussian dependence with arbitrary marginals and improves outlier robustness.

title: Meta-Gaussian Information Bottleneck

abstract: We propose a multiresolution Gaussian process to capture long-range, non-Markovian dependencies while allowing for abrupt changes. The multiresolution GP hierarchically couples a collection of smooth GPs, each defined over an element of a random nested partition. Long-range dependencies are captured by the top-level GP while the partition points define the abrupt changes. Due to the inherent conjugacy of the GPs, one can analytically marginalize the GPs and compute the conditional likelihood of the observations given the partition tree. This allows for efficient inference of the partition itself, for which we employ graph-theoretic techniques. We apply the multiresolution GP to the analysis of Magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings of brain activity.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a Gaussian process model for data that combine long-range dependence with abrupt changes. These two properties need distinct treatment within the representation: observations far apart can remain related, while local transitions can be sudden. The model accommodates both through a hierarchy of coupled smooth Gaussian processes.

Each process is defined on one element of a random nested partition. The process at the top of the hierarchy captures long-range dependencies, while partition boundaries determine where abrupt changes occur. The partition therefore has a direct modeling role: inferring its structure helps identify how the data divide into regions within the multiresolution description.

This supports efficient inference over the partition itself using graph-theoretic techniques. The model is applied to magnetoencephalography recordings of brain activity, illustrating a setting in which the combined treatment of long-range relationships and sudden changes can be used.
summary.tldr: Hierarchically coupled Gaussian processes model long-range dependencies and abrupt changes through an inferred nested partition.

title: Multiresolution Gaussian Processes

abstract: Bilinear approximation of a matrix is a powerful paradigm of unsupervised learning. In some applications, however, there is a natural hierarchy of concepts that ought to be reflected in the unsupervised analysis. For example, in the neurosciences image sequence considered here, there are the semantic concepts of pixel $\rightarrow$ neuron $\rightarrow$ assembly that should find their counterpart in the unsupervised analysis. Driven by this concrete problem, we propose a decomposition of the matrix of observations into a product of more than two sparse matrices, with the rank decreasing from lower to higher levels. In contrast to prior work, we allow for both hierarchical and heterarchical relations of lower-level to higher-level concepts. In addition, we learn the nature of these relations rather than imposing them. Finally, we describe an optimization scheme that allows to optimize the decomposition over all levels jointly, rather than in a greedy level-by-level fashion. The proposed bilevel SHMF (sparse heterarchical matrix factorization) is the first formalism that allows to simultaneously interpret a calcium imaging sequence in terms of the constituent neurons, their membership in assemblies, and the time courses of both neurons and assemblies. Experiments show that the proposed model fully recovers the structure from difficult synthetic data designed to imitate the experimental data. More importantly, bilevel SHMF yields plausible interpretations of real-world Calcium imaging data.

The paper develops a matrix decomposition that reflects this layered structure by expressing observations as a product of more than two sparse matrices, with rank decreasing toward higher levels.

The method learns relationships between levels and permits both hierarchical and heterarchical organization. This allows the representation to capture more than a prescribed hierarchy. Its optimization scheme adjusts all levels jointly, so the interpretation at one level can be learned together with the relationships and representations at the others.

title: Learning Multi-level Sparse Representations

abstract: Tetris is a popular video game that has been widely used as a benchmark for various optimization techniques including approximate dynamic programming (ADP) algorithms. A close look at the literature of this game shows that while ADP algorithms, that have been (almost) entirely based on approximating the value function (value function based), have performed poorly in Tetris, the methods that search directly in the space of policies by learning the policy parameters using an optimization black box, such as the cross entropy (CE) method, have achieved the best reported results. This makes us conjecture that Tetris is a game in which good policies are easier to represent, and thus, learn than their corresponding value functions. So, in order to obtain a good performance with ADP, we should use ADP algorithms that search in a policy space, instead of the more traditional ones that search in a value function space. In this paper, we put our conjecture to test by applying such an ADP algorithm, called classification-based modified policy iteration (CBMPI), to the game of Tetris. Our extensive experimental results show that for the first time an ADP algorithm, namely CBMPI, obtains the best results reported in the literature for Tetris in both small $10\times 10$ and large $10\times 20$ boards. Although the CBMPI's results are similar to those achieved by the CE method in the large board, CBMPI uses considerably fewer (almost 1/10) samples (call to the generative model of the game) than CE.

paragraphs: Tetris exposed a puzzle for approximate dynamic programming: methods centered on approximating value functions performed poorly, while methods directly optimizing policies achieved strong results. A value function describes how promising a situation is, whereas a policy determines what action to take. The authors conjecture that good Tetris policies are easier to represent and learn than their corresponding value functions.

They test that conjecture using classification-based modified policy iteration, or CBMPI. This brings approximate dynamic programming into a policy-search approach rather than relying on the traditional emphasis on searching a value-function space. The experiment asks whether changing what the algorithm learns can overcome the earlier disappointing performance.

CBMPI achieves the best Tetris results reported in the literature considered by the paper on both 10-by-10 and 10-by-20 boards. On the larger board, its results are similar to the cross-entropy method, but it uses about one tenth as many calls to the game's generative model. The findings support the proposed approach empirically; they do not turn the representational conjecture into a general theorem.
summary.tldr: Policy-focused approximate dynamic programming achieves leading reported Tetris results with substantially fewer samples than cross-entropy search on the larger board.

title: Approximate Dynamic Programming Finally Performs Well in the Game of Tetris

abstract: We consider the problem of learning to optimize an unknown Markov decision process (MDP). We show that, if the MDP can be parameterized within some known function class, we can obtain regret bounds that scale with the dimensionality, rather than cardinality, of the system. We characterize this dependence explicitly as $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d_K d_E T})$ where $T$ is time elapsed, $d_K$ is the Kolmogorov dimension and $d_E$ is the \emph{eluder dimension}. These represent the first unified regret bounds for model-based reinforcement learning and provide state of the art guarantees in several important settings. Moreover, we present a simple and computationally efficient algorithm \emph{posterior sampling for reinforcement learning} (PSRL) that satisfies these bounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning to act optimally in an unknown Markov decision process. Its central assumption is that the process can be parameterized within a known class of functions. Under this assumption, the authors derive regret bounds governed by dimensional measures of that class rather than by the cardinality of the system.

The bound scales as the square root of d_K times d_E times T, up to logarithmic factors. Here T is elapsed time, d_K is the Kolmogorov dimension, and d_E is the eluder dimension. This expression makes the dependence on model-class complexity explicit. It connects the cost of learning an unknown environment to two dimensions of its representation.

The authors present these as unified regret bounds for model-based reinforcement learning and report state-of-the-art guarantees in several important settings. They also give posterior sampling for reinforcement learning, or PSRL, as a simple and computationally efficient algorithm satisfying the bounds. The contribution therefore combines a theoretical characterization with an algorithm that achieves it under the stated model-class assumption.
summary.tldr: Under a known function-class assumption, PSRL achieves regret bounds controlled by Kolmogorov and eluder dimensions rather than system cardinality.

title: Model-based Reinforcement Learning and the Eluder Dimension

abstract: Tensor CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) decomposition has wide applications in statistical learning of latent variable models and in data mining. In this paper, we propose fast and randomized tensor CP decomposition algorithms based on sketching. We build on the idea of count sketches, but introduce many novel ideas which are unique to tensors. We develop novel methods for randomized com- putation of tensor contractions via FFTs, without explicitly forming the tensors. Such tensor contractions are encountered in decomposition methods such as ten- sor power iterations and alternating least squares. We also design novel colliding hashes for symmetric tensors to further save time in computing the sketches. We then combine these sketching ideas with existing whitening and tensor power iter- ative techniques to obtain the fastest algorithm on both sparse and dense tensors. The quality of approximation under our method does not depend on properties such as sparsity, uniformity of elements, etc. We apply the method for topic mod- eling and obtain competitive results.

paragraphs: Tensor CP decomposition is used in latent-variable learning and data mining, but its computations can be expensive. This paper develops randomized decomposition algorithms based on sketches: compact computational representations built using hashing. The authors start from count sketches and introduce techniques tailored to tensor operations.

A central contribution is computing randomized tensor contractions with fast Fourier transforms without explicitly constructing the tensors. These contractions appear in tensor power iterations and alternating least squares. The paper also introduces colliding hashes for symmetric tensors, reducing the time required to compute their sketches.

Combining these ideas with whitening and tensor power iteration yields what the authors describe as the fastest algorithm for both sparse and dense tensors. They state that approximation quality does not depend on properties such as sparsity or uniformity of tensor entries. An application to topic modeling gives competitive results. The contribution thus joins faster core computations with an approximation guarantee that is not tied to those particular tensor characteristics.
summary.tldr: Tensor-specific sketches accelerate CP decomposition by computing key contractions without explicitly forming tensors.

title: Fast and Guaranteed Tensor Decomposition via Sketching

abstract: Modern prediction problems arising in multilabel learning and learning to rank pose unique challenges to the classical theory of supervised learning. These problems have large prediction and label spaces of a combinatorial nature and involve sophisticated loss functions. We offer a general framework to derive mistake driven online algorithms and associated loss bounds. The key ingredients in our framework are a general loss function, a general vector space representation of predictions, and a notion of margin with respect to a general norm. Our general algorithm, Predtron, yields the perceptron algorithm and its variants when instantiated on classic problems such as binary classification, multiclass classification, ordinal regression, and multilabel classification. For multilabel ranking and subset ranking, we derive novel algorithms, notions of margins, and loss bounds. A simulation study confirms the behavior predicted by our bounds and demonstrates the flexibility of the design choices in our framework.

paragraphs: Prediction tasks such as multilabel learning and ranking can involve large combinatorial output spaces and losses more complicated than simple classification errors. This paper develops a general framework for deriving online algorithms that update in response to mistakes, together with bounds on their loss.

The framework combines a loss function, a vector-space representation of predictions, and a margin defined using a general norm. These choices determine an instance of the Predtron algorithm. On familiar tasks, including binary and multiclass classification, ordinal regression, and multilabel classification, the framework recovers the perceptron and its variants.

For multilabel ranking and subset ranking, the authors derive new algorithms, associated margin definitions, and loss bounds. A simulation study agrees with the behavior predicted by the bounds and illustrates flexibility in the framework’s design choices. The contribution is a common route from a prediction problem’s representation and loss to an online learning rule and a corresponding analysis of its performance.
summary.tldr: Predtron unifies perceptron-style online algorithms and derives new methods and loss bounds for structured ranking problems.

title: Predtron: A Family of Online Algorithms for General Prediction Problems

abstract: A key goal of computer vision is to recover the underlying 3D structure that gives rise to 2D observations of the world. If endowed with 3D understanding, agents can abstract away from the complexity of the rendering process to form stable, disentangled representations of scene elements. In this paper we learn strong deep generative models of 3D structures, and recover these structures from 2D images via probabilistic inference. We demonstrate high-quality samples and report log-likelihoods on several datasets, including ShapeNet, and establish the first benchmarks in the literature. We also show how these models and their inference networks can be trained jointly, end-to-end, and directly from 2D images without any use of ground-truth 3D labels. This demonstrates for the first time the feasibility of learning to infer 3D representations of the world in a purely unsupervised manner.

paragraphs: The paper investigates learning the three-dimensional structure underlying two-dimensional images. Its motivation is that a representation of scene structure can separate the underlying elements from the complexity of how they are rendered. The authors build deep generative models of 3D structures and use probabilistic inference to recover those structures from images.

A central result is that the generative models and their inference networks can be trained jointly, end to end, directly from 2D images. This training does not use ground-truth 3D labels. The model therefore learns both a representation of three-dimensional structure and a way to infer that structure through image-based training.

The authors demonstrate high-quality generated samples and report log-likelihoods on several datasets, including ShapeNet, establishing benchmarks for the approach. They present the work as a first demonstration that learning to infer 3D representations in a purely unsupervised manner is feasible. The significance is this demonstrated feasibility of recovering structured 3D representations without supplying labeled 3D targets during training.
summary.tldr: Deep generative models and inference networks can jointly learn to recover 3D structure from 2D images without ground-truth 3D labels.

title: Unsupervised Learning of 3D Structure from Images

abstract: Time series prediction problems are becoming increasingly high-dimensional in modern applications, such as climatology and demand forecasting. For example, in the latter problem, the number of items for which demand needs to be forecast might be as large as 50,000. In addition, the data is generally noisy and full of missing values. Thus, modern applications require methods that are highly scalable, and can deal with noisy data in terms of corruptions or missing values. However, classical time series methods usually fall short of handling these issues. In this paper, we present a temporal regularized matrix factorization (TRMF) framework which supports data-driven temporal learning and forecasting. We develop novel regularization schemes and use scalable matrix factorization methods that are eminently suited for high-dimensional time series data that has many missing values. Our proposed TRMF is highly general, and subsumes many existing approaches for time series analysis. We make interesting connections to graph regularization methods in the context of learning the dependencies in an autoregressive framework. Experimental results show the superiority of TRMF in terms of scalability and prediction quality. In particular, TRMF is two orders of magnitude faster than other methods on a problem of dimension 50,000, and generates better forecasts on real-world datasets such as Wal-mart E-commerce datasets.

Classical methods often struggle with this combination of scale and incomplete data. The paper introduces temporal regularized matrix factorization, or TRMF, to support learning temporal patterns and producing forecasts in such settings.

The framework combines scalable matrix factorization with new temporal regularization schemes. Temporal dependencies are learned from data, and the authors connect this process to graph regularization in an autoregressive framework. TRMF is sufficiently general to include many existing time-series approaches, giving the proposed formulation a role beyond a single specialized forecasting model.
