These findings support the framework's usefulness for large forecasting problems where computational cost and missing observations are central concerns.
summary.tldr: TRMF learns temporal structure through scalable matrix factorization, improving forecasting and achieving a reported hundredfold speedup on a 50,000-dimensional problem.

title: Temporal Regularized Matrix Factorization for High-dimensional Time Series Prediction

abstract: We consider empirical risk minimization for large-scale datasets. We introduce Ada Newton as an adaptive algorithm that uses Newton's method with adaptive sample sizes. The main idea of Ada Newton is to increase the size of the training set by a factor larger than one in a way that the minimization variable for the current training set is in the local neighborhood of the optimal argument of the next training set. This allows to exploit the quadratic convergence property of Newton's method and reach the statistical accuracy of each training set with only one iteration of Newton's method. We show theoretically that we can iteratively increase the sample size while applying single Newton iterations without line search and staying within the statistical accuracy of the regularized empirical risk. In particular, we can double the size of the training set in each iteration when the number of samples is sufficiently large. Numerical experiments on various datasets confirm the possibility of increasing the sample size by factor 2 at each iteration which implies that Ada Newton achieves the statistical accuracy of the full training set with about two passes over the dataset.

paragraphs: Ada Newton addresses large-scale empirical risk minimization by growing the training sample during optimization. Its target is statistical accuracy: solving each sample-based problem to the precision warranted by that sample. This shifts attention from repeatedly optimizing the full dataset to coordinating the amount of data with the progress of the optimizer.

The key is to enlarge the sample while keeping the current solution close enough to the next problem's optimum. In that local neighborhood, Newton's method can exploit quadratic convergence. The authors show theoretically how successive sample increases and single Newton updates can remain within the statistical accuracy of the regularized empirical risk, without requiring a line search at each stage.

Doubling the sample is supported when the number of observations is sufficiently large; it is not presented as an unconditional rule for every starting sample. Experiments on several datasets support doubling at each iteration. Under that progression, the authors report reaching the full dataset's statistical accuracy with about two passes over the data, connecting the convergence argument to reduced data-processing work.
summary.tldr: Ada Newton grows its training sample so single Newton updates can track statistical accuracy, enabling about two data passes in the reported experiments.

title: Adaptive Newton Method for Empirical Risk Minimization to Statistical Accuracy

abstract: Addressing the will to give a more complete picture than an average relationship provided by standard regression, a novel framework for estimating and predicting simultaneously several conditional quantiles is introduced. The proposed methodology leverages kernel-based multi-task learning to curb the embarrassing phenomenon of quantile crossing, with a one-step estimation procedure and no post-processing. Moreover, this framework comes along with theoretical guarantees and an efficient coordinate descent learning algorithm. Numerical experiments on benchmark and real datasets highlight the enhancements of our approach regarding the prediction error, the crossing occurrences and the training time.
originalAbstract: Addressing the will to give a more complete picture than an average relationship provided by standard regression, a novel framework for estimating and predicting simultaneously several conditional quantiles is introduced. The proposed methodology leverages kernel-based multi-task learning to curb the embarrassing phenomenon of quantile crossing, with a one-step estimation procedure and no post-processing. Moreover, this framework comes along with theoretical guarantees and an efficient coordinate descent learning algorithm. Numerical experiments on benchmark and real datasets highlight the enhancements of our approach regarding the prediction error, the crossing occurrences and the training time.

paragraphs: An average prediction can conceal how outcomes vary around that average. Quantile regression addresses this by predicting different positions within the conditional outcome distribution. This paper develops a framework that estimates several conditional quantiles simultaneously, aiming to provide a fuller picture of the relationship between inputs and outcomes.

A central difficulty is quantile crossing: predictions for supposedly lower quantiles can exceed predictions for higher ones. The authors use kernel-based multi-task learning to connect the quantile estimation problems and curb these crossings. The method estimates the quantiles in one procedure, without requiring a separate post-processing stage to repair their ordering afterward.

The framework includes theoretical guarantees and an efficient coordinate descent algorithm for learning. Experiments on benchmark and real datasets report improvements in prediction error, crossing occurrences, and training time. These findings support jointly learning the quantiles as a useful way to address predictive quality, consistency, and computation together. The stated goal is to reduce crossing, rather than an unconditional claim that crossings cannot occur.
summary.tldr: Joint kernel-based quantile regression reduces quantile crossing and improves prediction error and training time in the reported experiments.

title: Joint quantile regression in vector-valued RKHSs

abstract: This study deals with neural networks in the sense of geometric transformations acting on the coordinate representation of the underlying data manifold which the data is sampled from. It forms part of an attempt to construct a formalized general theory of neural networks in the setting of Riemannian geometry. From this perspective, the following theoretical results are developed and proven for feedforward networks. First it is shown that residual neural networks are finite difference approximations to dynamical systems of first order differential equations, as opposed to ordinary networks that are static. This implies that the network is learning systems of differential equations governing the coordinate transformations that represent the data. Second it is shown that a closed form solution of the metric tensor on the underlying data manifold can be found by backpropagating the coordinate representations learned by the neural network itself. This is formulated in a formal abstract sense as a sequence of Lie group actions on the metric fibre space in the principal and associated bundles on the data manifold. Toy experiments were run to confirm parts of the proposed theory, as well as to provide intuitions as to how neural networks operate on data.

The analysis develops and proves results for feedforward networks from this perspective.

One result identifies residual networks as finite-difference approximations to dynamical systems governed by first-order differential equations. In this interpretation, learning a residual network amounts to learning equations that govern transformations of the data's coordinates. This provides a dynamical reading of the network's successive transformations.

A second result gives a closed-form expression for the underlying manifold's metric tensor by backpropagating coordinate representations learned by the network. The formal treatment expresses this through Lie group actions and geometric bundles. Toy experiments confirm parts of the proposed theory and provide intuition about how networks transform data. Their role is to illustrate and support portions of the geometric account, while the principal contributions are the theoretical relationships.
summary.tldr: A geometric theory connects residual networks to differential equations and derives a manifold metric from learned coordinate transformations.

title: Principles of Riemannian Geometry in Neural Networks

abstract: Parallel implementations of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) have received significant research attention, thanks to its excellent scalability properties. A fundamental barrier when parallelizing SGD is the high bandwidth cost of communicating gradient updates between nodes; consequently, several lossy compresion heuristics have been proposed, by which nodes only communicate quantized gradients. Although effective in practice, these heuristics do not always guarantee convergence, and it is not clear whether they can be improved. In this paper, we propose Quantized SGD (QSGD), a family of compression schemes for gradient updates which provides convergence guarantees. QSGD allows the user to smoothly trade off \emph{communication bandwidth} and \emph{convergence time}: nodes can adjust the number of bits sent per iteration, at the cost of possibly higher variance. We show that this trade-off is inherent, in the sense that improving it past some threshold would violate information-theoretic lower bounds. QSGD guarantees convergence for convex and non-convex objectives, under asynchrony, and can be extended to stochastic variance-reduced techniques. When applied to training deep neural networks for image classification and automated speech recognition, QSGD leads to significant reductions in end-to-end training time. For example, on 16GPUs, we can train the ResNet152 network to full accuracy on ImageNet 1.8x faster than the full-precision variant.

summary.tldr: QSGD compresses gradient communication with convergence guarantees and an explicit bandwidth–variance trade-off, reducing reported training times.

title: QSGD: Communication-Efficient SGD via Gradient Quantization and Encoding

abstract: Learning with streaming data has attracted much attention during the past few years.Though most studies consider data stream with fixed features, in real practice the features may be evolvable. For example, features of data gathered by limited lifespan sensors will change when these sensors are substituted by new ones. In this paper, we propose a novel learning paradigm: Feature Evolvable Streaming Learning where old features would vanish and new features would occur. Rather than relying on only the current features, we attempt to recover the vanished features and exploit it to improve performance. Specifically, we learn two models from the recovered features and the current features, respectively. To benefit from the recovered features, we develop two ensemble methods. In the first method, we combine the predictions from two models and theoretically show that with the assistance of old features, the performance on new features can be improved. In the second approach, we dynamically select the best single prediction and establish a better performance guarantee when the best model switches. Experiments on both synthetic and real data validate the effectiveness of our proposal.

paragraphs: Streaming learning often assumes that the same features remain available over time. This paper considers a different situation: old features disappear and new ones arrive, as can happen when sensors are replaced. The proposed Feature Evolvable Streaming Learning framework seeks to preserve useful information from vanished features while learning from those currently available.

The method attempts to recover the old features and trains separate models using recovered and current features. It then offers two ways to use their predictions. One combines the models' outputs; the other dynamically selects a single prediction. These approaches let information associated with earlier features continue contributing after the observed feature set changes.

For the combination method, the authors theoretically show that assistance from old features can improve performance on new features. For dynamic selection, they establish a stronger performance guarantee when the best model changes over time. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the proposal's effectiveness, demonstrating the value of carrying information across feature transitions.
summary.tldr: Recovering vanished features and combining their predictions with current-feature models improves learning in streams whose feature sets change.

title: Learning with Feature Evolvable Streams

abstract: We show experimentally that the algorithm CLARANS of Ng and Han (1994) finds better K-medoids solutions than the Voronoi iteration algorithm of Hastie et al. (2001). This finding, along with the similarity between the Voronoi iteration algorithm and Lloyd's K-means algorithm, motivates us to use CLARANS as a K-means initializer. We show that CLARANS outperforms other algorithms on 23/23 datasets with a mean decrease over k-means++ of 30% for initialization mean squared error (MSE) and 3% for final MSE. We introduce algorithmic improvements to CLARANS which improve its complexity and runtime, making it a viable initialization scheme for large datasets.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a method for solving K-medoids can provide better starting points for K-means. It begins with an experimental comparison showing that CLARANS finds better K-medoids solutions than Voronoi iteration. Because Voronoi iteration resembles Lloyd's K-means algorithm, this finding motivates using CLARANS to initialize K-means.

These figures distinguish the immediate improvement in starting quality from the improvement that remains after K-means finishes.

The authors also improve CLARANS itself, reducing its complexity and runtime so that it becomes a viable initialization approach for large datasets. This computational contribution matters because initialization must justify its own cost. Taken together, the findings support CLARANS as a practical source of better K-means starting points, with measured benefits both before and after the subsequent clustering optimization.
summary.tldr: An improved CLARANS initializer lowers K-means error across 23 evaluated datasets, including a mean 3% reduction in final MSE versus k-means++.

title: K-Medoids For K-Means Seeding

abstract: Collecting large training datasets, annotated with high-quality labels, is costly and time-consuming. This paper proposes a novel framework for training deep convolutional neural networks from noisy labeled datasets that can be obtained cheaply. The problem is formulated using an undirected graphical model that represents the relationship between noisy and clean labels, trained in a semi-supervised setting. In our formulation, the inference over latent clean labels is tractable and is regularized during training using auxiliary sources of information. The proposed model is applied to the image labeling problem and is shown to be effective in labeling unseen images as well as reducing label noise in training on CIFAR-10 and MS COCO datasets.

paragraphs: Obtaining large image datasets with reliable labels is expensive, while cheaper annotations may contain mistakes. This paper develops a framework for training deep convolutional networks from such noisy labels. It treats the observed annotation and the underlying clean label as distinct quantities whose relationship should be modeled during learning.

The framework uses an undirected graphical model to connect noisy labels with latent clean labels and trains it in a semi-supervised setting. Inference over the clean labels is tractable, and auxiliary information regularizes that inference during training. This makes the estimation of cleaner supervision part of the training process rather than simply accepting every supplied annotation as correct.

The authors apply the method to image labeling on CIFAR-10 and MS COCO. They report effectiveness both in predicting labels for previously unseen images and in reducing noise in the training labels. These two outcomes address complementary parts of the problem: learning a useful image predictor and improving the uncertain supervision from which that predictor is learned.
summary.tldr: A semi-supervised graphical model learns latent clean labels alongside a convolutional network, improving image labeling and reducing training-label noise.

title: Toward Robustness against Label Noise in Training Deep Discriminative Neural Networks

abstract: Extrapolation methods use the last few iterates of an optimization algorithm to produce a better estimate of the optimum. They were shown to achieve optimal convergence rates in a deterministic setting using simple gradient iterates. Here, we study extrapolation methods in a stochastic setting, where the iterates are produced by either a simple or an accelerated stochastic gradient algorithm. We first derive convergence bounds for arbitrary, potentially biased perturbations, then produce asymptotic bounds using the ratio between the variance of the noise and the accuracy of the current point. Finally, we apply this acceleration technique to stochastic algorithms such as SGD, SAGA, SVRG and Katyusha in different settings, and show significant performance gains.

paragraphs: Extrapolation methods use several recent optimization iterates to construct a better estimate of the optimum. Although this strategy had strong convergence results in deterministic settings, stochastic optimization introduces noise into those iterates. This paper studies whether extrapolation can still improve progress when applied to ordinary or already accelerated stochastic gradient methods.

The analysis first derives convergence bounds allowing arbitrary perturbations, including perturbations that may be biased. It then develops asymptotic bounds in terms of the relationship between noise variance and the accuracy of the current point. This makes the noise level relative to optimization progress an explicit part of the theory, rather than treating stochastic iterates as if they were exact.

The authors apply the acceleration technique to SGD, SAGA, SVRG, and Katyusha in different settings and report significant performance gains. The findings show that extrapolation can complement several stochastic optimization procedures, including an accelerated one. The theoretical and experimental contributions together address how information across recent iterates remains useful despite perturbations.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes extrapolation under stochastic perturbations and reports acceleration gains for several stochastic optimization algorithms.

title: Nonlinear Acceleration of Stochastic Algorithms

abstract: Bayesian optimization usually assumes that a Bayesian prior is given. However, the strong theoretical guarantees in Bayesian optimization are often regrettably compromised in practice because of unknown parameters in the prior. In this paper, we adopt a variant of empirical Bayes and show that, by estimating the Gaussian process prior from offline data sampled from the same prior and constructing unbiased estimators of the posterior, variants of both GP-UCB and \emph{probability of improvement} achieve a near-zero regret bound, which decreases to a constant proportional to the observational noise as the number of offline data and the number of online evaluations increase. Empirically, we have verified our approach on challenging simulated robotic problems featuring task and motion planning.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization often begins by assuming a prior is already known. In practice, unknown prior parameters can weaken the relevance of its theoretical guarantees. This paper studies how to learn a Gaussian-process prior from offline data and then use it to guide online evaluations while retaining a regret guarantee.

The approach uses a variant of empirical Bayes. Its offline data must be sampled from the same prior as the online problem. The authors estimate that prior and construct unbiased estimators of the posterior, then develop variants of GP-UCB and probability of improvement. These selection methods use the learned probabilistic information to choose evaluations.

For both variants, the regret bound approaches a constant proportional to observational noise as offline data and online evaluations increase. Thus the stated near-zero guarantee retains a noise-dependent floor rather than promising zero regret under all observation conditions. Experiments on challenging simulated robotic task-and-motion-planning problems verify the approach empirically, connecting the prior-learning framework to a demanding optimization application.
summary.tldr: Learning a Gaussian-process prior from same-prior offline data enables Bayesian optimization regret bounds that approach a noise-proportional constant.

title: Regret bounds for meta Bayesian optimization with an unknown Gaussian process prior

abstract: This paper introduces Non-Autonomous Input-Output Stable Network (NAIS-Net), a very deep architecture where each stacked processing block is derived from a time-invariant non-autonomous dynamical system. Non-autonomy is implemented by skip connections from the block input to each of the unrolled processing stages and allows stability to be enforced so that blocks can be unrolled adaptively to a pattern-dependent processing depth. NAIS-Net induces non-trivial, Lipschitz input-output maps, even for an infinite unroll length. We prove that the network is globally asymptotically stable so that for every initial condition there is exactly one input-dependent equilibrium assuming tanh units, and multiple stable equilibria for ReL units. An efficient implementation that enforces the stability under derived conditions for both fully-connected and convolutional layers is also presented. Experimental results show how NAIS-Net exhibits stability in practice, yielding a significant reduction in generalization gap compared to ResNets.

NAIS-Net induces non-trivial, Lipschitz input-output maps, even for an infinite unroll length. paragraphs: NAIS-Net builds very deep neural networks from processing blocks derived from dynamical systems. Each block repeatedly receives its original input through skip connections to its unrolled stages. This non-autonomous construction allows the authors to enforce stability while adapting the processing depth to the particular input pattern.

The architecture produces nontrivial Lipschitz input-output maps even when a block is unrolled indefinitely. Such maps control how strongly outputs change in response to input changes. The authors prove global asymptotic stability, with exactly one input-dependent equilibrium for every initial condition when tanh units are used. With rectified linear units, the framework allows multiple stable equilibria.

The paper also presents an efficient implementation that enforces the derived stability conditions for fully connected and convolutional layers. Experiments demonstrate stable behavior in practice and a significant reduction in the generalization gap compared with ResNets. The contribution connects architectural design, mathematical stability, and observed generalization behavior, while explicitly distinguishing the equilibrium behavior of the two activation types.
summary.tldr: NAIS-Net uses input-connected dynamical blocks to enforce stability, support adaptive depth, and reduce the observed generalization gap relative to ResNets.

title: NAIS-Net: Stable Deep Networks from Non-Autonomous Differential Equations

abstract: Language encoding models help explain language processing in the human brain by learning functions that predict brain responses from the language stimuli that elicited them. Current word embedding-based approaches treat each stimulus word independently and thus ignore the influence of context on language understanding. In this work we instead build encoding models using rich contextual representations derived from an LSTM language model. Our models show a significant improvement in encoding performance relative to state-of-the-art embeddings in nearly every brain area. By varying the amount of context used in the models and providing the models with distorted context, we show that this improvement is due to a combination of better word embeddings learned by the LSTM language model and contextual information. We are also able to use our models to map context sensitivity across the cortex. These results suggest that LSTM language models learn high-level representations that are related to representations in the human brain.

Models based on independent word embeddings leave out how surrounding language changes a word's interpretation. This paper instead uses contextual representations from an LSTM language model to build predictors of brain responses, allowing the representation of a stimulus to incorporate its context.

The authors report significantly improved encoding performance relative to state-of-the-art embeddings in nearly every brain area. They investigate the source of this improvement by changing how much context the models receive and by distorting that context. These comparisons attribute the gains to both improved word embeddings learned by the LSTM and the contextual information it supplies.

The models also allow the authors to map sensitivity to context across the cortex. Together, the results suggest a relationship between the high-level representations learned by LSTM language models and representations in the human brain. That conclusion is a suggested correspondence grounded in predictive performance and context manipulations, preserving the exploratory strength of the paper's interpretation.
summary.tldr: LSTM-derived contextual language representations improve brain-response prediction and help map cortical sensitivity to context.

title: Incorporating Context into Language Encoding Models for fMRI

abstract: A limitation of Lasso-type estimators is that the optimal regularization parameter depends on the unknown noise level. Estimators such as the concomitant Lasso address this dependence by jointly estimating the noise level and the regression coefficients. Additionally, in many applications, the data is obtained by averaging multiple measurements: this reduces the noise variance, but it dramatically reduces sample sizes and prevents refined noise modeling. In this work, we propose a concomitant estimator that can cope with complex noise structure by using non-averaged measurements, its data-fitting term arising as a smoothing of the nuclear norm. The resulting optimization problem is convex and amenable, thanks to smoothing theory, to state-of-the-art optimization techniques that leverage the sparsity of the solutions. Practical benefits are demonstrated on toy datasets, realistic simulated data and real neuroimaging data.

paragraphs: Lasso-type regression methods face a tuning problem: the best regularization strength depends on an unknown noise level. Concomitant estimators address this by estimating noise and regression coefficients together. This paper also considers repeated measurements, which are often averaged to reduce noise variance but thereby lose sample size and information needed for more detailed noise modeling.

The proposed estimator works with measurements before averaging and can accommodate complex noise structure. Its data-fitting term comes from smoothing the nuclear norm. This provides a mathematical route to incorporating the available repeated observations while jointly addressing regression and noise estimation.

The resulting optimization problem is convex. Smoothing theory makes it compatible with advanced optimization methods that exploit sparse solutions, connecting the richer noise model to practical computation. The authors demonstrate benefits on toy datasets, realistic simulations, and real neuroimaging data. The contribution is a combination of noise-aware estimation and tractable sparse optimization that preserves information otherwise discarded by averaging, with practical support across the stated experimental settings.
summary.tldr: A convex concomitant estimator uses unaveraged repeated measurements to fit sparse regression models while handling complex noise.

title: Handling correlated and repeated measurements with the smoothed multivariate square-root Lasso

abstract: Learning the probability distribution of high-dimensional data is a challenging problem. To solve this problem, we formulate a deep energy adversarial network (DEAN), which casts the energy model learned from real data into an optimization of a goodness-of-fit (GOF) test statistic. DEAN can be interpreted as a GOF game between two generative networks, where one explicit generative network learns an energy-based distribution that fits the real data, and the other implicit generative network is trained by minimizing a GOF test statistic between the energy-based distribution and the generated data, such that the underlying distribution of the generated data is close to the energy-based distribution. We design a two-level alternative optimization procedure to train the explicit and implicit generative networks, such that the hyper-parameters can also be automatically learned. Experimental results show that DEAN achieves high quality generations compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.

Experimental results show that DEAN achieves high quality generations compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Learning a high-dimensional data distribution involves both describing which observations are plausible and producing new samples that follow that description. This paper introduces a deep energy adversarial network, or DEAN, that assigns these roles to two generative networks. Their interaction is formulated using a goodness-of-fit test statistic.

One network learns an explicit energy-based distribution fitted to real data. The other is an implicit generator that produces samples. It is trained to reduce the goodness-of-fit statistic comparing its generated data with the energy-based distribution, encouraging its output distribution to approach the learned energy model. The test statistic therefore connects distribution learning with sample generation.

The authors train the two networks through a two-level alternating optimization procedure that also allows hyperparameters to be learned automatically. Experiments report high-quality generated samples compared with state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is a coupled framework in which one model learns a target distribution and another learns to sample consistently with it, using statistical goodness of fit to define their relationship.
summary.tldr: DEAN couples an energy-based distribution learner with a sample generator through a goodness-of-fit objective and alternating optimization.

title: Two Generator Game: Learning to Sample via Linear Goodness-of-Fit Test

abstract: The computational cost of training with softmax cross entropy loss grows linearly with the number of classes. For the settings where a large number of classes are involved, a common method to speed up training is to sample a subset of classes and utilize an estimate of the loss gradient based on these classes, known as the sampled softmax method. However, the sampled softmax provides a biased estimate of the gradient unless the samples are drawn from the exact softmax distribution, which is again expensive to compute. Therefore, a widely employed practical approach involves sampling from a simpler distribution in the hope of approximating the exact softmax distribution. In this paper, we develop the first theoretical understanding of the role that different sampling distributions play in determining the quality of sampled softmax. Motivated by our analysis and the work on kernel-based sampling, we propose the Random Fourier Softmax (RF-softmax) method that utilizes the powerful Random Fourier Features to enable more efficient and accurate sampling from an approximate softmax distribution. We show that RF-softmax leads to low bias in estimation in terms of both the full softmax distribution and the full softmax gradient. Furthermore, the cost of RF-softmax scales only logarithmically with the number of classes.

However, the estimate is biased unless classes are sampled from the exact softmax distribution, and computing that distribution recreates the expense that sampling is intended to avoid.

This paper analyzes how the choice of sampling distribution affects the quality of sampled softmax. Guided by that analysis and kernel-based sampling, the authors introduce Random Fourier Softmax. It uses Random Fourier Features to sample efficiently from an approximation to the softmax distribution, aiming to improve the sampling quality without paying for the full distribution.

The authors show low estimation bias relative to both the full softmax distribution and its gradient. They also report that the method's cost scales logarithmically with the number of classes. The contribution links computational savings with an analysis of approximation quality: the proposed sampler seeks a more faithful learning signal while preserving the speed advantage of sampling.
summary.tldr: Random Fourier Softmax provides low-bias approximate softmax sampling with cost that scales logarithmically in the number of classes.

title: Sampled Softmax with Random Fourier Features

abstract: In this paper, we take attempt to incorporate the cyclic mechanism with the vision task of semi-supervised video object segmentation. By resorting to the accurate reference mask of the first frame, we try to mitigate the error propagation problem in most of current video object segmentation pipelines. Firstly, we propose a cyclic scheme for offline training of segmentation networks. Then, we extend the offline pipeline to an online method by introducing a simple gradient correction module while keeping high efficiency as other offline methods. Finally we develop cycle effective receptive field (cycle-ERF) from gradient correction to provide a new perspective for analyzing object-specific regions of interests. We conduct comprehensive experiments on benchmarks of DAVIS17 and Youtube-VOS, demonstrating that our introduced cyclic mechanism is helpful to boost the segmentation quality.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised video object segmentation uses an accurate object mask in the first frame as a reference for segmenting the video. A difficulty is error propagation: mistakes made as the video is processed can affect later segmentation. This paper introduces a cyclic mechanism intended to make better use of that reliable initial mask and reduce the propagation of errors.

The authors first incorporate the cyclic scheme into offline training of segmentation networks. They then extend the pipeline to an online method using a simple gradient correction module. The abstract reports that this extension maintains efficiency comparable to offline methods, making correction during video processing compatible with the approach's efficiency goals.

The gradient correction mechanism also motivates cycle effective receptive field, or cycle-ERF, a way to analyze regions of interest associated with particular objects. Thus, the cyclic idea serves both segmentation and analysis of object-specific regions. Experiments on DAVIS17 and YouTube-VOS show improved segmentation quality from adding the mechanism. The reported evidence supports its usefulness for the stated task, where an accurate first-frame mask provides the reference.
summary.tldr: A cyclic segmentation mechanism uses the first-frame reference mask to improve video object segmentation, with an efficient online correction extension.

title: Delving into the Cyclic Mechanism in Semi-supervised Video Object Segmentation

abstract: Previous literature offers limited clues on how to learn a periodic function using modern neural networks. We start with a study of the extrapolation properties of neural networks; we prove and demonstrate experimentally that the standard activations functions, such as ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, along with their variants, all fail to learn to extrapolate simple periodic functions. We hypothesize that this is due to their lack of a ``periodic" inductive bias. As a fix of this problem, we propose a new activation, namely, $x + \sin^2(x)$, which achieves the desired periodic inductive bias to learn a periodic function while maintaining a favorable optimization property of the $\relu$-based activations. Experimentally, we apply the proposed method to temperature and financial data prediction.

As a fix of this problem, we propose a new activation, namely, $x + \sin^2(x)$, which achieves the desired periodic inductive bias to learn a periodic function while maintaining a favorable optimization property of the $\relu$-based activations. paragraphs: Learning a repeating pattern involves more than matching observations within the training range. A model must also continue the repetition when asked to predict beyond that range. This paper studies that extrapolation problem and examines why neural networks with commonly used activation functions struggle with simple periodic functions.

The authors provide proofs and experiments showing failures of periodic extrapolation for ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, and their variants. They hypothesize that these failures arise because the activations lack a periodic inductive bias: their structure does not encourage continuation of a repeating pattern. That explanation is presented as a hypothesis motivating the proposed modification.

The proposed activation is x + sin²(x), which combines a linear term with a repeating component. The authors describe it as providing the desired periodic bias while retaining a favorable optimization property associated with ReLU-based activations. They apply the method experimentally to temperature and financial prediction. The contribution connects extrapolation behavior to activation design and supplies a concrete architectural change intended to make periodic structure easier to learn.
summary.tldr: The paper studies failures of periodic extrapolation and proposes x + sin²(x) as an activation with a periodic inductive bias.

title: Neural Networks Fail to Learn Periodic Functions and How to Fix It

abstract: Understanding the relationships between biomedical terms like viruses, drugs, and symptoms is essential in the fight against diseases. Many attempts have been made to introduce the use of machine learning to the scientific process of hypothesis generation (HG), which refers to the discovery of meaningful implicit connections between biomedical terms. However, most existing methods fail to truly capture the temporal dynamics of scientific term relations and also assume unobserved connections to be irrelevant (i.e., in a positive-negative (PN) learning setting). To break these limits, we formulate this HG problem as future connectivity prediction task on a dynamic attributed graph via positive-unlabeled (PU) learning. Then, the key is to capture the temporal evolution of node pair (term pair) relations from just the positive and unlabeled data. We propose a variational inference model to estimate the positive prior, and incorporate it in the learning of node pair embeddings, which are then used for link prediction. Experiment results on real-world biomedical term relationship datasets and case study analyses on a COVID-19 dataset validate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

paragraphs: Biomedical hypothesis generation looks for meaningful connections among terms such as drugs, viruses, and symptoms. This paper treats that process as predicting future connections in a changing graph. Two issues motivate the formulation: relationships evolve over time, and an unobserved relationship should not automatically be treated as irrelevant.

The method uses positive-unlabeled learning, separating established connections from connections whose status is unknown. A variational inference model estimates the positive prior, which describes the prevalence of positive relationships. That estimate is incorporated into learning representations of term pairs, with those representations then used to predict links.

The design connects uncertainty about unobserved relationships with the temporal evolution of term-pair relations. It therefore gives the prediction task a way to use known links without declaring every missing link negative. Experiments on real biomedical relationship datasets and case studies using a COVID-19 dataset support the model's effectiveness. These findings concern generating promising future connections through link prediction, the hypothesis-generation task the paper sets out to address.
summary.tldr: The method predicts future biomedical connections by modeling changing term relationships while treating missing links as unlabeled.

title: Temporal Positive-unlabeled Learning for Biomedical Hypothesis Generation via Risk Estimation

abstract: Saliency methods are used extensively to highlight the importance of input features in model predictions. These methods are mostly used in vision and language tasks, and their applications to time series data is relatively unexplored. In this paper, we set out to extensively compare the performance of various saliency-based interpretability methods across diverse neural architectures, including Recurrent Neural Network, Temporal Convolutional Networks, and Transformers in a new benchmark of synthetic time series data. We propose and report multiple metrics to empirically evaluate the performance of saliency methods for detecting feature importance over time using both precision (i.e., whether identified features contain meaningful signals) and recall (i.e., the number of features with signal identified as important). Through several experiments, we show that (i) in general, network architectures and saliency methods fail to reliably and accurately identify feature importance over time in time series data, (ii) this failure is mainly due to the conflation of time and feature domains, and (iii) the quality of saliency maps can be improved substantially by using our proposed two-step temporal saliency rescaling (TSR) approach that first calculates the importance of each time step before calculating the importance of each feature at a time step.

paragraphs: Saliency methods highlight which inputs matter to a model's prediction, but time series introduce two connected questions: which moments matter, and which features matter at those moments. This paper develops a synthetic time-series benchmark to assess how well saliency methods answer those questions across recurrent networks, temporal convolutional networks, and Transformers.

The evaluation uses multiple metrics covering precision and recall. Precision asks whether highlighted inputs actually contain meaningful signal; recall asks how much of the meaningful signal was identified. Across the experiments, the authors find that the tested architectures and saliency methods generally do not recover feature importance over time reliably or accurately.

The authors identify the mixing of time importance and feature importance as the main source of this failure. They propose temporal saliency rescaling, a two-stage procedure that first estimates the importance of each time step and then estimates feature importance within it. Reported improvements show that explicitly separating these questions can substantially improve saliency maps in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: A time-series benchmark reveals unreliable saliency maps and shows that separating time-step importance from feature importance can substantially improve them.

title: Benchmarking Deep Learning Interpretability in Time Series Predictions

abstract: In distributed second order optimization, a standard strategy is to average many local estimates, each of which is based on a small sketch or batch of the data. However, the local estimates on each machine are typically biased, relative to the full solution on all of the data, and this can limit the effectiveness of averaging. Here, we introduce a new technique for debiasing the local estimates, which leads to both theoretical and empirical improvements in the convergence rate of distributed second order methods. Our technique has two novel components: (1) modifying standard sketching techniques to obtain what we call a surrogate sketch; and (2) carefully scaling the global regularization parameter for local computations. Our surrogate sketches are based on determinantal point processes, a family of distributions for which the bias of an estimate of the inverse Hessian can be computed exactly. Based on this computation, we show that when the objective being minimized is $l_2$-regularized with parameter $\lambda$ and individual machines are each given a sketch of size $m$, then to eliminate the bias, local estimates should be computed using a shrunk regularization parameter given by $\lambda^\prime=\lambda(1-\frac{d_\lambda}{m})$, where $d_\lambda$ is the $\lambda$-effective dimension of the Hessian (or, for quadratic problems, the data matrix).

paragraphs: Distributed second-order optimization often combines estimates computed by separate machines from small data sketches or batches. Averaging these estimates can be less effective when each is systematically biased relative to the full-data solution. This paper addresses that bias directly, aiming to improve how quickly distributed optimization converges.

The method combines modified data sketches, called surrogate sketches, with a carefully adjusted regularization strength for local computations. The sketches use determinantal point processes, which allow the bias of an inverse-Hessian estimate to be calculated exactly. That calculation provides a principled basis for correcting local estimates before they are combined.

For an objective with l2 regularization strength lambda and local sketch size m, the derived local strength is lambda times one minus d_lambda divided by m. Here, d_lambda is the effective dimension of the Hessian, or of the data matrix for quadratic problems. The authors show that this adjustment eliminates bias in their formulation and report both theoretical and empirical improvements in convergence rates.
summary.tldr: Surrogate sketches and reduced local regularization remove estimation bias in the proposed formulation and improve distributed second-order convergence.

title: Debiasing Distributed Second Order Optimization with Surrogate Sketching and Scaled Regularization

abstract: Decentralized optimization has wide applications in machine learning, signal processing, and control. In this paper, we study the decentralized composite optimization problem with a non-smooth regularization term. Many proximal gradient based decentralized algorithms have been proposed in the past. However, these algorithms do not achieve near optimal computational complexity and communication complexity. In this paper, we propose a new method which establishes the optimal computational complexity and a near optimal communication complexity. Our empirical study shows that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

In this paper, we study the decentralized composite optimization problem with a non-smooth regularization term. Many proximal gradient based decentralized algorithms have been proposed in the past. However, these algorithms do not achieve near optimal computational complexity and communication complexity. In this paper, we propose a new method which establishes the optimal computational complexity and a near optimal communication complexity. Our empirical study shows that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies decentralized composite optimization, where a network must solve an optimization problem that includes a nonsmooth regularization term. The setting is relevant to machine learning, signal processing, and control. The regularization component is part of the problem the algorithm must handle, rather than something excluded to simplify the objective.

The authors focus on two separate measures of efficiency: computational complexity and communication complexity. These capture the work required to perform optimization and the exchanges required between network participants. Earlier decentralized methods based on proximal gradients did not achieve near-optimal complexity on both measures, motivating a method that improves their joint efficiency.

The proposed algorithm establishes optimal computational complexity and near-optimal communication complexity for the studied problem. That distinction is part of the result: the communication guarantee is near optimal, while the computation guarantee is optimal. An empirical study also reports better performance than existing leading algorithms. The contribution combines these theoretical efficiency guarantees with experimental evidence that the approach is useful in practice.
summary.tldr: A decentralized method handles nonsmooth regularization with optimal computational complexity and near-optimal communication complexity.

title: Decentralized Accelerated Proximal Gradient Descent

abstract: Parametric stochastic simulators are ubiquitous in science, often featuring high-dimensional input parameters and/or an intractable likelihood. Performing Bayesian parameter inference in this context can be challenging. We present a neural simulation-based inference algorithm which simultaneously offers simulation efficiency and fast empirical posterior testability, which is unique among modern algorithms. Our approach is simulation efficient by simultaneously estimating low-dimensional marginal posteriors instead of the joint posterior and by proposing simulations targeted to an observation of interest via a prior suitably truncated by an indicator function. Furthermore, by estimating a locally amortized posterior our algorithm enables efficient empirical tests of the robustness of the inference results. Since scientists cannot access the ground truth, these tests are necessary for trusting inference in real-world applications. We perform experiments on a marginalized version of the simulation-based inference benchmark and two complex and narrow posteriors, highlighting the simulator efficiency of our algorithm as well as the quality of the estimated marginal posteriors.

paragraphs: Scientific simulators can generate observations from parameters even when their likelihood is intractable, making Bayesian inference difficult. This paper introduces a neural simulation-based inference method designed to use simulations efficiently while allowing fast empirical checks of the resulting posterior estimates. It addresses both computational cost and the need to assess inference reliability.

The algorithm simultaneously estimates low-dimensional marginal posteriors instead of the full joint posterior. It also targets simulations toward an observation of interest by truncating the prior with an indicator function. These choices focus the estimation effort on selected parameter distributions and restrict where simulations are proposed.

The method estimates a locally amortized posterior, enabling efficient empirical tests of robustness rather than requiring access to the unknown real-world ground truth. Experiments use a marginalized version of a simulation-based inference benchmark and two complex, narrow posteriors. They highlight simulation efficiency and the quality of the estimated marginals. The contribution brings targeted inference and practical posterior checking into the same algorithm.
summary.tldr: Truncated marginal neural ratio estimation targets simulations and learns low-dimensional posteriors while supporting efficient empirical checks of inference robustness.

title: Truncated Marginal Neural Ratio Estimation

abstract: 3D pose transfer is one of the most challenging 3D generation tasks. It aims to transfer the pose of a source mesh to a target mesh and keep the identity (e.g., body shape) of the target mesh. Some previous works require key point annotations to build reliable correspondence between the source and target meshes, while other methods do not consider any shape correspondence between sources and targets, which leads to limited generation quality. In this work, we propose a correspondence-refinement network to achieve the 3D pose transfer for both human and animal meshes. The correspondence between source and target meshes is first established by solving an optimal transport problem. Then, we warp the source mesh according to the dense correspondence and obtain a coarse warped mesh. The warped mesh will be better refined with our proposed Elastic Instance Normalization, which is a conditional normalization layer and can help to generate high-quality meshes. Extensive experimental results show that the proposed architecture can effectively transfer the poses from source to target meshes and produce better results with satisfied visual performance than state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Pose transfer asks a system to give one three-dimensional mesh the posture of another while preserving the target's identity, such as its body shape. The difficult part is deciding which parts of the two meshes correspond. The paper addresses this with a network that explicitly learns correspondence and then refines the resulting geometry, for both human and animal meshes.

First, the method solves an optimal transport problem to establish dense matches between the source and target. It uses those matches to warp the source into a coarse mesh. A subsequent refinement stage uses Elastic Instance Normalization, a proposed conditional normalization layer, to improve the generated mesh. This separates establishing the geometric relationship from improving the initial warped result.

The reported experiments show effective pose transfer and better visual results than the state-of-the-art methods considered. The contribution is therefore a connected pipeline: correspondence supplies a structured starting point, while refinement improves its quality. The findings support this architecture for the evaluated human and animal meshes.
summary.tldr: A correspondence-and-refinement network transfers poses between human or animal meshes while preserving the target's shape.

title: 3D Pose Transfer with Correspondence Learning and Mesh Refinement

abstract: Recent work argues that robust training requires substantially larger datasets than those required for standard classification. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, this translates into a sizable robust-accuracy gap between models trained solely on data from the original training set and those trained with additional data extracted from the "80 Million Tiny Images" dataset (TI-80M). In this paper, we explore how generative models trained solely on the original training set can be leveraged to artificially increase the size of the original training set and improve adversarial robustness to $\ell_p$ norm-bounded perturbations. We identify the sufficient conditions under which incorporating additional generated data can improve robustness, and demonstrate that it is possible to significantly reduce the robust-accuracy gap to models trained with additional real data. Surprisingly, we even show that even the addition of non-realistic random data (generated by Gaussian sampling) can improve robustness. We evaluate our approach on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and TinyImageNet against $\ell_\infty$ and $\ell_2$ norm-bounded perturbations of size $\epsilon = 8/255$ and $\epsilon = 128/255$, respectively. We show large absolute improvements in robust accuracy compared to previous state-of-the-art methods. Against $\ell_\infty$ norm-bounded perturbations of size $\epsilon = 8/255$, our models achieve 66.10% and 33.49% robust accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, respectively (improving upon the state-of-the-art by +8.96% and +3.29%). Against $\ell_2$ norm-bounded perturbations of size $\epsilon = 128/255$, our model achieves 78.31% on CIFAR-10 (+3.81%). These results beat most prior works that use external data.

paragraphs: Training classifiers to resist adversarial perturbations can demand substantially more data than ordinary classification. This paper investigates whether synthetic examples can help when the generative model itself is trained only on the original training set. The aim is to improve robustness without relying on the additional external images used by many competing approaches.

The authors identify sufficient conditions under which adding generated data can improve robustness. Their experiments show that synthetic augmentation can substantially narrow the robust-accuracy gap to models using extra real data. They also find that Gaussian-generated random examples can help despite looking unrealistic, showing that visual realism is not required for every beneficial addition in the studied settings.

Evaluations cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and TinyImageNet under bounded perturbations. At an infinity-norm radius of 8/255, reported robust accuracy reaches 66.10% on CIFAR-10 and 33.49% on CIFAR-100. At a Euclidean-norm radius of 128/255, it reaches 78.31% on CIFAR-10. The results improve on the cited state of the art and exceed most prior work using external data.
summary.tldr: Synthetic data generated from the original training set can substantially improve adversarial robustness, with benefits even from Gaussian random examples in the studied settings.

title: Improving Robustness using Generated Data

abstract: We present SegFormer, a simple, efficient yet powerful semantic segmentation framework which unifies Transformers with lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) decoders. SegFormer has two appealing features: 1) SegFormer comprises a novel hierarchically structured Transformer encoder which outputs multiscale features. It does not need positional encoding, thereby avoiding the interpolation of positional codes which leads to decreased performance when the testing resolution differs from training. 2) SegFormer avoids complex decoders. The proposed MLP decoder aggregates information from different layers, and thus combining both local attention and global attention to render powerful representations. We show that this simple and lightweight design is the key to efficient segmentation on Transformers. We scale our approach up to obtain a series of models from SegFormer-B0 to Segformer-B5, which reaches much better performance and efficiency than previous counterparts.For example, SegFormer-B4 achieves 50.3% mIoU on ADE20K with 64M parameters, being 5x smaller and 2.2% better than the previous best method. Our best model, SegFormer-B5, achieves 84.0% mIoU on Cityscapes validation set and shows excellent zero-shot robustness on Cityscapes-C.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image pixel. SegFormer combines a hierarchical transformer encoder with a lightweight multilayer-perceptron decoder. The encoder produces features at multiple scales, while the decoder aggregates information across layers to bring local and global attention together in the final representation.

The encoder does not require positional encoding. This avoids interpolating positional codes when test images have a different resolution from training images, a process the paper associates with reduced performance. The lightweight decoder is the other main design choice: the authors attribute efficient transformer segmentation to this combination of multiscale encoding and simple aggregation.

The model family ranges from B0 to B5. On ADE20K, B4 achieves 50.3% mean intersection-over-union with 64 million parameters, reported as five times smaller and 2.2% better than the previous best method. B5 reaches 84.0% on Cityscapes validation and shows strong zero-shot robustness on Cityscapes-C. These results support the reported performance-efficiency gains of the architecture, alongside evidence of robustness in the stated evaluation.
summary.tldr: SegFormer pairs multiscale transformer features with a lightweight decoder to achieve strong reported segmentation accuracy, efficiency, and robustness.

title: SegFormer: Simple and Efficient Design for Semantic Segmentation with Transformers

abstract: Recent progress in model selection raises the question of the fundamental limits of these techniques. Under specific scrutiny has been model selection for general contextual bandits with nested policy classes, resulting in a COLT2020 open problem. It asks whether it is possible to obtain simultaneously the optimal single algorithm guarantees over all policies in a nested sequence of policy classes, or if otherwise this is possible for a trade-off $\alpha\in[\frac{1}{2},1)$ between complexity term and time: $\ln(|\Pi_m|)^{1-\alpha}T^\alpha$. We give a disappointing answer to this question. Even in the purely stochastic regime, the desired results are unobtainable. We present a Pareto frontier of up to logarithmic factors matching upper and lower bounds, thereby proving that an increase in the complexity term $\ln(|\Pi_m|)$ independent of $T$ is unavoidable for general policy classes.As a side result, we also resolve a COLT2016 open problem concerning second-order bounds in full-information games.

It asks whether it is possible to obtain simultaneously the optimal single algorithm guarantees over all policies in a nested sequence of policy classes, or if otherwise this is possible for a trade-off $\alpha\in[\frac{1}{2},1)$ between complexity term and time: $\ln(|\Pi_m|)^{1-\alpha}T^\alpha$. We give a disappointing answer to this question. Even in the purely stochastic regime, the desired results are unobtainable. paragraphs: Model selection for contextual bandits asks whether one learning algorithm can adapt to policy classes of different complexity. This paper considers nested classes and asks whether an algorithm can simultaneously achieve the optimal guarantees available for each class. It also examines a proposed tradeoff involving log(|Pi_m|)^(1-alpha) T^alpha, for alpha between one-half and one.

The authors show that these desired guarantees are unattainable for general policy classes, even when the environment is purely stochastic. They characterize the achievable compromises through a Pareto frontier, providing upper and lower bounds that match up to logarithmic factors. This identifies both attainable performance and barriers that no algorithm can avoid in the studied setting.

A central consequence is that an increase in the policy-class complexity term, independent of the time horizon T, is unavoidable. Adaptation therefore carries a cost beyond the proposed tradeoff. The negative result concerns general classes, preserving the scope of the impossibility claim. As an additional contribution, the paper resolves an open problem about second-order bounds in full-information games, extending its theoretical findings beyond contextual-bandit model selection.
summary.tldr: Matching upper and lower bounds show unavoidable complexity costs when adapting across general nested policy classes in contextual bandits.

title: The Pareto Frontier of model selection for general Contextual Bandits

abstract: It is difficult to use subsampling with variational inference in hierarchical models since the number of local latent variables scales with the dataset. Thus, inference in hierarchical models remains a challenge at a large scale. It is helpful to use a variational family with a structure matching the posterior, but optimization is still slow due to the huge number of local distributions. Instead, this paper suggests an amortized approach where shared parameters simultaneously represent all local distributions. This approach is similarly accurate as using a given joint distribution (e.g., a full-rank Gaussian) but is feasible on datasets that are several orders of magnitude larger. It is also dramatically faster than using a structured variational distribution.

Thus, inference in hierarchical models remains a challenge at a large scale. It is helpful to use a variational family with a structure matching the posterior, but optimization is still slow due to the huge number of local distributions. Instead, this paper suggests an amortized approach where shared parameters simultaneously represent all local distributions. paragraphs: Hierarchical models can contain local hidden variables whose number grows with the dataset. Variational inference approximates uncertainty about these variables using distributions that must be optimized. Even when the approximation has a structure well matched to the posterior, the growing collection of local distributions makes optimization expensive and complicates the use of data subsampling.

This paper proposes sharing parameters across those local distributions through an amortized approach. Instead of treating every local approximation as a separate optimization burden, a common parameterization represents them together. The approach directly targets the scaling problem caused by increasing numbers of local latent variables while retaining the goal of an accurate distributional approximation.

The authors report accuracy similar to that obtained with a given joint approximation, such as a full-rank Gaussian, while handling datasets several orders of magnitude larger. They also report a substantial speed advantage over structured variational inference. The contribution therefore concerns making comparable approximate inference computationally feasible at much larger scales in the hierarchical models studied.
summary.tldr: Sharing parameters across local variational distributions makes inference in simple hierarchical models much faster and more scalable while retaining similar accuracy.

title: Amortized Variational Inference for Simple Hierarchical Models

abstract: Error correction techniques have been used to refine the output sentences from automatic speech recognition (ASR) models and achieve a lower word error rate (WER) than original ASR outputs. Previous works usually use a sequence-to-sequence model to correct an ASR output sentence autoregressively, which causes large latency and cannot be deployed in online ASR services. A straightforward solution to reduce latency, inspired by non-autoregressive (NAR) neural machine translation, is to use an NAR sequence generation model for ASR error correction, which, however, comes at the cost of significantly increased ASR error rate. In this paper, observing distinctive error patterns and correction operations (i.e., insertion, deletion, and substitution) in ASR, we propose FastCorrect, a novel NAR error correction model based on edit alignment. In training, FastCorrect aligns each source token from an ASR output sentence to the target tokens from the corresponding ground-truth sentence based on the edit distance between the source and target sentences, and extracts the number of target tokens corresponding to each source token during edition/correction, which is then used to train a length predictor and to adjust the source tokens to match the length of the target sentence for parallel generation. In inference, the token number predicted by the length predictor is used to adjust the source tokens for target sequence generation. Experiments on the public AISHELL-1 dataset and an internal industrial-scale ASR dataset show the effectiveness of FastCorrect for ASR error correction: 1) it speeds up the inference by 6-9 times and maintains the accuracy (8-14% WER reduction) compared with the autoregressive correction model; and 2) it outperforms the popular NAR models adopted in neural machine translation and text edition by a large margin.

paragraphs: Speech recognition output can be improved by a second model that corrects its text. Producing corrections one token at a time adds substantial latency, while straightforward parallel generation can sacrifice accuracy. FastCorrect addresses this tradeoff by organizing parallel correction around the insertion, deletion, and substitution patterns found in recognition errors.

From that alignment, FastCorrect extracts how many target tokens correspond to each source token. title: FastCorrect: Fast Error Correction with Edit Alignment for Automatic Speech Recognition

abstract: Mainstream approaches for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) learn domain-invariant representations to narrow the domain shift, which are empirically effective but theoretically challenged by the hardness or impossibility theorems. Recently, self-training has been gaining momentum in UDA, which exploits unlabeled target data by training with target pseudo-labels. However, as corroborated in this work, under distributional shift, the pseudo-labels can be unreliable in terms of their large discrepancy from target ground truth. In this paper, we propose Cycle Self-Training (CST), a principled self-training algorithm that explicitly enforces pseudo-labels to generalize across domains. CST cycles between a forward step and a reverse step until convergence. In the forward step, CST generates target pseudo-labels with a source-trained classifier. In the reverse step, CST trains a target classifier using target pseudo-labels, and then updates the shared representations to make the target classifier perform well on the source data. We introduce the Tsallis entropy as a confidence-friendly regularization to improve the quality of target pseudo-labels. We analyze CST theoretically under realistic assumptions, and provide hard cases where CST recovers target ground truth, while both invariant feature learning and vanilla self-training fail. Empirical results indicate that CST significantly improves over the state-of-the-arts on visual recognition and sentiment analysis benchmarks.

paragraphs: Self-training adapts a model to unlabeled target data by treating its predictions as training labels. Under distribution shift, however, those pseudo-labels can disagree substantially with the true target labels. Cycle Self-Training addresses this problem by explicitly encouraging the information learned from target pseudo-labels to generalize back across domains.

The algorithm alternates forward and reverse steps until convergence. First, a classifier trained on source data produces target pseudo-labels. Next, a target classifier learns from those labels, and the shared representation is updated so that this target classifier performs well on source data. Tsallis entropy supplies an additional regularizer intended to improve pseudo-label quality while accommodating confident predictions.

The paper analyzes the method under stated assumptions and constructs difficult cases where it recovers target ground truth while invariant representation learning and ordinary self-training fail. Those cases establish a meaningful distinction without implying universal recovery. Experiments on visual recognition and sentiment analysis benchmarks report significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods.
summary.tldr: Cycle Self-Training improves domain adaptation by requiring learning from target pseudo-labels to transfer back successfully to source data.

title: Cycle Self-Training for Domain Adaptation

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation which aims to adapt models trained on a labeled source domain to a completely unlabeled target domain has attracted much attention in recent years. While many domain adaptation techniques have been proposed for images, the problem of unsupervised domain adaptation in videos remains largely underexplored. In this paper, we introduce Contrast and Mix (CoMix), a new contrastive learning framework that aims to learn discriminative invariant feature representations for unsupervised video domain adaptation. First, unlike existing methods that rely on adversarial learning for feature alignment, we utilize temporal contrastive learning to bridge the domain gap by maximizing the similarity between encoded representations of an unlabeled video at two different speeds as well as minimizing the similarity between different videos played at different speeds. Second, we propose a novel extension to the temporal contrastive loss by using background mixing that allows additional positives per anchor, thus adapting contrastive learning to leverage action semantics shared across both domains. Moreover, we also integrate a supervised contrastive learning objective using target pseudo-labels to enhance discriminability of the latent space for video domain adaptation. Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach over state-of-the-art methods. Project page: https://cvir.github.io/projects/comix.

paragraphs: CoMix addresses video recognition when labels are available in a source domain but entirely absent in the target domain. The goal is to learn features that still distinguish actions while remaining useful across this change in data. The paper brings temporal information into this adaptation problem through contrastive learning.

Its first objective pulls together representations of the same unlabeled video played at different speeds and pushes apart representations of different videos played at different speeds. Background mixing supplies additional positive examples for the contrastive objective, helping it use action semantics shared between domains. These components encourage the representation to connect related action content despite changes in playback speed or background.

The framework also uses target pseudo-labels in a supervised contrastive objective. These are model-provided labels, allowing target videos to contribute to learning a more discriminative feature space despite the absence of target annotations. Experiments on several benchmark datasets show improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The reported results support combining temporal consistency, background mixing, and pseudo-label supervision for unsupervised video adaptation.
summary.tldr: CoMix combines playback-speed contrast, background mixing, and target pseudo-labels to improve video adaptation without target-domain annotations.

title: Contrast and Mix: Temporal Contrastive Video Domain Adaptation with Background Mixing

abstract: It is well known that vision classification models suffer from poor calibration in the face of data distribution shifts. In this paper, we take a geometric approach to this problem. We propose Geometric Sensitivity Decomposition (GSD) which decomposes the norm of a sample feature embedding and the angular similarity to a target classifier into an instance-dependent and an instance-independent com-ponent. The instance-dependent component captures the sensitive information about changes in the input while the instance-independent component represents the insensitive information serving solely to minimize the loss on the training dataset. Inspired by the decomposition, we analytically derive a simple extension to current softmax-linear models, which learns to disentangle the two components during training. On several common vision models, the disentangled model out-performs other calibration methods on standard calibration metrics in the face of out-of-distribution (OOD) data and corruption with significantly less complexity. Specifically, we surpass the current state of the art by 30.8% relative improvement on corrupted CIFAR100 in Expected Calibration Error.

paragraphs: A classifier's confidence can become unreliable when images differ from its training data. This paper studies that calibration problem through the geometry of the model's internal features. It asks how the size of a feature representation and its angular alignment with a classifier contribute to confidence when inputs change.

The proposed Geometric Sensitivity Decomposition separates these geometric quantities into components that depend on the individual input and components that do not. The input-dependent part captures information sensitive to changes in the image. The other part serves to reduce training loss without representing that sensitivity. From this decomposition, the authors derive a simple extension of softmax-linear models that learns to separate the two components during training.

Across several vision models, the resulting approach improves standard calibration measurements under distribution shifts and image corruption, with lower complexity than comparison methods. On corrupted CIFAR100, it reports a 30.8% relative improvement in Expected Calibration Error over the previous state of the art. The findings connect confidence reliability to how models organize their feature geometry.
summary.tldr: Separating input-sensitive and input-insensitive feature geometry improves neural confidence calibration under distribution shifts and corruption.

title: A Geometric Perspective towards Neural Calibration via Sensitivity Decomposition

abstract: Popular feature importance techniques compute additive approximations to nonlinear models by first defining a cooperative game describing the value of different subsets of the model's features, then calculating the resulting game's Shapley values to attribute credit additively between the features. However, the specific modeling settings in which the Shapley values are a poor approximation for the true game have not been well-described. In this paper we utilize an interpretation of Shapley values as the result of an orthogonal projection between vector spaces to calculate a residual representing the kernel component of that projection. We provide an algorithm for computing these residuals, characterize different modeling settings based on the value of the residuals, and demonstrate that they capture information about model predictions that Shapley values cannot. Shapley residuals can thus act as a warning to practitioners against overestimating the degree to which Shapley-value-based explanations give them insight into a model.
