paragraphs: This paper considers minimizing a Lipschitz convex function when gradient information is noisy. Its key assumption concerns the shape of that noise: errors are bounded with high probability in every direction. The authors call this isotropic noise and investigate how this directional control can improve optimization complexity.

They develop an algorithm that improves on prior results by a factor equal to the dimension d in certain regimes. A consequence is a new state-of-the-art complexity for sub-exponential noise. Matching lower bounds, up to polylogarithmic factors, show that both results are close to the achievable limits under the analyzed conditions. The dimensional improvement is therefore tied to a specified noise setting and parameter regimes.

The paper also introduces a quantum isotropifier. This algorithm takes a quantum sampling oracle with bounded variance and converts it into one producing unbiased estimates with isotropic error. Combining that conversion with the optimization results yields improved dimension-dependent rates for quantum stochastic convex optimization. The quantum contribution makes the useful noise structure available from a different starting guarantee.
summary.tldr: Directional control of gradient noise enables near-optimal convex optimization improvements, with a quantum procedure extending the benefits to quantum sampling.

title: Isotropic Noise in Stochastic and Quantum Convex Optimization

abstract: Combinatorial problems on graphs have attracted extensive efforts from the machine learning community over the past decade. Despite notable progress in this area under the umbrella of ML4CO, a comprehensive categorization, unified reproducibility, and transparent evaluation protocols are still lacking for the emerging and immense pool of neural CO solvers. In this paper, we establish a modular and streamlined framework benchmarking prevalent neural CO methods, dissecting their design choices via a tri-leveled "paradigm-model-learning'' taxonomy to better characterize different approaches. Further, we integrate their shared features and respective strengths to form 3 unified solvers representing global prediction (GP), local construction (LC), and adaptive expansion (AE) mannered neural solvers. We also collate a total of 65 datasets for 7 mainstream CO problems (including both edge-oriented tasks: TSP, ATSP, CVRP, as well as node-oriented: MIS, MCl, MVC, MCut) across scales to facilitate more comparable results among literature. Extensive experiments upon our benchmark reveal a fair and exact performance exhibition indicative of the raw contribution of the learning components in each method, rethinking and insisting that pre- and post-inference heuristic tricks are not supposed to compensate for sub-par capability of the data-driven counterparts. Under this unified benchmark, an up-to-date replication of typical ML4CO methods is maintained, hoping to provide convenient reference and insightful guidelines for both engineering development and academic exploration of the ML4CO community in the future. Code is available at https://github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/ML4CO-Bench-101, and the dataset is at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ML4CO/ML4CO-Bench-101-SL.

paragraphs: Neural methods for graph-based combinatorial optimization have proliferated, making their results difficult to compare consistently. This paper builds a common benchmarking framework to clarify how these solvers differ and what their learned components actually contribute. It organizes methods at three levels: their overall paradigm, model design, and learning approach.

The framework also consolidates shared features into three unified solvers representing global prediction, local construction, and adaptive expansion. These provide common implementations for examining different styles of solving a problem. A collection of 65 datasets covers seven optimization problems across multiple scales, including both edge-oriented and node-oriented tasks.

The experiments emphasize separating the contribution of learning from the benefits of heuristics applied before or after model inference. That distinction matters because a strong overall solver result can otherwise obscure a weak learned component. The authors maintain replications of representative methods within the benchmark, aiming to make comparisons more reproducible and transparent. The contribution is both a practical evaluation resource and a clearer basis for attributing progress to particular design choices.
summary.tldr: ML4CO-Bench-101 standardizes neural graph-optimization evaluation to clarify design differences and isolate the contribution of learned components.

title: ML4CO-Bench-101: Benchmark Machine Learning for Classic Combinatorial Problems on Graphs

abstract: Multimodal learning (MML) is significantly constrained by modality imbalance, leading to suboptimal performance in practice. While existing approaches primarily focus on balancing the learning of different modalities to address this issue, they fundamentally overlook the inherent disproportion in model classification ability, which serves as the primary cause of this phenomenon. In this paper, we propose a novel multimodal learning approach to dynamically balance the classification ability of weak and strong modalities by incorporating the principle of boosting. Concretely, we first propose a sustained boosting algorithm in multimodal learning by simultaneously optimizing the classification and residual errors. Subsequently, we introduce an adaptive classifier assignment strategy to dynamically facilitate the classification performance of the weak modality. Furthermore, we theoretically analyze the convergence property of the cross-modal gap function, ensuring the effectiveness of the proposed boosting scheme. To this end, the classification ability of strong and weak modalities is expected to be balanced, thereby mitigating the imbalance issue. Empirical experiments on widely used datasets reveal the superiority of our method through comparison with various state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal learning baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/njustkmg/NeurIPS25-AUG.

paragraphs: Multimodal systems can become dominated by one strong modality while another contributes little. This paper attributes that imbalance to differences in classification ability, arguing that merely balancing training signals may not fix the underlying disparity.

The proposed sustained boosting procedure jointly optimizes classification and residual errors. An adaptive classifier-assignment strategy then helps the weaker modality improve, making the learning arrangement respond to each modality’s current capabilities.

A convergence analysis of the cross-modal gap supports the boosting mechanism, and experiments outperform several state-of-the-art multimodal baselines. The contribution reframes balancing as a capability-improvement problem: useful cooperation requires the weaker channel to become a better predictor, rather than simply receiving an equal share of optimization effort regardless of what it can currently explain.
summary.tldr: A boosting-based multimodal method strengthens weak modalities by adapting their classifiers and residual learning.

title: Rethinking Multimodal Learning from the Perspective of Mitigating Classification Ability Disproportion

abstract: While there has been significant progress in the field of 3D avatar creation from visual observations, modeling physically plausible dynamics of humans with loose garments remains a challenging problem. Although a few existing works address this problem by leveraging physical simulation, they suffer from limited accuracy or robustness to novel animation inputs. In this work, we present MPMAvatar, a framework for creating 3D human avatars from multi-view videos that supports highly realistic, robust animation, as well as photorealistic rendering from free viewpoints. For accurate and robust dynamics modeling, our key idea is to use a Material Point Method-based simulator, which we carefully tailor to model garments with complex deformations and contact with the underlying body by incorporating an anisotropic constitutive model and a novel collision handling algorithm. We combine this dynamics modeling scheme with our canonical avatar that can be rendered using 3D Gaussian Splatting with quasi-shadowing, enabling high-fidelity rendering for physically realistic animations. In our experiments, we demonstrate that MPMAvatar significantly outperforms the existing state-of-the-art physics-based avatar in terms of (1) dynamics modeling accuracy, (2) rendering accuracy, and (3) robustness and efficiency. Additionally, we present a novel application in which our avatar generalizes to unseen interactions in a zero-shot manner—which was not achievable with previous learning-based methods due to their limited simulation generalizability. Our code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: MPMAvatar builds human avatars from multi-view videos, focusing on the difficult dynamics of loose clothing. An avatar must capture how garments deform and contact the body while also rendering convincingly from different viewpoints. The paper addresses limitations in the accuracy of existing physical simulations and their robustness to new animation inputs.

Its central component is a Material Point Method simulator adapted for garments. The simulator includes an anisotropic constitutive model, allowing material behavior to depend on direction, and a new collision-handling algorithm for contact with the body. The authors also demonstrate an application involving unseen interactions without additional training. That result illustrates the value of the simulator's generalization: the avatar can handle interaction conditions beyond those demonstrated during learning in the reported application.
summary.tldr: MPMAvatar combines tailored garment physics with Gaussian rendering to produce accurate, robust human-avatar animations.

title: MPMAvatar: Learning 3D Gaussian Avatars with Accurate and Robust Physics-Based Dynamics

abstract: The scaling law for large language models (LLMs) depicts that the path towards machine intelligence necessitates training at large scale. Thus, companies continuously build large-scale GPU clusters, and launch training jobs that span over thousands of computing nodes. However, LLM pre-training presents unique challenges due to its complex communication patterns, where GPUs exchange data in sparse yet high-volume bursts within specific groups. Inefficient resource scheduling exacerbates bandwidth contention, leading to suboptimal training performance. This paper presents Arnold, a scheduling system summarizing our experience to effectively align LLM communication patterns to data center topology at scale. In-depth characteristic study is performed to identify the impact of physical network topology to LLM pre-training jobs. Based on the insights, we develop a scheduling algorithm to effectively align communication patterns to physical network topology in data centers. Through simulation experiments, we show the effectiveness of our algorithm in reducing the maximum spread of communication groups by up to $1.67$x. In production training, our scheduling system improves the end-to-end performance by $10.6\%$ when training with more than $9600$ Hopper GPUs, a significant improvement for our training pipeline.

When scheduling places those groups poorly across a data-center network, their traffic can compete for bandwidth and reduce training performance. This paper studies that scheduling problem at large scale.

The authors introduce Arnold, a scheduling system that aligns training communication patterns with physical network topology. They first characterize how the network’s physical organization affects pretraining jobs, then use those observations to design the scheduling algorithm. summary.tldr: Arnold aligns GPU communication groups with data-center topology, improving end-to-end production training performance by 10.6% on more than 9,600 GPUs.

title: Efficient Pre-Training of LLMs via Topology-Aware Communication Alignment on More Than 9600 GPUs

abstract: Recent advances in multimodal Reward Models (RMs) have shown significant promise in delivering reward signals to align vision models with human preferences. However, current RMs are generally restricted to providing direct responses or engaging in shallow reasoning processes with limited depth, often leading to inaccurate reward signals. We posit that incorporating explicit long chains of thought (CoT) into the reward reasoning process can significantly strengthen their reliability and robustness. Furthermore, we believe that once RMs internalize CoT reasoning, their direct response accuracy can also be improved through implicit reasoning capabilities. To this end, this paper proposes UnifiedReward-Think, the first unified multimodal CoT-based reward model, capable of multi-dimensional, step-by-step long-chain reasoning for both visual understanding and generation reward tasks. Specifically, we adopt an exploration-driven reinforcement fine-tuning approach to elicit and incentivize the model's latent complex reasoning ability: (1) We first use a small amount of image generation preference data to distill the reasoning process of GPT-4o, which is then used for the model's cold start to learn the format and structure of CoT reasoning. (2) Subsequently, by leveraging the model's prior knowledge and generalization capabilities, we prepare large-scale unified multimodal preference data to elicit the model's reasoning process across various vision tasks. During this phase, correct reasoning outputs are retained for rejection sampling to refine the model (3) while incorrect predicted samples are finally used for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) based reinforcement fine-tuning, enabling the model to explore diverse reasoning paths and optimize for correct and robust solutions. Extensive experiments confirm that incorporating long CoT reasoning significantly enhances the accuracy of reward signals. Notably, after mastering CoT reasoning, the model exhibits implicit reasoning capabilities, allowing it to surpass existing baselines even without explicit reasoning traces.

paragraphs: Reward models help align vision systems with human preferences, so inaccurate judgments can provide misleading training signals. UnifiedReward-Think investigates whether longer, explicit reasoning improves those judgments. It supports both visual understanding and image-generation evaluation, using step-by-step reasoning across multiple dimensions of a response or output.

The model then reasons over a larger collection of multimodal preference data spanning vision tasks. This stage encourages exploration of alternative reasoning paths.

After this training, the model also exceeds existing baselines when giving answers without explicit reasoning traces. The findings support both the immediate value of explicit reasoning for evaluation and the possibility that learning to reason can improve later direct judgments. The framework thus connects reasoning-focused training with more accurate multimodal feedback.
summary.tldr: UnifiedReward-Think improves multimodal reward accuracy through reasoning-focused training and retains gains even without explicit reasoning traces.

title: Unified Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reward Model through Reinforcement Fine-Tuning

abstract: The physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are widely applied in solving differential equations. However, few studies have discussed their consistency. In this paper, we consider the consistency of PINNs when applied to second-order elliptic equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We first provide the necessary and sufficient condition for the consistency of the physics-informed kernel gradient flow algorithm, and then as a direct corollary, when the neural network is sufficiently wide, we obtain a necessary and sufficient condition for the consistency of PINNs based on the neural tangent kernel theory. We also estimate the non-asymptotic loss bounds of physics-informed kernel gradient flow and PINN under suitable stronger assumptions. Finally, these results inspires us to construct a notable pathological example where the PINN method is inconsistent.

paragraphs: This paper studies the consistency of physics-informed neural networks when solving second-order elliptic equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. The central concern is whether the method reliably approaches the intended solution, rather than simply being usable as a numerical procedure. The boundary conditions and equation class define the setting in which the authors develop their guarantees.

The analysis first establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for consistency of a related physics-informed kernel gradient flow algorithm. Using neural tangent kernel theory, the authors then obtain a corresponding necessary and sufficient condition for PINNs when the network is sufficiently wide. The width requirement matters because it is part of the stated bridge from the kernel analysis to neural network training.

Under stronger assumptions, the paper also provides non-asymptotic loss bounds for both methods, addressing behavior before an asymptotic limit. Finally, the theory guides construction of a pathological example in which a PINN is inconsistent. Together, these results characterize when consistency holds in the analyzed setting and demonstrate that it cannot be taken for granted.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes PINN consistency for a specified elliptic-equation setting and constructs an example where consistency fails.

title: Consistency of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Second-Order Elliptic Equations

abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems involving multiple agents are notoriously challenging due to their NP-hard nature and the necessity for effective agent coordination. Despite advancements in learning-based methods, existing approaches often face critical limitations, including suboptimal agent coordination, poor generalization, and high computational latency. To address these issues, we propose PARCO (Parallel AutoRegressive Combinatorial Optimization), a general reinforcement learning framework designed to construct high-quality solutions for multi-agent combinatorial tasks efficiently. To this end, PARCO integrates three key novel components: (1) transformer-based communication layers to enable effective agent collaboration during parallel solution construction, (2) a multiple pointer mechanism for low-latency, parallel agent decision-making, and (3) priority-based conflict handlers to resolve decision conflicts via learned priorities. We evaluate PARCO in multi-agent vehicle routing and scheduling problems, where our approach outperforms state-of-the-art learning methods, demonstrating strong generalization ability and remarkable computational efficiency. We make our source code publicly available to foster future research: https://github.com/ai4co/parco.

paragraphs: Routing and scheduling with multiple agents require both difficult combinatorial choices and coordination between decision-makers. Learning-based methods can struggle to coordinate agents, generalize to other instances, or produce solutions quickly. PARCO is a reinforcement learning framework designed to construct high-quality multi-agent solutions efficiently by allowing agents to make decisions in parallel.

Three components support this design. Transformer-based communication layers let agents exchange information while building solutions. A multiple pointer mechanism enables parallel choices with low latency. When those choices conflict, a priority-based handler resolves the conflict using learned priorities. These components connect simultaneous decision-making with explicit mechanisms for communication and conflict resolution.

The authors evaluate PARCO on multi-agent vehicle routing and scheduling problems. In those evaluations, it outperforms state-of-the-art learning methods and shows strong generalization and computational efficiency. The approach matters because parallel construction needs coordination to yield useful collective solutions. PARCO places that coordination inside the learned solution-building process, addressing both the quality of the resulting decisions and the time required to produce them.
summary.tldr: PARCO combines parallel agent decisions, learned communication, and conflict resolution to improve routing and scheduling performance in the reported evaluations.

title: PARCO: Parallel AutoRegressive Models for Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Generative modeling of time series is a central challenge in time series analysis, particularly under data-scarce conditions. Despite recent advances in generative modeling, a comprehensive understanding of how state-of-the-art generative models perform under limited supervision remains lacking. In this work, we conduct the first large-scale study evaluating leading generative models in data-scarce settings, revealing a substantial performance gap between full-data and data-scarce regimes. To close this gap, we propose a unified diffusion-based generative framework that can synthesize high-fidelity time series across diverse domains using just a few examples. Our model is pretrained on a large, heterogeneous collection of time series datasets, enabling it to learn generalizable temporal representations. It further incorporates architectural innovations such as dynamic convolutional layers for flexible channel adaptation and dataset token conditioning for domain-aware generation. Without requiring abundant supervision, our unified model achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot settings—outperforming domain-specific baselines across a wide range of subset sizes. Remarkably, it also surpasses all baselines even when tested on full datasets benchmarks, highlighting the strength of pretraining and cross-domain generalization. We hope this work encourages the community to revisit few-shot generative modeling as a key problem in time series research and pursue unified solutions that scale efficiently across domains. Code is available at https://github.com/azencot-group/ImagenFew.

paragraphs: This paper studies time-series generation when only a few examples are available for a target setting. A large-scale evaluation finds a substantial gap between leading generative models trained with full datasets and those operating under limited supervision. The proposed response is a unified diffusion model pretrained across a large, heterogeneous collection of time-series datasets.

Pretraining is intended to capture temporal representations that transfer across domains. Dynamic convolutional layers let the architecture adapt flexibly to different channel configurations, while dataset tokens condition generation on the domain. These components allow one framework to accommodate varied time-series datasets while drawing on shared knowledge learned during pretraining.

The model achieves state-of-the-art few-shot results in the reported evaluations, outperforming domain-specific baselines across a range of subset sizes. It also exceeds all evaluated baselines on full-dataset benchmarks. The findings support cross-domain pretraining as a useful foundation for generation with scarce target examples. The small-example claim concerns adaptation to the target setting, alongside substantial pretraining on other time-series data.
summary.tldr: A diffusion model pretrained across diverse time series generates strong few-shot results and also outperforms evaluated baselines on full-dataset benchmarks.

title: Time Series Generation Under Data Scarcity: A Unified Generative Modeling Approach

abstract: Active testing enables label-efficient evaluation of predictive models through careful data acquisition, but it can pose a significant computational cost. We identify cost-saving measures that enable active testing to be scaled up to large language models (LLMs). In particular we show that the surrogate model used to guide data acquisition can be constructed cheaply using in-context learning, does not require updating within an active-testing loop, and can be smaller than the target model. We even find we can make good data-acquisition decisions without making predictions with the target model. As a result we are able to achieve much more accurate evaluations of LLM performance relative to using randomly acquired data. We additionally introduce a bootstrap estimator of evaluation error, which we show to be a useful indicator of how well active testing is working within a single run.

paragraphs: Evaluating a language model can require many labeled examples. Active testing aims to use labels more efficiently by carefully choosing which examples to acquire, but the selection process can itself be computationally expensive. This paper identifies ways to reduce that overhead so active testing can be used at language-model scale.

The authors find that the surrogate model guiding acquisition can be built cheaply through in-context learning. It can be smaller than the model being evaluated and can remain unchanged throughout the active-testing loop. They also find that useful acquisition decisions can be made without obtaining target-model predictions for those decisions, further reducing the computational burden of selection.

With these cost-saving measures, active testing produces substantially more accurate estimates of language-model performance than random data acquisition. The paper also introduces a bootstrap estimator of evaluation error, which serves as a useful indicator of how well a single active-testing run is working. Together, these results address both the cost of choosing evaluation examples and the need to assess the resulting estimate’s reliability.
summary.tldr: Cheap, fixed surrogate models make active testing practical for LLMs and improve evaluation accuracy relative to random data acquisition.

title: Scaling Up Active Testing to Large Language Models

abstract: In many fields one encounters the challenge of identifying, out of a pool of possible designs, those that simultaneously optimize multiple objectives. This means that usually there is not one optimal design but an entire set of Pareto-optimal ones with optimal tradeoffs in the objectives. In many applications, evaluating one design is expensive; thus, an exhaustive search for the Pareto-optimal set is unfeasible. To address this challenge, we propose the Pareto Active Learning (PAL) algorithm, which intelligently samples the design space to predict the Pareto-optimal set. Key features of PAL include (1) modeling the objectives as samples from a Gaussian process distribution to capture structure and accommodate noisy evaluation; (2) a method to carefully choose the next design to evaluate to maximize progress; and (3) the ability to control prediction accuracy and sampling cost. We provide theoretical bounds on PAL’s sampling cost required to achieve a desired accuracy. Further, we show an experimental evaluation on three real-world data sets. The results show PAL’s effectiveness; in particular it improves significantly over a state-of-the-art evolutionary algorithm, saving in many cases about 33%.

paragraphs: When designs must satisfy several objectives, there may be no single best choice. Instead, the goal is a Pareto-optimal set: designs offering tradeoffs that cannot be improved in one objective without sacrificing another. Evaluating every candidate can be too expensive, so the paper asks how to identify this set using selective measurements.

The proposed Pareto Active Learning algorithm models the objectives with Gaussian processes. These models capture structure across the design space and accommodate noisy evaluations. PAL uses them to choose the next design to evaluate, aiming to make progress toward predicting the Pareto set while allowing control over accuracy and sampling cost.

The authors provide theoretical bounds on the sampling required for a desired accuracy. On three real-world datasets, PAL also improves significantly over the evolutionary algorithm used for comparison, with savings of about 33% in many cases. These findings support targeted evaluation as a way to reduce the expense of discovering useful tradeoffs, rather than exhaustively testing the design pool.
summary.tldr: Pareto Active Learning selectively evaluates designs to identify good multi-objective tradeoffs with controlled accuracy and sampling cost.

title: Active Learning for Multi-Objective Optimization

abstract: To be tractable and robust to data noise, existing metric learning algorithms commonly rely on PCA as a pre-processing step. How can we know, however, that PCA, or any other specific dimensionality reduction technique, is the method of choice for the problem at hand? The answer is simple: We cannot! To address this issue, in this paper, we develop a Riemannian framework to jointly learn a mapping performing dimensionality reduction and a metric in the induced space. Our experiments evidence that, while we directly work on high-dimensional features, our approach yields competitive runtimes with and higher accuracy than state-of-the-art metric learning algorithms.

To address this issue, in this paper, we develop a Riemannian framework to jointly learn a mapping performing dimensionality reduction and a metric in the induced space. paragraphs: Metric learning seeks a useful way to measure distances between data points. For tractability and robustness to noise, existing methods commonly first reduce the data’s dimension using PCA. The paper questions whether that independently chosen reduction is the right representation for the particular metric-learning problem.

The authors develop a Riemannian framework that learns two components together: a mapping into a lower-dimensional space and a metric within that space. Joint learning allows the dimensionality-reduction mapping and the distance measure to be selected as parts of the same problem. This directly addresses the uncertainty introduced by fixing a preprocessing method in advance.

Experiments show higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art metric-learning algorithms considered, with competitive running times despite starting directly from high-dimensional features. These findings support learning the representation and metric together as a practical alternative to separate preprocessing. The reported advantage is empirical and concerns the evaluated settings, rather than establishing that any particular reduction method is always unsuitable.
summary.tldr: A Riemannian framework jointly learns dimensionality reduction and a distance metric, improving accuracy with competitive runtimes in experiments.

title: Joint Dimensionality Reduction and Metric Learning: A Geometric Take

abstract: Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) are a family of probabilistic models that have a repulsive behavior, and lend themselves naturally to many tasks in machine learning where returning a diverse set of objects is important. While there are fast algorithms for sampling, marginalization and conditioning, much less is known about learning the parameters of a DPP. Our contribution is twofold: (i) we establish the optimal sample complexity achievable in this problem and show that it is governed by a natural parameter, which we call the cycle sparsity; (ii) we propose a provably fast combinatorial algorithm that implements the method of moments efficiently and achieves optimal sample complexity. Finally, we give experimental results that confirm our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes are probabilistic models whose repulsive behavior makes them useful when an application needs a diverse set of objects. Efficient procedures already exist for sampling from these models and computing several related probabilities. This paper addresses a less understood problem: learning the model's parameters from observed data.

The authors establish the optimal sample complexity, describing the amount of data needed for learning. They show that this requirement is governed by a structural parameter they call cycle sparsity. This identifies a property of the learning problem that determines its statistical difficulty, connecting the data requirement to the structure being recovered.

They also provide a provably fast combinatorial algorithm that efficiently implements the method of moments and attains the optimal sample complexity. Experimental results support the theoretical findings. The combined contribution is both statistical and computational: it characterizes the achievable data requirement and supplies an efficient learning procedure that reaches that requirement.
summary.tldr: Cycle sparsity governs optimal DPP learning sample complexity, which a fast combinatorial method-of-moments algorithm achieves.

title: Learning Determinantal Point Processes with Moments and Cycles

abstract: Parameter inference for stochastic differential equations is challenging due to the presence of a latent diffusion process. Working with an Euler-Maruyama discretisation for the diffusion, we use variational inference to jointly learn the parameters and the diffusion paths. We use a standard mean-field variational approximation of the parameter posterior, and introduce a recurrent neural network to approximate the posterior for the diffusion paths conditional on the parameters. This neural network learns how to provide Gaussian state transitions which bridge between observations in a very similar way to the conditioned diffusion process. The resulting black-box inference method can be applied to any SDE system with light tuning requirements. We illustrate the method on a Lotka-Volterra system and an epidemic model, producing accurate parameter estimates in a few hours.

paragraphs: Inferring the parameters of a stochastic differential equation is difficult because observations leave the intervening diffusion path hidden. This paper learns both the parameters and those unobserved paths through variational inference. Its starting point is an Euler–Maruyama discretization, so inference operates on a discrete approximation to the diffusion process.

The method uses two different approximations for the two parts of the problem. A mean-field distribution represents uncertainty about parameters, while a recurrent neural network represents diffusion paths conditional on those parameters. The network learns Gaussian state transitions that bridge observations, behaving similarly to the diffusion process conditioned on the observed data.

This learned bridge is the central mechanism for making inference broadly reusable rather than requiring extensive tuning for each system. The authors present the resulting method as applicable to any SDE system with light tuning. Demonstrations on a Lotka–Volterra system and an epidemic model produce accurate parameter estimates within a few hours, supporting its usefulness on those examples.
summary.tldr: A recurrent network learns hidden diffusion paths alongside model parameters to enable broadly applicable variational inference for stochastic differential equations.

title: Black-Box Variational Inference for Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: A probabilistic framework based on the covariate-dependent relational gamma process is developed to analyze relational data arising from longitudinal networks. The proposed framework characterizes networked nodes by nonnegative node-group memberships, which allow each node to belong to multiple latent groups simultaneously, and encodes edge probabilities between each pair of nodes using a Bernoulli Poisson link to the embedded latent space. Within the latent space, our framework models the birth and death dynamics of individual groups via a thinning function. Our framework also captures the evolution of individual node-group memberships over time using gamma Markov processes. Exploiting the recent advances in data augmentation and marginalization techniques, a simple and efficient Gibbs sampler is proposed for posterior computation. Experimental results on a simulation study and three real-world temporal network data sets demonstrate the model’s capability, competitive performance and scalability compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic model for networks observed over time. Each node has nonnegative memberships in hidden groups, and it may belong to several groups simultaneously. These memberships form a latent representation of the network. A Bernoulli Poisson link connects that representation to the probability of an edge between a pair of nodes.

The framework represents two kinds of temporal change. A thinning function models groups appearing and disappearing, while gamma Markov processes model changes in individual nodes' group memberships. Keeping both mechanisms allows the model to describe changes in which groups exist as well as changes in how nodes participate in those groups.

For inference, the authors develop a Gibbs sampler using data augmentation and marginalization techniques. They evaluate the framework in a simulation and on three real temporal network datasets. The experiments demonstrate competitive performance and scalability relative to state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a unified account of overlapping memberships, changing group populations, and evolving network connections.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic temporal-network model tracks overlapping node memberships alongside the appearance and disappearance of latent groups.

title: Dependent Relational Gamma Process Models for Longitudinal Networks

abstract: Virtual democracy is an approach to automating decisions, by learning models of the preferences of individual people, and, at runtime, aggregating the predicted preferences of those people on the dilemma at hand. One of the key questions is which aggregation method – or voting rule – to use; we offer a novel statistical viewpoint that provides guidance. Specifically, we seek voting rules that are robust to prediction errors, in that their output on people’s true preferences is likely to coincide with their output on noisy estimates thereof. We prove that the classic Borda count rule is robust in this sense, whereas any voting rule belonging to the wide family of pairwise-majority consistent rules is not. Our empirical results further support, and more precisely measure, the robustness of Borda count.

One of the key questions is which aggregation method – or voting rule – to use; we offer a novel statistical viewpoint that provides guidance. Specifically, we seek voting rules that are robust to prediction errors, in that their output on people’s true preferences is likely to coincide with their output on noisy estimates thereof. We prove that the classic Borda count rule is robust in this sense, whereas any voting rule belonging to the wide family of pairwise-majority consistent rules is not. paragraphs: Virtual democracy makes decisions by predicting individual preferences and then aggregating those predictions through a voting rule. Prediction errors create an additional challenge: even a useful preference model may lead to a different collective outcome from the one obtained using people's true preferences. The paper studies voting rules from this statistical perspective.

Its robustness criterion asks whether a rule's output on noisy preference estimates is likely to match its output on the underlying true preferences. This focuses on the stability of the final decision, connecting the preference-prediction stage with the aggregation stage. The choice of voting rule therefore affects how prediction errors propagate into collective choices.

The authors prove that Borda count is robust in this sense, whereas rules in the broad pairwise-majority-consistent family are not. Empirical results further support and quantify Borda's robustness. These findings guide aggregation when predicted preferences are noisy; they concern the paper's statistical robustness criterion rather than establishing that Borda is superior according to every possible goal for collective decision-making.
summary.tldr: Borda count is robust to preference-prediction errors under the paper's criterion, while pairwise-majority-consistent voting rules are not.

title: Statistical Foundations of Virtual Democracy

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) achieve the state-of-the-art results on a wide range of image processing tasks, however, the majority of such solutions are problem-specific, like most AI algorithms. The One Network to Solve Them All (OneNet) procedure has been suggested to resolve this issue by exploiting a DNN as the proximal operator in Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) solvers for various imaging problems. In this work, we make two contributions, both facilitating end-to-end learning using backpropagation. First, we generalize OneNet to videos by augmenting its convolutional prior network with bidirectional recurrent connections; second, we extend the fixed fully connected linear ADMM data step with another trainable bidirectional convolutional recurrent network. In our computational experiments on the Rotated MNIST, Scanned CIFAR-10 and UCF-101 data sets, the proposed modifications improve performance by a large margin compared to end-to-end convolutional OneNet and 3D Wavelet sparsity on several video processing problems: pixelwise inpainting-denoising, blockwise inpainting, scattered inpainting, super resolution, compressive sensing, deblurring, frame interpolation, frame prediction and colorization. Our two contributions are complementary, and using them together yields the best results.

paragraphs: Many neural image-processing solutions are designed for a single problem. OneNet offers a more reusable approach by placing a neural network inside an ADMM optimization solver as a proximal operator. This paper extends that framework to video and makes two components suitable for end-to-end learning through backpropagation.

First, the authors add bidirectional recurrent connections to the convolutional prior network, allowing its processing to incorporate temporal information in both directions. Second, they replace the fixed linear data step with a trainable bidirectional convolutional recurrent network. The changes bring learned video processing into both the prior component and the solver’s data step.

Experiments on Rotated MNIST, Scanned CIFAR-10, and UCF-101 cover tasks including inpainting, super resolution, deblurring, frame interpolation, prediction, and colorization. The modifications substantially improve performance over end-to-end convolutional OneNet and 3D Wavelet sparsity in the reported experiments. The two changes are complementary, with their combination producing the best results, supporting the value of adapting both solver components to video.
summary.tldr: VideoOneNet adds bidirectional recurrence and a trainable data step to OneNet, producing complementary improvements across multiple video-processing tasks.

title: VideoOneNet: Bidirectional Convolutional Recurrent OneNet with Trainable Data Steps for Video Processing

abstract: Generative autoencoders offer a promising approach for controllable text generation by leveraging their learned sentence representations. However, current models struggle to maintain coherent latent spaces required to perform meaningful text manipulations via latent vector operations. Specifically, we demonstrate by example that neural encoders do not necessarily map similar sentences to nearby latent vectors. A theoretical explanation for this phenomenon establishes that high-capacity autoencoders can learn an arbitrary mapping between sequences and associated latent representations. To remedy this issue, we augment adversarial autoencoders with a denoising objective where original sentences are reconstructed from perturbed versions (referred to as DAAE). We prove that this simple modification guides the latent space geometry of the resulting model by encouraging the encoder to map similar texts to similar latent representations. In empirical comparisons with various types of autoencoders, our model provides the best trade-off between generation quality and reconstruction capacity. Moreover, the improved geometry of the DAAE latent space enables \emph{zero-shot} text style transfer via simple latent vector arithmetic.

paragraphs: Text autoencoders learn sentence representations that could support editing through operations on latent vectors. But successful reconstruction does not necessarily give those vectors a useful arrangement. The paper demonstrates that similar sentences need not be encoded near one another and explains theoretically why high-capacity autoencoders can associate sequences with arbitrary latent representations.

The proposed remedy adds a denoising objective to an adversarial autoencoder. Instead of only reconstructing a sentence from its own representation, the model learns to reconstruct the original sentence from a perturbed version. The authors prove that this modification encourages similar texts to receive similar representations, giving the latent space a more coherent geometry.

In empirical comparisons with several autoencoder types, the resulting DAAE model offers the best reported balance between generation quality and reconstruction capacity. Its improved latent geometry also enables zero-shot text style transfer through simple vector arithmetic. The findings show why the organization of representations matters alongside reconstruction: a space that preserves relationships among texts can support meaningful manipulations of those texts.
summary.tldr: Adding denoising to adversarial text autoencoders encourages coherent latent geometry and enables zero-shot style transfer through vector arithmetic.

title: Educating Text Autoencoders: Latent Representation Guidance via Denoising

abstract: Learning composable policies for environments with complex rules and tasks is a challenging problem. We introduce a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework called the Logical Options Framework (LOF) that learns policies that are satisfying, optimal, and composable. LOF efficiently learns policies that satisfy tasks by representing the task as an automaton and integrating it into learning and planning. We provide and prove conditions under which LOF will learn satisfying, optimal policies. And lastly, we show how LOF’s learned policies can be composed to satisfy unseen tasks with only 10-50 retraining steps on our benchmarks. We evaluate LOF on four tasks in discrete and continuous domains, including a 3D pick-and-place environment.

paragraphs: Complex reinforcement-learning tasks can involve rules that a policy must satisfy as well as behavior it should optimize. The Logical Options Framework addresses this through hierarchical learning, with the additional goal that learned policies can be combined for new tasks. It connects task structure directly to learning and planning.

The framework represents a task as an automaton, making its logical requirements part of the decision process. The authors provide and prove conditions under which the framework learns policies that both satisfy the task and are optimal. Those conditions matter: the theoretical claim is a conditional guarantee, rather than a promise for every possible environment or specification.

The paper also evaluates whether previously learned policies can be composed to handle unseen tasks. Across its benchmarks, this requires only 10–50 retraining steps. Evaluation covers four tasks in discrete and continuous domains, including a three-dimensional pick-and-place environment. These findings support the practical value of learning reusable policies whose composition is guided by an explicit representation of task requirements.
summary.tldr: The Logical Options Framework uses task automata to learn composable policies, with conditional optimality guarantees and limited retraining on unseen benchmark tasks.

title: The Logical Options Framework

abstract: Recursive Neural Networks (RvNNs), which compose sequences according to their underlying hierarchical syntactic structure, have performed well in several natural language processing tasks compared to similar models without structural biases. However, traditional RvNNs are incapable of inducing the latent structure in a plain text sequence on their own. Several extensions have been proposed to overcome this limitation. Nevertheless, these extensions tend to rely on surrogate gradients or reinforcement learning at the cost of higher bias or variance. In this work, we propose Continuous Recursive Neural Network (CRvNN) as a backpropagation-friendly alternative to address the aforementioned limitations. This is done by incorporating a continuous relaxation to the induced structure. We demonstrate that CRvNN achieves strong performance in challenging synthetic tasks such as logical inference (Bowman et al., 2015b) and ListOps (Nangia & Bowman, 2018). We also show that CRvNN performs comparably or better than prior latent structure models on real-world tasks such as sentiment analysis and natural language inference.

paragraphs: Recursive neural networks combine parts of a sequence according to a hierarchy, making structural relationships part of their computation. Traditional versions cannot discover that hidden hierarchy from plain text on their own. Extensions that learn structure often use surrogate gradients or reinforcement learning, introducing difficulties associated with higher bias or variance.

The proposed Continuous Recursive Neural Network makes the induced structure continuous through a relaxation. This allows structure learning to work with backpropagation, providing an alternative way to train a recursive model from sequences. The key idea is to retain hierarchical composition while changing how the model represents its structural choices during learning.

The authors report strong performance on synthetic logical inference and ListOps tasks, which test structured sequence processing. On sentiment analysis and natural language inference, the model performs comparably to or better than earlier latent-structure models. These findings support continuous relaxation as a practical route to learning hidden hierarchies while preserving the structural bias that motivates recursive networks.
summary.tldr: Continuous relaxation lets recursive neural networks learn latent hierarchies through backpropagation, with strong results on structured language tasks.

title: Modeling Hierarchical Structures with Continuous Recursive Neural Networks

abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly seen as a viable approach for building compiler optimization heuristics, but many ML methods cannot replicate even the simplest of the data flow analyses that are critical to making good optimization decisions. We posit that if ML cannot do that, then it is insufficiently able to reason about programs. We formulate data flow analyses as supervised learning tasks and introduce a large open dataset of programs and their corresponding labels from several analyses. We use this dataset to benchmark ML methods and show that they struggle on these fundamental program reasoning tasks. We propose ProGraML - Program Graphs for Machine Learning - a language-independent, portable representation of program semantics. ProGraML overcomes the limitations of prior works and yields improved performance on downstream optimization tasks.

paragraphs: Machine learning can guide compiler optimization, but useful decisions require understanding properties of programs. The authors argue that reproducing basic data-flow analyses is an important test of that understanding. If a method struggles with these foundational tasks, its ability to reason about programs is insufficient for the optimization decisions that depend on them.

The paper turns data-flow analyses into supervised learning problems and introduces a large open dataset pairing programs with analysis labels. Benchmarking existing machine learning methods on these tasks exposes their difficulties. This creates a concrete way to assess program reasoning, using targets derived from analyses that matter to compilers.

The proposed ProGraML representation expresses program semantics as graphs and is designed to be portable and independent of programming language. The authors report that it addresses limitations of earlier representations and improves performance on downstream optimization tasks. The contribution combines a diagnostic benchmark with a new representation, connecting foundational program-analysis ability to the practical goal of making better compiler optimization decisions.
summary.tldr: ProGraML combines graph-based program semantics with data-flow benchmarks to improve machine learning for compiler optimization.

title: ProGraML: A Graph-based Program Representation for Data Flow Analysis and Compiler Optimizations

abstract: In batched multi-armed bandit problems, the learner can adaptively pull arms and adjust strategy in batches. In many real applications, not only the regret but also the batch complexity need to be optimized. Existing batched bandit algorithms usually assume that the time horizon T is known in advance. However, many applications involve an unpredictable stopping time. In this paper, we study the anytime batched multi-armed bandit problem. We propose an anytime algorithm that achieves the asymptotically optimal regret for exponential families of reward distributions with $O(\log \log T \ilog^{\alpha} (T))$ \footnote{Notation \ilog^{\alpha} (T) is the result of iteratively applying the logarithm function on T for \alpha times, e.g., \ilog^{3} (T)=\log\log\log T.} batches, where $\alpha\in O_{T}(1)$. Moreover, we prove that for any constant c>0, no algorithm can achieve the asymptotically optimal regret within c\log\log T batches.

paragraphs: Batched bandit learning balances two costs: losses from choosing inferior arms and the number of batches used to organize decisions. Many existing methods require the total number of decisions in advance. This paper studies an anytime setting, where the learner must operate without knowing when the process will stop.

For reward distributions in exponential families, the authors propose an anytime algorithm with asymptotically optimal regret. Its batch count is bounded by log log T multiplied by an iterated logarithm of T. An iterated logarithm means applying the logarithm repeatedly, with the number of applications held constant as the horizon T grows.

The paper also establishes a lower bound: in the studied setting, no algorithm can achieve asymptotically optimal regret using at most c times log log T batches for any fixed positive constant c. Thus, the extra slowly growing factor in the proposed bound addresses a real obstruction. The result explains how nearly optimal batching can coexist with optimal long-run regret when the stopping time is unknown.
summary.tldr: An anytime batched bandit algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal regret with a batch count close to a proved lower bound.

title: Almost Optimal Anytime Algorithm for Batched Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: Making predictions and quantifying their uncertainty when the input data is sequential is a fundamental learning challenge, recently attracting increasing attention. We develop SigGPDE, a new scalable sparse variational inference framework for Gaussian Processes (GPs) on sequential data. Our contribution is twofold. First, we construct inducing variables underpinning the sparse approximation so that the resulting evidence lower bound (ELBO) does not require any matrix inversion. Second, we show that the gradients of the GP signature kernel are solutions of a hyperbolic partial differential equation (PDE). This theoretical insight allows us to build an efficient back-propagation algorithm to optimize the ELBO. We showcase the significant computational gains of SigGPDE compared to existing methods, while achieving state-of-the-art performance for classification tasks on large datasets of up to 1 million multivariate time series.

paragraphs: Learning from sequences requires models that can make predictions while representing uncertainty about them. SigGPDE develops a scalable sparse variational framework for applying Gaussian processes to sequential data. Its contribution focuses on making the approximation and its optimization computationally efficient enough for large collections of time series.

The second is a theoretical connection: gradients of the Gaussian-process signature kernel solve a hyperbolic partial differential equation. The authors use this connection to build an efficient back-propagation algorithm for optimizing that objective.

These two components address complementary parts of the training computation: evaluating the sparse learning objective and obtaining the gradients needed to improve it. The reported evaluations show substantial computational gains over existing methods alongside state-of-the-art classification performance. The experiments include datasets containing up to one million multivariate time series, demonstrating the framework at a large sequential-data scale.
summary.tldr: SigGPDE combines an inversion-free variational objective with PDE-based kernel gradients to scale Gaussian processes to large time-series datasets.

title: SigGPDE: Scaling Sparse Gaussian Processes on Sequential Data

abstract: Answering complex natural language questions on knowledge graphs (KGQA) is a challenging task. It requires reasoning with the input natural language questions as well as a massive, incomplete heterogeneous KG. Prior methods obtain an abstract structured query graph/tree from the input question and traverse the KG for answers following the query tree. However, they inherently cannot deal with missing links in the KG. Here we present LEGO, a Latent Execution-Guided reasOning framework to handle this challenge in KGQA. LEGO works in an iterative way, which alternates between (1) a Query Synthesizer, which synthesizes a reasoning action and grows the query tree step-by-step, and (2) a Latent Space Executor that executes the reasoning action in the latent embedding space to combat against the missing information in KG. To learn the synthesizer without step-wise supervision, we design a generic latent execution guided bottom-up search procedure to find good execution traces efficiently in the vast query space. Experimental results on several KGQA benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework compared with previous state of the art.

paragraphs: Answering complex questions over a knowledge graph requires connecting natural-language meaning with multiple reasoning steps. Missing graph links create a particular difficulty for methods that execute a structured query by traversing existing edges. LEGO addresses this problem by combining incremental query construction with execution in a learned latent space.

The framework alternates between two components. A Query Synthesizer proposes a reasoning action and extends the query tree one step at a time. A Latent Space Executor carries out that action using embeddings, helping the reasoning process cope with missing graph information. Query construction and execution therefore proceed together throughout the reasoning sequence.

To train the synthesizer without supervision for every intermediate step, the authors introduce a bottom-up search procedure guided by latent execution. It efficiently seeks useful execution traces within a large space of possible queries. Experiments on several knowledge-graph question-answering benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness relative to previous state-of-the-art methods. The contribution connects structured reasoning with latent execution while also providing a way to learn the reasoning sequence without stepwise labels.
summary.tldr: LEGO alternates query synthesis with latent-space execution to answer multi-hop questions over incomplete knowledge graphs.

title: LEGO: Latent Execution-Guided Reasoning for Multi-Hop Question Answering on Knowledge Graphs

abstract: Object-centric world models provide structured representation of the scene and can be an important backbone in reinforcement learning and planning. However, existing approaches suffer in partially-observable environments due to the lack of belief states. In this paper, we propose Structured World Belief, a model for learning and inference of object-centric belief states. Inferred by Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), our belief states provide multiple object-centric scene hypotheses. To synergize the benefits of SMC particles with object representations, we also propose a new object-centric dynamics model that considers the inductive bias of object permanence. This enables tracking of object states even when they are invisible for a long time. To further facilitate object tracking in this regime, we allow our model to attend flexibly to any spatial location in the image which was restricted in previous models. In experiments, we show that object-centric belief provides a more accurate and robust performance for filtering and generation. Furthermore, we show the efficacy of structured world belief in improving the performance of reinforcement learning, planning and supervised reasoning.

paragraphs: Representing a scene as objects can help an agent reason and plan, but partial visibility creates uncertainty about what those objects are doing. A single scene representation may not capture that uncertainty. Structured World Belief learns object-centric belief states that maintain multiple possible explanations of the scene.

The method uses Sequential Monte Carlo to infer these hypotheses and combines it with an object-centric dynamics model designed around object permanence. This enables it to track object states even during long periods of invisibility. It also allows attention to move flexibly to any image location, helping object tracking in circumstances where previous models restricted that flexibility.

Experiments show more accurate and robust filtering and generation with the object-centric beliefs. The authors also demonstrate improvements in reinforcement learning, planning, and supervised reasoning. The findings connect structured uncertainty to downstream usefulness: maintaining several plausible object states can improve both the model’s account of a partially observed world and the tasks that depend on that account.
summary.tldr: Structured World Belief tracks multiple object-centric scene hypotheses to improve inference and decision-making under partial observability.

title: Structured World Belief for Reinforcement Learning in POMDP

abstract: Scalable training of large models (like BERT and GPT-3) requires careful optimization rooted in model design, architecture, and system capabilities. From a system standpoint, communication has become a major bottleneck, especially on commodity systems with standard TCP interconnects that offer limited network bandwidth. Communication compression is an important technique to reduce training time on such systems. One of the most effective ways to compress communication is via error compensation compression, which offers robust convergence speed, even under 1-bit compression. However, state-of-the-art error compensation techniques only work with basic optimizers like SGD and momentum SGD, which are linearly dependent on the gradients. They do not work with non-linear gradient-based optimizers like Adam, which offer state-of-the-art convergence efficiency and accuracy for models like BERT. In this paper, we propose 1-bit Adam that reduces the communication volume by up to 5x, offers much better scalability, and provides the same convergence speed as uncompressed Adam. Our key finding is that Adam’s variance becomes stable (after a warmup phase) and can be used as a fixed precondition for the rest of the training (compression phase). We performed experiments on up to 256 GPUs and show that 1-bit Adam enables up to 3.3x higher throughput for BERT-Large pre-training and up to 2.9x higher throughput for SQuAD fine-tuning. In addition, we provide theoretical analysis for 1-bit Adam.

paragraphs: Training large models across many GPUs requires frequent communication, which can become a bottleneck when network bandwidth is limited. Compressing the exchanged information helps, but existing error compensation techniques do not directly accommodate Adam’s nonlinear dependence on gradients. This paper develops 1-bit Adam to combine communication compression with Adam’s convergence efficiency.

These are reported maximum gains, rather than uniform improvements across configurations. The paper also supplies theoretical analysis, connecting its systems improvements with an analysis of the optimization method.
summary.tldr: 1-bit Adam fixes a stabilized variance estimate after warmup to compress distributed training communication while retaining Adam’s reported convergence speed.

title: 1-bit Adam: Communication Efficient Large-Scale Training with Adam’s Convergence Speed

abstract: We investigate the robustness of stochastic approximation approaches against data poisoning attacks. We focus on two-layer neural networks with ReLU activation and show that under a specific notion of separability in the RKHS induced by the infinite-width network, training (finite-width) networks with stochastic gradient descent is robust against data poisoning attacks. Interestingly, we find that in addition to a lower bound on the width of the network, which is standard in the literature, we also require a distribution-dependent upper bound on the width for robust generalization. We provide extensive empirical evaluations that support and validate our theoretical results.
originalAbstract: We investigate the robustness of stochastic approximation approaches against data poisoning attacks. We focus on two-layer neural networks with ReLU activation and show that under a specific notion of separability in the RKHS induced by the infinite-width network, training (finite-width) networks with stochastic gradient descent is robust against data poisoning attacks. Interestingly, we find that in addition to a lower bound on the width of the network, which is standard in the literature, we also require a distribution-dependent upper bound on the width for robust generalization. We provide extensive empirical evaluations that support and validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Data poisoning attacks interfere with learning through the training data. This paper investigates when stochastic approximation methods can withstand such attacks, focusing on finite-width, two-layer neural networks with ReLU activations. Its main result gives a robustness guarantee for stochastic gradient descent under a particular condition on the learning problem.

That condition is a notion of separability in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated with the corresponding infinite-width network. The analysis uses this infinite-width representation to establish a result about training finite-width networks. Separability is therefore a substantive assumption behind the guarantee, tying resistance to poisoning to the structure of the data in that induced space.

The width requirements have an unusual feature: robust generalization needs both a lower bound and a distribution-dependent upper bound on network width. The result does not simply prescribe making the model wider. Extensive empirical evaluations support the theoretical findings. Together, the analysis and experiments identify a role for controlling model width when seeking robustness to poisoned training data under the stated separability condition.
summary.tldr: Under a specific separability assumption, SGD-trained two-layer ReLU networks resist data poisoning when width satisfies both lower and distribution-dependent upper bounds.

title: Robust Learning for Data Poisoning Attacks

abstract: Likelihood is a standard estimate for outlier detection. The specific role of the normalization constraint is to ensure that the out-of-distribution (OOD) regime has a small likelihood when samples are learned using maximum likelihood. Because autoencoders do not possess such a process of normalization, they often fail to recognize outliers even when they are obviously OOD. We propose the Normalized Autoencoder (NAE), a normalized probabilistic model constructed from an autoencoder. The probability density of NAE is defined using the reconstruction error of an autoencoder, which is differently defined in the conventional energy-based model. In our model, normalization is enforced by suppressing the reconstruction of negative samples, significantly improving the outlier detection performance. Our experimental results confirm the efficacy of NAE, both in detecting outliers and in generating in-distribution samples.

paragraphs: An autoencoder learns to reconstruct inputs, but successful reconstruction does not necessarily mean an input belongs to the training distribution. The paper identifies missing probability normalization as a reason ordinary autoencoders can reconstruct obvious outliers well. This weakens their usefulness when reconstruction behavior is used to decide whether an example is unusual.

The proposed Normalized Autoencoder turns an autoencoder into a normalized probabilistic model. Its probability density is defined through reconstruction error, connecting the model’s ability to reproduce an input with the probability it assigns to that input. To enforce normalization, training suppresses reconstruction of negative samples. This introduces pressure against reconstructing those samples well, alongside learning the observed data.

The authors report a substantial improvement in outlier detection and experiments supporting both outlier recognition and generation of in-distribution samples. The central idea is that reconstruction becomes more informative when it is part of a normalized probability model. The same construction supports judging whether an input fits the distribution and producing samples that do.
summary.tldr: The Normalized Autoencoder uses reconstruction-based probabilities and negative samples to improve outlier detection while supporting in-distribution generation.

title: Autoencoding Under Normalization Constraints

abstract: Boundary based blackbox attack has been recognized as practical and effective, given that an attacker only needs to access the final model prediction. However, the query efficiency of it is in general high especially for high dimensional image data. In this paper, we show that such efficiency highly depends on the scale at which the attack is applied, and attacking at the optimal scale significantly improves the efficiency. In particular, we propose a theoretical framework to analyze and show three key characteristics to improve the query efficiency. We prove that there exists an optimal scale for projective gradient estimation. Our framework also explains the satisfactory performance achieved by existing boundary black-box attacks. Based on our theoretical framework, we propose Progressive-Scale enabled projective Boundary Attack (PSBA) to improve the query efficiency via progressive scaling techniques. In particular, we employ Progressive-GAN to optimize the scale of projections, which we call PSBA-PGAN. We evaluate our approach on both spatial and frequency scales. Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet against different models including a real-world face recognition API show that PSBA-PGAN significantly outperforms existing baseline attacks in terms of query efficiency and attack success rate. We also observe relatively stable optimal scales for different models and datasets. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/AI-secure/PSBA.

paragraphs: Boundary-based black-box attacks seek adversarial inputs using only a model's final predictions. For high-dimensional images, the number of required queries is a central practical concern. This paper studies how that query requirement depends on the scale at which an attack operates, rather than treating the scale as an incidental design choice.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for projective gradient estimation and prove that an optimal scale exists within that framework. Their analysis also explains successful behavior of existing boundary attacks. They turn these findings into Progressive-Scale Boundary Attack, or PSBA, and use Progressive-GAN to optimize projection scale in the PSBA-PGAN variant.

These results support scale selection as an effective component of the studied black-box attacks.
summary.tldr: PSBA progressively adjusts projection scale to improve the query efficiency and success of boundary-based black-box attacks.

title: Progressive-Scale Boundary Blackbox Attack via Projective Gradient Estimation

abstract: While extensive-form games (EFGs) can be converted into normal-form games (NFGs), doing so comes at the cost of an exponential blowup of the strategy space. So, progress on NFGs and EFGs has historically followed separate tracks, with the EFG community often having to catch up with advances (\eg last-iterate convergence and predictive regret bounds) from the larger NFG community. In this paper we show that the Optimistic Multiplicative Weights Update (OMWU) algorithm—the premier learning algorithm for NFGs—can be simulated on the normal-form equivalent of an EFG in linear time per iteration in the game tree size using a kernel trick. The resulting algorithm, Kernelized OMWU (KOMWU) , applies more broadly to all convex games whose strategy space is a polytope with 0/1 integral vertices, as long as the kernel can be evaluated efficiently. In the particular case of EFGs, KOMWU closes several standing gaps between NFG and EFG learning, by enabling direct, black-box transfer to EFGs of desirable properties of learning dynamics that were so far known to be achievable only in NFGs. Specifically, KOMWU gives the first algorithm that guarantees at the same time last-iterate convergence, lower dependence on the size of the game tree than all prior algorithms, and $\tilde{\bigOh}(1)$ regret when followed by all players.

The resulting algorithm, Kernelized OMWU (KOMWU) , applies more broadly to all convex games whose strategy space is a polytope with 0/1 integral vertices, as long as the kernel can be evaluated efficiently. The paper shows how to simulate a leading normal-form algorithm without paying that expansion cost.

title: Kernelized Multiplicative Weights for 0/1-Polyhedral Games: Bridging the Gap Between Learning in Extensive-Form and Normal-Form Games

abstract: Recently, some accelerated stochastic variance reduction algorithms such as Katyusha and ASVRG-ADMM achieve faster convergence than non-accelerated methods such as SVRG and SVRG-ADMM. However, there are still some gaps between the oracle complexities and their lower bounds. To fill in these gaps, this paper proposes a novel Directly Accelerated stochastic Variance reductIon (DAVIS) algorithm with two Snapshots for non-strongly convex (non-SC) unconstrained problems. Our theoretical results show that DAVIS achieves the optimal convergence rate O(1/(nS^2)) and optimal gradient complexity O(n+\sqrt{nL/\epsilon}), which is identical to its lower bound. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first directly accelerated algorithm that attains the optimal lower bound and improves the convergence rate from O(1/S^2) to O(1/(nS^2)). Moreover, we extend DAVIS and theoretical results to non-SC problems with a structured regularizer, and prove that the proposed algorithm with double-snapshots also attains the optimal convergence rate O(1/(nS)) and optimal oracle complexity O(n+L/\epsilon) for such problems, and it is at least a factor n/S faster than existing accelerated stochastic algorithms, where n\gg S in general.

paragraphs: Accelerated variance-reduction methods improve optimization speed, but their theoretical costs can still exceed known lower bounds. This paper targets those gaps for non-strongly convex problems. It introduces DAVIS, a directly accelerated stochastic variance-reduction algorithm with two snapshots, and analyzes both an unconstrained formulation and an extension involving a structured regularizer.

For the structured-regularizer extension, the paper proves a rate of O(1/(nS)) and oracle complexity of O(n + L/epsilon), again described as optimal. It also reports a theoretical speed advantage of at least n/S over existing accelerated stochastic algorithms in that setting. The size of that comparison depends on n relative to S, with the abstract emphasizing the regime where n is much larger.
summary.tldr: DAVIS uses direct acceleration and two snapshots to attain stated optimal complexity bounds for non-strongly convex optimization settings.

title: Kill a Bird with Two Stones: Closing the Convergence Gaps in Non-Strongly Convex Optimization by Directly Accelerated SVRG with Double Compensation and Snapshots

abstract: Solving a reinforcement learning (RL) problem poses two competing challenges: fitting a potentially discontinuous value function, and generalizing well to new observations. In this paper, we analyze the learning dynamics of temporal difference algorithms to gain novel insight into the tension between these two objectives. We show theoretically that temporal difference learning encourages agents to fit non-smooth components of the value function early in training, and at the same time induces the second-order effect of discouraging generalization. We corroborate these findings in deep RL agents trained on a range of environments, finding that neural networks trained using temporal difference algorithms on dense reward tasks exhibit weaker generalization between states than randomly initialized networks and networks trained with policy gradient methods. Finally, we investigate how post-training policy distillation may avoid this pitfall, and show that this approach improves generalization to novel environments in the ProcGen suite and improves robustness to input perturbations.
