paragraphs: Reinforcement learning must fit value functions that may change abruptly while also producing behavior that generalizes to new observations. This paper studies the tension between those goals through the learning dynamics of temporal-difference algorithms. It asks how the training process itself shapes what an agent learns, beyond whether it fits the value function.

The theoretical analysis shows that temporal-difference learning favors fitting non-smooth value components early in training and creates a second-order effect that discourages generalization. Experiments corroborate these findings across environments. On dense-reward tasks, networks trained with temporal-difference methods generalize less well between states than randomly initialized networks and networks trained using policy gradients.

The authors then investigate distilling the policy after training as a way to avoid this problem. They report improved generalization to new ProcGen environments and greater robustness to input perturbations. The results connect a particular learning dynamic to weaker generalization and identify post-training distillation as a useful response in the tested settings. They do not imply that fitting a value function and generalizing are always incompatible.
summary.tldr: Temporal-difference learning can discourage generalization, while post-training policy distillation improves transfer and input robustness in the reported evaluations.

title: Learning Dynamics and Generalization in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Policy optimization methods are one of the most widely used classes of Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms. However, theoretical understanding of these methods remains insufficient. Even in the episodic (time-inhomogeneous) tabular setting, the state-of-the-art theoretical result of policy-based method in Shani et al. (2020) is only $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{S^2AH^4K})$ where $S$ is the number of states, $A$ is the number of actions, $H$ is the horizon, and $K$ is the number of episodes, and there is a $\sqrt{SH}$ gap compared with the information theoretic lower bound $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{SAH^3K})$ (Jin et al., 2018). To bridge such a gap, we propose a novel algorithm Reference-based Policy Optimization with Stable at Any Time guarantee (RPO-SAT), which features the property “Stable at Any Time”. We prove that our algorithm achieves $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{SAH^3K} + \sqrt{AH^4K})$ regret. When $S > H$, our algorithm is minimax optimal when ignoring logarithmic factors. To our best knowledge, RPO-SAT is the first computationally efficient, nearly minimax optimal policy-based algorithm for tabular RL.

paragraphs: Policy optimization directly improves an agent’s behavior, but its theoretical guarantees have lagged behind the best achievable learning rates. This paper examines episodic tabular reinforcement learning, where states and actions are explicitly enumerated and behavior can vary within an episode. It introduces Reference-based Policy Optimization with Stable at Any Time guarantee, or RPO-SAT, to narrow that gap.

The authors prove a regret bound of approximately √(SAH³K) + √(AH⁴K), suppressing logarithmic factors. Here S counts states, A counts actions, H is episode length, and K counts episodes. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to optimal behavior. The first term matches the information-theoretic lower-bound scaling stated in the abstract, while the second contributes an additional cost.

When the number of states exceeds the episode length, the algorithm is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. That condition is part of the optimality claim. The authors describe RPO-SAT as, to their knowledge, the first computationally efficient policy-based algorithm that is nearly minimax optimal for tabular reinforcement learning, strengthening the theoretical case for this widely used algorithm family.
summary.tldr: RPO-SAT gives nearly optimal policy-optimization regret in tabular reinforcement learning, achieving minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors when states outnumber the horizon.

title: Nearly Optimal Policy Optimization with Stable at Any Time Guarantee

abstract: Transformer architectures are now central to sequence modeling tasks. At its heart is the attention mechanism, which enables effective modeling of long-term dependencies in a sequence. Recently, transformers have been successfully applied in the computer vision domain, where 2D images are first segmented into patches and then treated as 1D sequences. Such linearization, however, impairs the notion of spatial locality in images, which bears important visual clues. To bridge the gap, we propose ripple attention , a sub-quadratic attention mechanism for vision transformers. Built upon the recent kernel-based efficient attention mechanisms, we design a novel dynamic programming algorithm that weights contributions of different tokens to a query with respect to their relative spatial distances in the 2D space in linear observed time. Extensive experiments and analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of ripple attention on various visual tasks.

Such linearization, however, impairs the notion of spatial locality in images, which bears important visual clues. paragraphs: Vision Transformers often convert an image into a sequence of patches. While this allows sequence-based attention to process images, it weakens the explicit representation of spatial locality: nearby patches carry visual relationships that a one-dimensional ordering does not fully express. Ripple attention is designed to bring two-dimensional spatial distance into efficient attention computation.

The method builds on kernel-based efficient attention and introduces a dynamic programming algorithm. For each query, contributions from other tokens are weighted according to their relative distances in the image plane. This makes spatial arrangement part of the attention mechanism while targeting a cost below the quadratic complexity associated with full pairwise attention.

The authors describe ripple attention as subquadratic and report linear observed runtime for the proposed computation. Experiments and analyses across visual tasks demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both spatial and computational: it gives attention an explicit way to use image locality while retaining efficient processing. The observed linear behavior is an empirical runtime statement, distinct from the broader subquadratic characterization of the mechanism.
summary.tldr: Ripple attention incorporates two-dimensional spatial distance into efficient vision attention, with subquadratic complexity and observed linear runtime.

title: Ripple Attention for Visual Perception with Sub-quadratic Complexity

abstract: We study a variation of vanilla stochastic gradient descent where the optimizer only has access to a Markovian sampling scheme. These schemes encompass applications that range from decentralized optimization with a random walker (token algorithms), to RL and online system identification problems. We focus on obtaining rates of convergence under the least restrictive assumptions possible on the underlying Markov chain and on the functions optimized. We first unveil the theoretical lower bound for methods that sample stochastic gradients along the path of a Markov chain, making appear a dependency in the hitting time of the underlying Markov chain. We then study Markov chain SGD (MC-SGD) under much milder regularity assumptions than prior works. We finally introduce MC-SAG, an alternative to MC-SGD with variance reduction, that only depends on the hitting time of the Markov chain, therefore obtaining a communication-efficient token algorithm.

These schemes encompass applications that range from decentralized optimization with a random walker (token algorithms), to RL and online system identification problems. We focus on obtaining rates of convergence under the least restrictive assumptions possible on the underlying Markov chain and on the functions optimized. We first unveil the theoretical lower bound for methods that sample stochastic gradients along the path of a Markov chain, making appear a dependency in the hitting time of the underlying Markov chain. We then study Markov chain SGD (MC-SGD) under much milder regularity assumptions than prior works. paragraphs: Stochastic gradient methods sometimes obtain samples by following a Markov chain, so successive samples depend on the sampling process's current state. This occurs in settings such as random-walker-based decentralized optimization, reinforcement learning, and online system identification. The paper studies convergence when the optimizer has access only to this kind of sampling.

The authors first establish a theoretical lower bound for methods that collect gradients along a Markov-chain path. The bound reveals a dependence on the chain's hitting time, connecting optimization difficulty to how the sampling process reaches states. They then analyze Markov-chain SGD under much milder regularity assumptions than earlier work.

The paper also introduces MC-SAG, a variance-reduced alternative to MC-SGD. Its dependence on the Markov chain is only through hitting time, leading to a communication-efficient token algorithm. Together, the lower bound and algorithmic results clarify how the sampling process constrains optimization and how variance reduction can address this setting. The work emphasizes obtaining guarantees while imposing fewer restrictions on both the chain and the optimized functions.
summary.tldr: The paper links optimization under Markovian sampling to hitting time and introduces a variance-reduced method for communication-efficient decentralized learning.

title: Stochastic Gradient Descent under Markovian Sampling Schemes

abstract: Training classifiers is difficult with severe class imbalance, but many rare events are the culmination of a sequence with much more common intermediate outcomes. For example, in online marketing a user first sees an ad, then may click on it, and finally may make a purchase; estimating the probability of purchases is difficult because of their rarity. We show both theoretically and through data experiments that the more abundant data in earlier steps may be leveraged to improve estimation of probabilities of rare events. We present PRESTO, a relaxation of the proportional odds model for ordinal regression. Instead of estimating weights for one separating hyperplane that is shifted by separate intercepts for each of the estimated Bayes decision boundaries between adjacent pairs of categorical responses, we estimate separate weights for each of these transitions. We impose an L1 penalty on the differences between weights for the same feature in adjacent weight vectors in order to shrink towards the proportional odds model. We prove that PRESTO consistently estimates the decision boundary weights under a sparsity assumption. Synthetic and real data experiments show that our method can estimate rare probabilities in this setting better than both logistic regression on the rare category, which fails to borrow strength from more abundant categories, and the proportional odds model, which is too inflexible.

paragraphs: Rare outcomes can be difficult to predict because few examples are available. Many occur at the end of a sequence with more common intermediate outcomes, such as seeing an advertisement, clicking it, and purchasing. The paper shows theoretically and experimentally that earlier outcomes can help estimate the probability of the rare final event.

PRESTO relaxes the proportional-odds model used for ordered categories. Instead of sharing one set of feature weights across all category boundaries, it learns separate weights for each transition. An L1 penalty encourages corresponding weights in adjacent transitions to remain similar, allowing information sharing without requiring identical effects everywhere.

The authors prove consistent estimation of the boundary weights under a sparsity assumption. Synthetic and real-data experiments show better rare-probability estimation than logistic regression trained on the rare category and the more restrictive proportional-odds model. The results illustrate the benefit of balancing flexibility with shared structure: common stages contribute information, while each transition can retain its own relationship to the features.
summary.tldr: PRESTO improves rare-event probability estimation by sharing information across ordered outcomes while allowing their feature effects to differ.

title: Predicting Rare Events by Shrinking Towards Proportional Odds

abstract: Existing research on task incremental learning in continual learning has primarily focused on preventing catastrophic forgetting (CF). Although several techniques have achieved learning with no CF, they attain it by letting each task monopolize a sub-network in a shared network, which seriously limits knowledge transfer (KT) and causes over-consumption of the network capacity, i.e., as more tasks are learned, the performance deteriorates. The goal of this paper is threefold: (1) overcoming CF, (2) encouraging KT, and (3) tackling the capacity problem. A novel technique (called SPG) is proposed that soft-masks (partially blocks) parameter updating in training based on the importance of each parameter to old tasks. Each task still uses the full network, i.e., no monopoly of any part of the network by any task, which enables maximum KT and reduction in capacity usage. To our knowledge, this is the first work that soft-masks a model at the parameter-level for continual learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SPG in achieving all three objectives. More notably, it attains significant transfer of knowledge not only among similar tasks (with shared knowledge) but also among dissimilar tasks (with little shared knowledge) while mitigating CF.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a network to learn successive tasks without losing earlier knowledge. Some approaches prevent forgetting by reserving separate parts of the network for each task. The paper argues that this restricts knowledge transfer and consumes capacity, making it harder to maintain performance as the sequence of tasks grows.

The proposed technique, SPG, adjusts how much each parameter can change according to its importance for previous tasks. This soft masking partially blocks updates instead of giving tasks exclusive ownership of subnetworks. Every task continues to use the full network, creating opportunities to reuse learned knowledge while limiting changes to parameters that matter for earlier tasks.

Experiments evaluate the three linked objectives of reducing forgetting, encouraging transfer, and managing network capacity. The authors report effectiveness on all three, including significant knowledge transfer between both similar and dissimilar tasks. Their findings support parameter-level protection as a way to balance retaining old capabilities with learning new ones. The reported outcome is mitigation of catastrophic forgetting, rather than a universal guarantee that forgetting disappears.
summary.tldr: SPG partially restricts updates to important parameters, mitigating forgetting while supporting knowledge transfer and more efficient use of network capacity.

title: Parameter-Level Soft-Masking for Continual Learning

abstract: Inference from large autoregressive models like Transformers is slow - decoding K tokens takes K serial runs of the model. In this work we introduce speculative decoding - an algorithm to sample from autoregressive models faster without any changes to the outputs, by computing several tokens in parallel. At the heart of our approach lie the observations that (1) hard language-modeling tasks often include easier subtasks that can be approximated well by more efficient models, and (2) using speculative execution and a novel sampling method, we can make exact decoding from the large models faster, by running them in parallel on the outputs of the approximation models, potentially generating several tokens concurrently, and without changing the distribution. Our method can accelerate existing off-the-shelf models without retraining or architecture changes. We demonstrate it on T5-XXL and show a 2X-3X acceleration compared to the standard T5X implementation, with identical outputs.

paragraphs: Large autoregressive models ordinarily generate tokens sequentially, requiring another model run for each token. This creates a speed bottleneck even when substantial parallel computing capacity is available. The paper introduces speculative decoding to generate several tokens concurrently while preserving the large model's output distribution.

The approach relies on the observation that some portions of a difficult language-modeling task are easier to approximate than others. More efficient models produce candidate continuations, and the large model processes those candidates in parallel. A sampling procedure makes this speculative computation compatible with exact sampling from the large model, so the approximation can accelerate generation without changing the target distribution.

The method works with existing models and does not require retraining or changes to their architecture. On T5-XXL, the authors report a two- to threefold acceleration over the standard T5X implementation, with identical outputs. This demonstration shows that changing the decoding procedure can yield a substantial speed improvement while retaining the original model's generation behavior.
summary.tldr: Speculative decoding uses efficient approximation models and parallel verification to accelerate generation while preserving the large model's output distribution.

title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding

abstract: The output distribution of a neural network (NN) over the entire input space captures the complete input-output mapping relationship, offering in- sights toward a more comprehensive NN under- standing. Exhaustive enumeration or traditional Monte Carlo methods for the entire input space can exhibit impractical sampling time, especially for high-dimensional inputs. To make such difficult sampling computationally feasible, in this paper, we propose a novel Gradient-based Wang-Landau (GWL) sampler. We first draw the connection between the output distribution of a NN and the density of states (DOS) of a physical system. Then, we renovate the classic sampler for the DOS problem, Wang-Landau algorithm, by re-placing its random proposals with gradient-based Monte Carlo proposals. This way, our GWL sampler investigates the under-explored subsets of the input space much more efficiently. Extensive experiments have verified the accuracy of the output distribution generated by GWL and also showcased several interesting findings - for example, in a binary image classification task, both CNN and ResNet mapped the majority of human unrecognizable images to very negative logit values.

paragraphs: This paper examines the distribution of a neural network’s outputs across its entire input space. This is a finding from that experiment, illustrating how broad input-space sampling can expose behavior beyond familiar examples.
summary.tldr: Gradient-based Wang-Landau sampling estimates neural network output distributions by exploring neglected regions of the input space more efficiently.

title: Gradient-based Wang-Landau Algorithm: A Novel Sampler for Output Distribution of Neural Networks over the Input Space

abstract: Language models (LMs) are increasingly being used in open-ended contexts, where the opinions they reflect in response to subjective queries can have a profound impact, both on user satisfaction, and shaping the views of society at large. We put forth a quantitative framework to investigate the opinions reflected by LMs – by leveraging high-quality public opinion polls. Using this framework, we create OpinionQA, a dataset for evaluating the alignment of LM opinions with those of 60 US demographic groups over topics ranging from abortion to automation. Across topics, we find substantial misalignment between the views reflected by current LMs and those of US demographic groups: on par with the Democrat-Republican divide on climate change. Notably, this misalignment persists even after explicitly steering the LMs towards particular groups. Our analysis not only confirms prior observations about the left-leaning tendencies of some human feedback-tuned LMs, but also surfaces groups whose opinions are poorly reflected by current LMs (e.g., 65+ and widowed individuals).

This paper develops a quantitative way to examine those differences using public opinion polls. Its dataset, OpinionQA, compares model responses with opinions from 60 US demographic groups across subjects ranging from abortion to automation.

The authors find substantial misalignment across topics between the evaluated models and these demographic groups. They contextualize its size by comparing it with the Democrat-Republican divide on climate change. Explicitly steering models toward particular demographic groups does not eliminate the mismatch, showing that such instructions do not necessarily make responses representative of the requested population.

The analysis also confirms left-leaning tendencies in some models tuned with human feedback and identifies poorly represented groups, including people aged 65 and older and widowed individuals. These findings concern the views expressed in model responses. They make demographic representation measurable and show why a model's answers to subjective questions should not automatically be treated as reflecting its users' opinions.
summary.tldr: OpinionQA finds substantial gaps between language-model responses and US demographic opinions, even when models are prompted to represent specific groups.

title: Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?

abstract: In this work, we propose a novel prior learning method for advancing generalization and uncertainty estimation in deep neural networks. The key idea is to exploit scalable and structured posteriors of neural networks as informative priors with generalization guarantees. Our learned priors provide expressive probabilistic representations at large scale, like Bayesian counterparts of pre-trained models on ImageNet, and further produce non-vacuous generalization bounds. We also extend this idea to a continual learning framework, where the favorable properties of our priors are desirable. Major enablers are our technical contributions: (1) the sums-of-Kronecker-product computations, and (2) the derivations and optimizations of tractable objectives that lead to improved generalization bounds. Empirically, we exhaustively show the effectiveness of this method for uncertainty estimation and generalization.

paragraphs: The paper proposes learning informative priors for neural networks to improve generalization and uncertainty estimation. Its core idea is to reuse scalable, structured posterior distributions as priors. This carries forward a probabilistic representation of what a model has learned, providing a Bayesian counterpart to the role played by pretrained models.

The approach supports expressive representations at large scale and produces non-vacuous generalization bounds. These are bounds that remain informative rather than becoming too loose to say anything useful. Two technical components make this possible: computations involving sums of Kronecker products, and tractable training objectives whose derivation and optimization improve the resulting bounds.

The authors also extend the method to continual learning, where information learned previously can inform subsequent learning. Empirical evaluations report benefits for both uncertainty estimation and generalization. The contribution therefore combines a reusable probabilistic representation with mathematical guarantees, rather than treating predictive accuracy and uncertainty as entirely separate goals.
summary.tldr: Structured neural-network posteriors become expressive learned priors, supporting improved uncertainty estimation, generalization, and informative theoretical bounds.

title: Learning Expressive Priors for Generalization and Uncertainty Estimation in Neural Networks

abstract: In this paper, we study risk-sensitive Reinforcement Learning (RL), focusing on the objective of Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) with risk tolerance $\tau$. Starting with multi-arm bandits (MABs), we show the minimax CVaR regret rate is $\Omega(\sqrt{\tau^{-1}AK})$, where $A$ is the number of actions and $K$ is the number of episodes, and that it is achieved by an Upper Confidence Bound algorithm with a novel Bernstein bonus. For online RL in tabular Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), we show a minimax regret lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{\tau^{-1}SAK})$ (with normalized cumulative rewards), where $S$ is the number of states, and we propose a novel bonus-driven Value Iteration procedure. We show that our algorithm achieves the optimal regret of $\widetilde O(\sqrt{\tau^{-1}SAK})$ under a continuity assumption and in general attains a near-optimal regret of $\widetilde O(\tau^{-1}\sqrt{SAK})$, which is minimax-optimal for constant $\tau$. This improves on the best available bounds. By discretizing rewards appropriately, our algorithms are computationally efficient.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, as its objective and tau as the risk-tolerance parameter. It asks how much regret is unavoidable and designs efficient algorithms approaching those limits. The analysis begins with multi-armed bandits before extending to tabular Markov decision processes.

For bandits with A actions and K episodes, the authors establish a minimax regret rate of order sqrt(AK/tau). An upper-confidence-bound algorithm using a new Bernstein bonus achieves that rate. For tabular reinforcement learning with S states and normalized cumulative rewards, they establish a lower bound of order sqrt(SAK/tau) and propose a bonus-based value iteration procedure.

The reinforcement learning procedure matches that dependence up to logarithmic factors under a continuity assumption. In general, its bound is instead of order sqrt(SAK)/tau, again up to logarithmic factors, and is minimax-optimal for constant tau. The distinction makes clear where the stronger risk-tolerance dependence requires additional structure. Appropriate reward discretization also makes the proposed algorithms computationally efficient.
summary.tldr: New CVaR learning algorithms attain optimal bandit regret and near-optimal tabular RL regret, with stronger RL guarantees under a continuity assumption.

title: Near-Minimax-Optimal Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with CVaR

abstract: We study the problem of estimating the distribution of the return of a policy using an offline dataset that is not generated from the policy, i.e., distributional offline policy evaluation (OPE). We propose an algorithm called Fitted Likelihood Estimation (FLE), which conducts a sequence of Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and has the flexibility of integrating any state-of-the-art probabilistic generative models as long as it can be trained via MLE. FLE can be used for both finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted settings where rewards can be multi-dimensional vectors. Our theoretical results show that for both finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted settings, FLE can learn distributions that are close to the ground truth under total variation distance and Wasserstein distance, respectively. Our theoretical results hold under the conditions that the offline data covers the test policy’s traces and that the supervised learning MLE procedures succeed. Experimentally, we demonstrate the performance of FLE with two generative models, Gaussian mixture models and diffusion models. For the multi-dimensional reward setting, FLE with diffusion models is capable of estimating the complicated distribution of the return of a test policy.

paragraphs: Evaluating a policy from existing data becomes harder when that data was collected using a different policy. This paper estimates the full distribution of the target policy’s return, rather than only a single average. It also allows rewards to have several components, making the object of prediction a potentially complicated joint distribution.

The proposed Fitted Likelihood Estimation algorithm repeatedly solves maximum-likelihood learning problems. This design can incorporate probabilistic generative models provided they can be trained through maximum likelihood. The framework covers both finite-horizon problems and infinite-horizon problems with discounted rewards, giving the same broad estimation strategy a role in two different decision-making settings.

The guarantees depend on offline data covering the target policy’s trajectories and on successful maximum-likelihood learning. Under those conditions, the estimated distributions approach the truth in total variation distance for the finite-horizon case and Wasserstein distance for the discounted infinite-horizon case. Experiments use Gaussian mixture and diffusion models. In particular, the diffusion-based version demonstrates the ability to estimate complicated return distributions when rewards are multidimensional.
summary.tldr: Fitted Likelihood Estimation learns policy-return distributions from offline data, with error guarantees conditional on coverage and successful likelihood training.

title: Distributional Offline Policy Evaluation with Predictive Error Guarantees

abstract: We consider an average reward reinforcement learning (RL) problem and work with asymptotic variance as a risk measure to model safety-critical applications. We design a temporal-difference (TD) type algorithm tailored for policy evaluation in this context. Our algorithm is based on linear stochastic approximation of an equivalent formulation of the asymptotic variance in terms of the solution of the Poisson equation. We consider both the tabular and linear function approximation settings, and establish $\tilde {O}(1/k)$ finite time convergence rate, where $k$ is the number of steps of the algorithm. Our work paves the way for developing actor-critic style algorithms for variance-constrained RL. To the best of our knowledge, our result provides the first sequential estimator for asymptotic variance of a Markov chain with provable finite sample guarantees, which is of independent interest.

paragraphs: An average reward describes long-run performance but does not capture all of its variability. This paper uses asymptotic variance as a risk measure for average-reward reinforcement learning, motivated by safety-critical applications. It focuses on policy evaluation: estimating this risk for a policy, providing information that future policy-learning methods could use.

The authors derive a temporal-difference-style algorithm from a formulation of asymptotic variance involving the solution of a Poisson equation. They use linear stochastic approximation to turn that formulation into a sequential estimator. The analysis covers both tabular representations and linear function approximation, so the contribution includes two common ways of representing the quantities being estimated.

The paper establishes a finite-time convergence rate of approximately 1/k, with logarithmic factors suppressed, after k algorithm steps. The authors identify their result, to their knowledge, as the first sequential estimator of Markov-chain asymptotic variance with finite-sample guarantees. It also supplies a foundation for future actor-critic algorithms that constrain variance, rather than itself presenting the completed variance-constrained control method.
summary.tldr: A temporal-difference-style estimator evaluates asymptotic variance in average-reward reinforcement learning with finite-sample convergence guarantees.

title: Policy Evaluation for Variance in Average Reward Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Random probabilities are a key component to many nonparametric methods in Statistics and Machine Learning. To quantify comparisons between different laws of random probabilities several works are starting to use the elegant Wasserstein over Wasserstein distance. In this paper we prove that the infinite dimensionality of the space of probabilities drastically deteriorates its sample complexity, which is slower than any polynomial rate in the sample size. We propose a new distance that preserves many desirable properties of the former while achieving a parametric rate of convergence. In particular, our distance 1) metrizes weak convergence; 2) can be estimated numerically through samples with low complexity; 3) can be bounded analytically from above and below. The main ingredient are integral probability metrics, which lead to the name hierarchical IPM.

paragraphs: Some statistical methods treat a probability distribution itself as a random object. Comparing such objects requires a distance between laws of random probability measures, adding a level beyond comparing ordinary distributions. This paper examines the Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein distance used for that purpose and identifies a substantial obstacle to estimating it from samples.

The authors prove that the infinite-dimensional space of probability measures severely worsens this distance’s sample complexity. Its convergence is slower than any polynomial rate in sample size. Consequently, the appeal of the distance’s mathematical structure comes with a demanding statistical estimation problem in the setting analyzed.

They introduce hierarchical integral probability metrics as an alternative that retains many desirable properties while achieving a parametric convergence rate. The new distance metrizes weak convergence, meaning that convergence under the distance captures that statistical notion of convergence. It also supports low-complexity numerical estimation from samples and analytical upper and lower bounds. Together, these properties make the proposal useful for both estimating comparisons and reasoning about them mathematically.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical integral probability metrics compare random probability measures with substantially better sample convergence than Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein.

title: Hierarchical Integral Probability Metrics: A distance on random probability measures with low sample complexity

abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo methods have become popular in statistics as versatile techniques to sample from complicated probability distributions. In this work, we propose a method to parameterize and train transition kernels of Markov chains to achieve efficient sampling and good mixing. This training procedure minimizes the total variation distance between the stationary distribution of the chain and the empirical distribution of the data. Our approach leverages involutive Metropolis-Hastings kernels constructed from reversible neural networks that ensure detailed balance by construction. We find that reversibility also implies $C_2$-equivariance of the discriminator function which can be used to restrict its function space.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo generates samples from complicated probability distributions by repeatedly moving between states. The rules governing those moves strongly influence how efficiently the chain explores the distribution. This paper proposes learning those transition rules, with the aim of obtaining efficient sampling and good mixing rather than specifying every aspect of the sampler manually.

The training objective minimizes total variation distance between the chain's stationary distribution and the empirical data distribution. The method builds involutive Metropolis-Hastings kernels from reversible neural networks. These constructions ensure detailed balance by design, embedding an important mathematical property of the sampler directly into its architecture.

Reversibility also has consequences for the adversarial training component. The authors show that it implies a C2 symmetry requirement for the discriminator, allowing its possible functions to be restricted accordingly. The contribution therefore connects learned sampling with structural guarantees: reversibility shapes both the transition mechanism and the discriminator used to train it.
summary.tldr: Ai-sampler learns Markov chain transitions using reversible neural networks that enforce detailed balance and constrain adversarial training.

title: Ai-sampler: Adversarial Learning of Markov kernels with involutive maps

abstract: Spectral Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), alternatively known as graph filters, have gained increasing prevalence for heterophily graphs. Optimal graph filters rely on Laplacian eigendecomposition for Fourier transform. In an attempt to avert prohibitive computations, numerous polynomial filters have been proposed. However, polynomials in the majority of these filters are predefined and remain fixed across different graphs, failing to accommodate the varying degrees of heterophily. Addressing this gap, we demystify the intrinsic correlation between the spectral property of desired polynomial bases and the heterophily degrees via thorough theoretical analyses. Subsequently, we develop a novel adaptive heterophily basis wherein the basis vectors mutually form angles reflecting the heterophily degree of the graph. We integrate this heterophily basis with the homophily basis to construct a universal polynomial basis UniBasis, which devises a polynomial filter based graph neural network – UniFilter. It optimizes the convolution and propagation in GNN, thus effectively limiting over-smoothing and alleviating over-squashing. Our extensive experiments, conducted on datasets with a diverse range of heterophily, support the superiority of UniBasis in the universality but also its proficiency in graph explanation.

paragraphs: Spectral graph neural networks use graph filters to control how information moves through a graph. Polynomial filters avoid the expensive eigendecomposition used by optimal spectral filters, but many rely on polynomial bases that stay fixed across graphs. This can be restrictive when graphs differ in heterophily, the extent to which connected nodes have different characteristics or labels.

The paper theoretically analyzes how suitable polynomial bases relate to a graph’s degree of heterophily. It then constructs an adaptive basis whose vectors form angles reflecting that degree. Combining this with a homophily basis produces UniBasis, which supports a polynomial-filter graph neural network called UniFilter. The design makes the filter’s building blocks responsive to graph structure.

The authors report that this approach limits over-smoothing and alleviates over-squashing, two problems affecting information propagation in graph networks. Experiments across datasets with different degrees of heterophily support the basis’s broad applicability and usefulness for graph explanation. The contribution connects a mathematical property of the filter basis to the kinds of neighborhood relationships present in the data.
summary.tldr: UniBasis adapts polynomial graph filters to heterophily, supporting broad graph performance while reducing propagation problems.

title: How Universal Polynomial Bases Enhance Spectral Graph Neural Networks: Heterophily, Over-smoothing, and Over-squashing

abstract: We introduce Stereo Risk, a new deep-learning approach to solve the classical stereo-matching problem in computer vision. As it is well-known that stereo matching boils down to a per-pixel disparity estimation problem, the popular state-of-the-art stereo-matching approaches widely rely on regressing the scene disparity values, yet via discretization of scene disparity values. Such discretization often fails to capture the nuanced, continuous nature of scene depth. Stereo Risk departs from the conventional discretization approach by formulating the scene disparity as an optimal solution to a continuous risk minimization problem, hence the name "stereo risk". We demonstrate that $L^1$ minimization of the proposed continuous risk function enhances stereo-matching performance for deep networks, particularly for disparities with multi-modal probability distributions. Furthermore, to enable the end-to-end network training of the non-differentiable $L^1$ risk optimization, we exploited the implicit function theorem, ensuring a fully differentiable network. A comprehensive analysis demonstrates our method’s theoretical soundness and superior performance over the state-of-the-art methods across various benchmark datasets, including KITTI 2012, KITTI 2015, ETH3D, SceneFlow, and Middlebury 2014.

paragraphs: Stereo matching estimates the displacement, or disparity, of corresponding scene points between two images. This gives a per-pixel estimation problem whose underlying values vary continuously. Many deep approaches nevertheless use discretized disparity values, which can miss finer distinctions in the scene's continuous depth structure.

Stereo Risk defines each estimated disparity as the solution of a continuous risk-minimization problem. The paper shows that minimizing its proposed L1 risk improves stereo-matching performance, especially when the disparity distribution has multiple plausible peaks. This makes the shape of uncertainty over possible disparities central to how the final prediction is chosen.

The L1 optimization introduces a challenge for end-to-end learning because it is non-differentiable. The authors use the implicit function theorem to make the overall network differentiable and trainable. Their analysis supports the formulation theoretically, and benchmark evaluations report superior performance on KITTI 2012, KITTI 2015, ETH3D, SceneFlow, and Middlebury 2014. The work connects continuous disparity estimation, a risk-based decision rule, and a mechanism for learning through that rule.
summary.tldr: Stereo Risk estimates continuous disparities through L1 risk minimization and enables end-to-end training through implicit differentiation.

title: Stereo Risk: A Continuous Modeling Approach to Stereo Matching

abstract: Supervised contrastive representation learning has been shown to be effective in various transfer learning scenarios. However, while asymmetric non-contrastive learning (ANCL) often outperforms its contrastive learning counterpart in self-supervised representation learning, the extension of ANCL to supervised scenarios is less explored. To bridge the gap, we study ANCL for supervised representation learning, coined SupSiam and SupBYOL, leveraging labels in ANCL to achieve better representations. The proposed supervised ANCL framework improves representation learning while avoiding collapse. Our analysis reveals that providing supervision to ANCL reduces intra-class variance, and the contribution of supervision should be adjusted to achieve the best performance. Experiments demonstrate the superiority of supervised ANCL across various datasets and tasks. The code is available at: https://github.com/JH-Oh-23/Sup-ANCL.

paragraphs: This paper examines how class labels can improve asymmetric non-contrastive learning, or ANCL, a family of methods for learning representations of data. The motivation is a gap between learning settings: ANCL often outperforms contrastive approaches in self-supervised learning, but its use with explicit supervision has received less attention.

The authors introduce supervised ANCL methods called SupSiam and SupBYOL. These methods incorporate labels into representation learning. The proposed framework improves the learned representations while avoiding collapse, the failure in which representations lose the distinctions that make them useful. This makes retaining useful differences an important part of the reported result.

Their analysis finds that supervision reduces variation among representations belonging to the same class. In plain language, examples sharing a label become more alike in the learned representation. However, the authors also find that the contribution of supervision should be adjusted to obtain the best performance; the finding does not imply that stronger supervision is always better.

Experiments report advantages for supervised ANCL across multiple datasets and tasks. These findings support incorporating labels into ANCL, with the balance of supervision playing a role in how effectively the resulting representations perform.
summary.tldr: SupSiam and SupBYOL incorporate labels into asymmetric non-contrastive learning, improving representations without collapse while showing that the contribution of supervision should be adjusted.

title: On the Effectiveness of Supervision in Asymmetric Non-Contrastive Learning

abstract: Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is a ubiquitous task in machine learning applications. Given a query vector and $n$ other vectors in $d$ dimensions, the MIPS problem is to find the atom that has the highest inner product with the query vector. Existing MIPS algorithms scale at least as $O(\sqrt{d})$ with respect to $d$, which becomes computationally prohibitive in high-dimensional settings. In this work, we present BanditMIPS, a novel randomized algorithm that provably improves the state-of-the-art complexity from $O(\sqrt{d})$ to $O(1)$ with respect to $d$. We validate the scaling of BanditMIPS and demonstrate that BanditMIPS outperforms prior state-of-the-art MIPS algorithms in sample complexity, wall-clock time, and precision/speedup tradeoff across a variety of experimental settings. Furthermore, we propose a variant of our algorithm, named BanditMIPS-$\alpha$, which improves upon BanditMIPS by employing non-uniform sampling across coordinates. We also demonstrate the usefulness of BanditMIPS in problems for which MIPS is a subroutine, including Matching Pursuit and Fourier analysis. Finally, we demonstrate that BanditMIPS can be used in conjunction with preprocessing techniques to improve its complexity with respect to $n$. All of our experimental results are reproducible via a 1-line script at github.com/ThrunGroup/BanditMIPS.

paragraphs: Maximum Inner Product Search finds the vector with the largest inner product with a query among a collection of candidates. Its computational burden can grow with both the number of vectors and their dimension. This paper targets the dimension dependence, which becomes especially costly when each vector has many coordinates.

The authors introduce BanditMIPS, a randomized algorithm with a proved improvement from O(√d) to O(1) complexity with respect to dimension d. This claim concerns scaling in dimension; the number of candidate vectors remains a separate consideration. A variant, BanditMIPS-α, further improves the method by sampling coordinates non-uniformly.

Experiments validate the reported scaling and show advantages in sample complexity, runtime, and the trade-off between precision and speedup across the evaluated settings. The authors also demonstrate uses in Matching Pursuit and Fourier analysis, where inner-product search is a component of a larger calculation. Finally, they show that preprocessing techniques can be combined with BanditMIPS to improve dependence on the number of candidates, connecting its dimensional savings with a separate avenue for accelerating search.
summary.tldr: BanditMIPS improves the dimension dependence of maximum inner-product search and demonstrates practical speed and sampling benefits.

title: Faster Maximum Inner Product Search in High Dimensions

abstract: Binarized image super-resolution (SR) has attracted much research attention due to its potential to drastically reduce parameters and operations. However, most binary SR works binarize network weights directly, which hinders high-frequency information extraction. Furthermore, as a pixel-wise reconstruction task, binarization often results in heavy representation content distortion. To address these issues, we propose a flexible residual binarization (FRB) method for image SR. We first propose a second-order residual binarization (SRB), to counter the information loss caused by binarization. In addition to the primary weight binarization, we also binarize the reconstruction error, which is added as a residual term in the prediction. Furthermore, to narrow the representation content gap between the binarized and full-precision networks, we propose Distillation-guided Binarization Training (DBT). We uniformly align the contents of different bit widths by constructing a normalized attention form. Finally, we generalize our method by applying our FRB to binarize convolution and Transformer-based SR networks, resulting in two binary baselines: FRBC and FRBT. We conduct extensive experiments and comparisons with recent leading binarization methods. Our proposed baselines, FRBC and FRBT, achieve superior performance both quantitatively and visually. The code and model will be released.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution reconstructs detailed images, making information loss from binary network representations particularly consequential. Directly binarizing weights can weaken the extraction of high-frequency information and distort the content represented inside the model. Flexible Residual Binarization addresses these problems while retaining the computational motivation for binary networks.

Its second-order residual binarization adds a correction to the primary binary weight representation. The method also binarizes the reconstruction error and uses that result as a residual contribution to the prediction. A complementary training method uses distillation to narrow the content gap between binary and full-precision networks, aligning representations of different bit widths through normalized attention.

The authors apply this combination to convolutional and Transformer super-resolution networks, producing FRBC and FRBT. Extensive experiments report stronger quantitative results and better visual outcomes than recent leading binarization methods. Together, the results support addressing both weight approximation error and representation distortion when compressing super-resolution models, rather than expecting the initial binary weight approximation to preserve all necessary image detail.
summary.tldr: FRB improves binary super-resolution networks through residual error correction and distillation that aligns binary and full-precision representations.

title: Flexible Residual Binarization for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: We initiate a systematic study of worst-group risk minimization under $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy (DP). The goal is to privately find a model that approximately minimizes the maximal risk across $p$ sub-populations (groups) with different distributions, where each group distribution is accessed via a sample oracle. We first present a new algorithm that achieves excess worst-group population risk of $\tilde{O}(\frac{p\sqrt{d}}{K\epsilon} + \sqrt{\frac{p}{K}})$, where $K$ is the total number of samples drawn from all groups and $d$ is the problem dimension. Our rate is nearly optimal when each distribution is observed via a fixed-size dataset of size $K/p$. Our result is based on a new stability-based analysis for the generalization error. In particular, we show that $\Delta$-uniform argument stability implies $\tilde{O}(\Delta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}})$ generalization error w.r.t. the worst-group risk, where $n$ is the number of samples drawn from each sample oracle. Next, we propose an algorithmic framework for worst-group population risk minimization using any DP online convex optimization algorithm as a subroutine. Hence, we give another excess risk bound of $\tilde{O}\left( \sqrt{\frac{d^{1/2}}{\epsilon K}} +\sqrt{\frac{p}{K\epsilon^2}} + \sqrt{\frac{p}{K}} \right)$. Assuming the typical setting of $\epsilon=\Theta(1)$, this bound is more favorable than our first bound in a certain range of $p$ as a function of $K$ and $d$. Finally, we study differentially private worst-group empirical risk minimization in the offline setting, where each group distribution is observed by a fixed-size dataset. We present a new algorithm with nearly optimal excess risk of $\tilde{O}(\frac{p\sqrt{d}}{K\epsilon})$.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to train a differentially private model while minimizing its largest risk across several population groups. Each group has its own distribution, accessed through a sampling oracle. The objective makes the worst-performing group central to optimization, while differential privacy constrains how the procedure can use individual data.

The first algorithm has an excess population-risk bound combining a privacy term proportional to p√d/(Kε) and a sampling term proportional to √(p/K), up to logarithmic factors. Here p counts groups, d is dimension, and K is the total sample count. The rate is nearly optimal when each group is represented by a fixed dataset containing K/p samples. A new stability-based generalization analysis supports this result.

The authors also give a framework using private online convex optimization as a subroutine. For constant-order ε, its bound improves on the first in a particular range of group counts relative to sample size and dimension. Finally, they study offline empirical risk and obtain a nearly optimal excess-risk bound. These results distinguish population generalization from optimization on fixed datasets.
summary.tldr: The paper develops private worst-group learning algorithms with risk bounds that track privacy, sample size, dimension, and group count.

title: Differentially Private Worst-group Risk Minimization

abstract: This paper proposes a family of permutation-invariant graph embeddings, generalizing the Skew Spectrum of graphs of Kondor & Borgwardt (2008). Grounded in group theory and harmonic analysis, our method introduces a new class of graph invariants that are isomorphism-invariant and capable of embedding richer graph structures - including attributed graphs, multilayer graphs, and hypergraphs - which the Skew Spectrum could not handle. Our generalization further defines a family of functions that enables a trade-off between computational complexity and expressivity. By applying generalization-preserving heuristics to this family, we improve the Skew Spectrum’s expressivity at the same computational cost. We formally prove the invariance of our generalization, demonstrate its improved expressiveness through experiments, and discuss its efficient computation.

paragraphs: A graph representation should remain unchanged when its nodes are renamed, while still capturing useful structural differences. This paper develops a family of graph embeddings with that invariance property. It generalizes the existing Skew Spectrum using group theory and harmonic analysis to cover a wider range of graph structures.

The extension handles attributed graphs, multilayer graphs, and hypergraphs, which the original Skew Spectrum could not represent in this way. It also defines a family of functions that offers choices between computational cost and expressivity. This makes the representation adaptable to how much computation is available and how much structural information needs to be distinguished.

The authors formally prove invariance and demonstrate improved expressiveness experimentally. They also apply generalization-preserving heuristics to improve expressivity at the same computational cost as the original Skew Spectrum, and discuss efficient computation. The result combines a wider domain of supported structures with a flexible computational tradeoff. Its formal guarantee concerns invariance to graph isomorphism, while the reported experiments provide evidence for the improvement in expressive power.
summary.tldr: A generalized Skew Spectrum provides invariant embeddings for richer graph types and adjustable tradeoffs between expressivity and computation.

title: The Generalized Skew Spectrum of Graphs

abstract: A widespread strategy to obtain a language model that performs well on a target domain is to finetune a pretrained model to perform unsupervised next-token prediction on data from that target domain. Finetuning presents two challenges: (i) if the amount of target data is limited, as in most practical applications, the model will quickly overfit, and (ii) the model will drift away from the original model, forgetting the pretraining data and the generic knowledge that comes with it. Our goal is to derive scaling laws that quantify these two phenomena for various target domains, amounts of available target data, and model scales. We measure the efficiency of injecting pretraining data into the finetuning data mixture to avoid forgetting and mitigate overfitting. A key practical takeaway from our study is that injecting as little as $1%$ of pretraining data in the finetuning data mixture prevents the model from forgetting the pretraining set.

paragraphs: Finetuning a language model on a target domain through next-token prediction can improve specialization, but it introduces two related problems. Limited target data can lead to rapid overfitting, and continued training can move the model away from its pretrained behavior. That drift can cause it to forget pretraining data and associated general knowledge.

The study aims to quantify these effects with scaling laws across target domains, target-data amounts, and model sizes. It also evaluates mixing pretraining data into the finetuning stream. This mixture gives training continued exposure to the original material while the model adapts to the target domain, and the authors measure its effectiveness against forgetting and overfitting.

A key reported finding is that a pretraining-data share as small as 1% prevents forgetting of the pretraining set in the study. This makes the composition of the training mixture a consequential practical choice. The finding specifically concerns retention of the pretraining set; the broader investigation examines how retention and specialization behave as data availability and model scale change.
summary.tldr: The study quantifies finetuning-related forgetting and finds that a 1% pretraining-data mixture can prevent pretraining-set forgetting.

title: Scaling Laws for Forgetting during Finetuning with Pretraining Data Injection

abstract: Bias problems in the estimation of Q-values are a well-known obstacle that slows down convergence of Q-learning and actor-critic methods. One of the reasons of the success of modern RL algorithms is partially a direct or indirect overestimation reduction mechanism. We introduce an easy to implement method built on top of distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithms to deal with the overestimation in a locally adaptive way. Our framework ADDQ is simple to implement, existing DRL implementations can be improved with a few lines of code. We provide theoretical backup and experimental results in tabular, Atari, and MuJoCo environments, comparisons with state-of-the-art methods, and a proof of convergence in the tabular case.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning methods can learn slowly when their estimates of action values are biased. These Q-values represent how rewarding actions are expected to be, so overestimating them can distort learning. The paper focuses on reducing this overestimation, a mechanism the authors identify as contributing to the success of several modern reinforcement learning algorithms.

ADDQ builds on distributional reinforcement learning, which represents a distribution of possible returns. Its central idea is to handle overestimation in a locally adaptive way. This makes the adjustment responsive to local circumstances within learning. The authors present the framework as straightforward to integrate into existing distributional implementations, requiring only a small amount of additional code.

The work combines theoretical support with experiments in tabular environments, Atari, and MuJoCo, including comparisons with leading methods. It also proves convergence in the tabular case. That guarantee has a specific scope: it supports convergence for the tabular setting, while the broader experiments examine how the framework behaves in more complex environments.
summary.tldr: ADDQ adds a locally adaptive overestimation correction to distributional reinforcement learning, with a convergence proof for the tabular setting.

title: ADDQ: Adaptive distributional double Q-learning

abstract: Constrained Reinforcement Learning (CRL) aims to maximize cumulative rewards while satisfying constraints. However, existing CRL algorithms often encounter significant constraint violations during training, limiting their applicability in safety-critical scenarios. In this paper, we identify the underestimation of the cost value function as a key factor contributing to these violations. To address this issue, we propose the Memory-driven Intrinsic Cost Estimation (MICE) method, which introduces intrinsic costs to mitigate underestimation and control bias to promote safer exploration. Inspired by flashbulb memory, where humans vividly recall dangerous experiences to avoid risks, MICE constructs a memory module that stores previously explored unsafe states to identify high-cost regions. The intrinsic cost is formulated as the pseudo-count of the current state visiting these risk regions. Furthermore, we propose an extrinsic-intrinsic cost value function that incorporates intrinsic costs and adopts a bias correction strategy. Using this function, we formulate an optimization objective within the trust region, along with corresponding optimization methods. Theoretically, we provide convergence guarantees for the proposed cost value function and establish the worst-case constraint violation for the MICE update. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MICE significantly reduces constraint violations while preserving policy performance comparable to baselines.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning seeks high rewards while respecting limits on costly or unsafe behavior. Yet an agent can violate those limits during training. This paper identifies underestimating the cost value function as an important contributor: if predicted costs are too low, the learner can treat risky behavior as more acceptable than it really is.

MICE addresses this problem with a memory of previously explored unsafe states. That memory identifies high-cost regions, and a pseudo-count associated with visits to those regions defines an additional intrinsic cost. The method combines this signal with the external cost in a cost value function and applies bias correction. It then uses that function to formulate a trust-region optimization objective and corresponding update methods.

The theoretical analysis provides convergence guarantees for the proposed cost value function and a worst-case constraint-violation result for the update. Experiments show substantially fewer constraint violations while maintaining policy performance comparable to baselines. The contribution is therefore a method for reducing unsafe exploration through better cost estimation, with both theoretical analysis and empirical support.
summary.tldr: MICE remembers unsafe states and corrects cost estimates to reduce training-time constraint violations while preserving comparable policy performance.

title: Controlling Underestimation Bias in Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Safe Exploration

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training with privacy preservation but is vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious clients degrade model performance on targeted inputs. These attacks exploit FL decentralized nature, while existing defenses, based on isolated behaviors and fixed rules, can be bypassed by adaptive attackers. To address these limitations, we propose SPMC, a marginal collaboration defense mechanism that leverages intrinsic consistency across clients to estimate inter-client marginal contributions. This allows the system to dynamically reduce the influence of clients whose behavior deviates from the collaborative norm, thus maintaining robustness even as the number of attackers changes. In addition to overcoming proxy-dependent purification’s weaknesses, we introduce a self-purification process that locally adjusts suspicious gradients. By aligning them with margin-based model updates, we mitigate the effect of local poisoning. Together, these two modules significantly improve the adaptability and resilience of FL systems, both at the client and server levels. Experimental results on a variety of classification benchmarks demonstrate that SPMC achieves strong defense performance against sophisticated backdoor attacks without sacrificing accuracy on benign tasks. The code is posted at: https://github.com/WenddHe0119/SPMC.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train collaboratively, but malicious participants can implant backdoors that affect targeted inputs. Defenses based on isolated client behavior and fixed rules can be bypassed by adaptive attackers. SPMC instead uses consistency across collaborating clients to estimate their marginal contributions and determine how strongly their updates should influence learning.

Its collaboration mechanism dynamically reduces the influence of clients whose behavior departs from the collaborative norm. The authors present this as a way to remain robust when the number of attackers changes. A second, local self-purification mechanism adjusts suspicious gradients by aligning them with margin-based model updates, reducing the effect of poisoning within clients.

Together, the two mechanisms address defense at both server and client levels and tackle weaknesses associated with proxy-dependent purification. Experiments on several classification benchmarks show strong protection against sophisticated backdoor attacks while preserving accuracy on benign tasks. The reported results support combining adaptive contribution assessment with local gradient correction to strengthen federated learning against the evaluated attacks.
summary.tldr: SPMC defends federated learning by reducing anomalous clients’ influence and locally correcting suspicious gradients.

title: SPMC: Self-Purifying Federated Backdoor Defense via Margin Contribution

abstract: Auction plays a crucial role in many modern trading environments, including online advertising and public resource allocation. As the number of competing bidders increases, learning Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (BNE) in auctions faces significant scalability challenges. Existing methods often experience slow convergence in large-scale auctions. For example, in a classic symmetric auction setting, the convergence rate depends on the number of bidders quadratically. To address this issue, we propose the Approximate Best Response Gradient method, a new approach for learning BNE efficiently in auction games. We leverage an analytic solution for gradient estimation to enable efficient gradient computation during optimization. Moreover, we introduce the Best Response Distance objective, which serves as an upper bound of approximation quality to BNE. By optimizing the new objective, our method is proven to achieve a local convergence rate independent of bidder numbers and circumvent the traditional quadratic complexity in the classic symmetric setting. Extensive experiments across various auction formats demonstrate that our approach accelerates convergence and enhances learning efficiency in complex auction settings.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in an auction becomes harder as more bidders compete. The paper highlights slow convergence in existing methods, including a quadratic dependence on bidder count in a classic symmetric auction setting. This creates a scaling problem for learning equilibrium behavior in larger auction games.

The proposed Approximate Best Response Gradient method uses an analytic solution for gradient estimation to make optimization more efficient. It also introduces a Best Response Distance objective that upper-bounds approximation quality relative to equilibrium. This objective provides a quantity to optimize with a stated connection to how well the learned behavior approximates a Bayesian Nash equilibrium.

The authors prove a local convergence rate independent of bidder count and show that their approach avoids the traditional quadratic dependence in the classic symmetric setting. The local qualification matters: the stated result concerns convergence near the relevant solution. Experiments across different auction formats report faster convergence and improved learning efficiency, supporting the method’s usefulness beyond the motivating symmetric example.
summary.tldr: Approximate Best Response Gradient accelerates auction-equilibrium learning, with a proven local convergence rate independent of bidder count.

title: Learning Bayesian Nash Equilibrium in Auction Games via Approximate Best Response

abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) show promise in solving complex mathematical tasks, existing evaluation paradigms rely solely on a coarse measure of overall answer accuracy, which are insufficient for assessing their authentic capabilities. In this paper, we propose CogMath, which comprehensively assesses LLMs’ mathematical abilities through the lens of human cognition. Specifically, inspired by psychological theories, CogMath formalizes human reasoning process into 3 stages: problem comprehension, problem solving, and solution summarization. Within these stages, we investigate perspectives such as numerical calculation, knowledge, and counterfactuals, and design a total of 9 fine-grained evaluation dimensions. In each dimension, we develop an “Inquiry-Judge-Reference” multi-agent system to generate inquiries that assess LLMs’ mastery from this dimension. An LLM is considered to truly master a problem only when excelling in all inquiries from the 9 dimensions. By applying CogMath on three benchmarks, we reveal that the mathematical capabilities of 7 mainstream LLMs are overestimated by 30%-40%. Moreover, we locate their strengths and weaknesses across specific stages/dimensions, offering in-depth insights to further enhance their reasoning abilities.

paragraphs: A correct mathematical answer gives limited information about how thoroughly a language model understands a problem. CogMath evaluates that understanding through a framework inspired by human cognition. It divides reasoning into understanding the problem, solving it, and summarizing the solution, then examines these stages through nine more specific dimensions.

Those dimensions include perspectives involving numerical calculation, knowledge, and counterfactuals. For each dimension, an Inquiry-Judge-Reference multi-agent system generates questions intended to probe the model’s mastery. Under CogMath’s definition, a model masters a problem only when it excels across all the inquiries in all nine dimensions. This makes the evaluation more demanding than checking the final answer alone.

Applied to three benchmarks and seven mainstream language models, CogMath finds that mathematical capabilities are overestimated by 30–40% under the comparison reported in the paper. That result is tied to its broader criterion for mastery. The framework also identifies strengths and weaknesses at particular stages and dimensions, giving a more detailed picture of where reasoning succeeds and where improvement is needed.
summary.tldr: CogMath probes nine dimensions of mathematical understanding and finds that final-answer evaluations overestimate the assessed models’ capabilities.

title: CogMath: Assessing LLMs’ Authentic Mathematical Ability from a Human Cognitive Perspective

abstract: Hierarchical classification offers an approach to incorporate the concept of mistake severity by leveraging a structured, labeled hierarchy. However, decoding in such settings frequently relies on heuristic decision rules, which may not align with task-specific evaluation metrics. In this work, we propose a framework for the optimal decoding of an output probability distribution with respect to a target metric. We derive optimal decision rules for increasingly complex prediction settings, providing universal algorithms when candidates are limited to the set of nodes. In the most general case of predicting a subset of nodes, we focus on rules dedicated to the hierarchical $\mathrm{hF}_{\beta}$ scores, tailored to hierarchical settings. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we conduct extensive empirical evaluations, showcasing the superiority of our proposed optimal strategies, particularly in underdetermined scenarios. These results highlight the potential of our methods to enhance the performance and reliability of hierarchical classifiers in real-world applications.

paragraphs: Hierarchical classification organizes labels into a structure that can distinguish more serious mistakes from less serious ones. Yet the rule that converts predicted probabilities into a final answer is often heuristic. This paper develops a framework for choosing that answer optimally with respect to the metric used to evaluate it, aligning decoding with the task’s objective.

The authors derive decision rules for prediction settings of increasing complexity. When candidate answers are individual hierarchy nodes, they provide universal algorithms. When an answer may contain a subset of nodes, they develop rules specifically for hierarchical hF-beta scores. That distinction matters because the available answer space changes the optimization problem.

Extensive empirical evaluations show benefits from the proposed optimal decoding strategies, especially in underdetermined scenarios. The contribution focuses on what to do with an already produced probability distribution: different evaluation metrics can call for different final decisions. By making the target metric part of decoding, the framework provides a principled alternative to a fixed heuristic rule and offers a route to improved hierarchical-classifier performance.
summary.tldr: Metric-specific optimal decoding improves how hierarchical classifiers convert probability distributions into node or node-subset predictions.

title: To Each Metric Its Decoding: Post-Hoc Optimal Decision Rules of Probabilistic Hierarchical Classifiers

abstract: Multi-view clustering has gained significant attention for integrating multi-view information in multimedia applications. With the growing complexity of graph data, multi-view graph clustering (MVGC) has become increasingly important. Existing methods primarily use Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to encode structural and feature information, but applying GNNs within contrastive learning poses specific challenges, such as integrating graph data with node features and handling both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. To address these challenges, this paper introduces Node-Guided Contrastive Encoding (NGCE), a novel MVGC approach that leverages node features to guide embedding generation. NGCE enhances compatibility with GNN filtering, effectively integrates homophilic and heterophilic information, and strengthens contrastive learning across views. Extensive experiments demonstrate its robust performance on six homophilic and heterophilic multi-view benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Multi-view graph clustering groups nodes using several views of their features and relationships. A central difficulty is combining node information with graph structure when connected nodes may be similar or dissimilar. These two patterns, called homophily and heterophily, create different demands on graph neural networks and on learning representations that agree across views.

The paper introduces Node-Guided Contrastive Encoding, or NGCE. Its key choice is to let node features guide embedding generation. The authors describe this guidance as improving compatibility with graph neural network filtering, integrating information from both homophilic and heterophilic structures, and strengthening the contrastive learning process that connects representations across views.

Experiments on six multi-view benchmark datasets demonstrate robust performance across both graph types. The finding matters because a clustering representation must reconcile what a node looks like with how it connects to others, and those signals need not align in the same way everywhere. NGCE provides a feature-guided approach to that reconciliation, supported by the reported benchmark evaluations.
summary.tldr: NGCE uses node features to guide contrastive graph representations, supporting clustering across views with both similar and dissimilar connected nodes.

title: Multi-View Graph Clustering via Node-Guided Contrastive Encoding

abstract: This paper studies off-policy evaluation (OPE) in reinforcement learning with a focus on behavior policy estimation for importance sampling. Prior work has shown empirically that estimating a history-dependent behavior policy can lead to lower mean squared error (MSE) even when the true behavior policy is Markovian. However, the question of why the use of history should lower MSE remains open. In this paper, we theoretically demystify this paradox by deriving a bias-variance decomposition of the MSE of ordinary importance sampling (IS) estimators, demonstrating that history-dependent behavior policy estimation decreases their asymptotic variances while increasing their finite-sample biases. Additionally, as the estimated behavior policy conditions on a longer history, we show a consistent decrease in variance. We extend these findings to a range of other OPE estimators, including the sequential IS estimator, the doubly robust estimator and the marginalized IS estimator, with the behavior policy estimated either parametrically or non-parametrically.

In this paper, we theoretically demystify this paradox by deriving a bias-variance decomposition of the MSE of ordinary importance sampling (IS) estimators, demonstrating that history-dependent behavior policy estimation decreases their asymptotic variances while increasing their finite-sample biases.
